body.translated_text: <s>Śrī</s> (Auspiciousness).
May <s>Śrī Hari</s> be victorious!
Salutations to the glorious <s>Rāmānuja</s>!

children.translated_text: In the <s>Siddhitraya</s> (Three Proofs), graced by the supreme teacher, the venerable sage <s>Yāmuna</s> —
<s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s> (The Proof of Cognition).

body.translated_text: Accompanied by the commentary named <s>Siddhāñjana</s>.
That <s>Brahman</s> is one only, without a second — [so says] the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> statement.
Does it not deny the existence of anything other than <s>Brahman</s>? // 1 //

children.text: (vyākhyā) īṣṭe viśvasya nityaṃ vyapagatatulanāyogyavastvantaro yo vidye yasyādhigatyai vidurupaniṣado dve parāṃ cāparāṃ ca /
children.translated_text: (Commentary) May the Lord <s>Śrīmān</s> — who eternally rules the universe, who is beyond any object worthy of comparison, who is known [only] through the two <s>Upaniṣads</s>, the higher (<s>parā</s>) and the lower (<s>aparā</s>) [<s>vidyā</s>],

children.text: yo viśvasvāntavāsī prathayati ca dhiyaṃ tasya tasyānurūpāṃ devaḥ śrīmān sa mahyaṃ pradiśatu dayayā dhīvikāsaṃ samantāt // 1 //
children.translated_text: who dwells in the hearts of all the world and manifests understanding appropriate to each and every [being] — may he, out of compassion, grant me the full blossoming of intellect! // 1 //
Having meditated upon <s>Lakṣmaṇayogin</s>, who knows the intent of <s>Yāmuna</s>,
I shall comment upon the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s>, the work of the noble <s>Yāmuna</s>. // 2 //

body.text:
pramāṇaphalarūpāyāḥ saṃvidaḥ prameyatattvavyavasthāpikāyāḥ svarūpādiviśodhyate 'tra saṃvistiddhau /
iyamādimā siddhitraye ślokavārtikacchlokamālikārūpā /
tantravārtikavaccātmeśvarasiddhī /
atra copakramamadhyāvasāneṣu bhūyān granthabhāgo luptaḥ /
upalabhyamānasaṃvitsiddhibhāge ca bahulamadvaitimatanirāso dṛśyate /
advaitino hi

children.translated_text: 'In the beginning, dear one, this was Being alone, one only, without a second' —
from hearing the 'non-duality' (<s>advitīyatva</s>) of the supreme <s>Brahman</s> designated by the word 'Being' (<s>sat</s>) which is the cause [of the universe], and
'<s>Brahman</s> is truth, knowledge, infinite' —

children.text:
ti jñānamātratvaśravaṇācca sajātīyavijātīyasvagatabhedasāmānyaśūnyaṃ brahmaiva cinmātraṃ sat paramārthaḥ, anyatsarvaṃ tatraivāvidyayā parikalpitaṃ mithyābhūtamityāmananti /
tatrādvitīyaśrutestadabhimatārthapratipādakatvāsambhavaṃ varṇayitumādau tanmatamanuvadati
children.translated_text: from hearing [<s>Brahman</s> described as] mere knowledge (<s>jñānamātra</s>), they hold that <s>Brahman</s> alone, as pure consciousness (<s>cinmātra</s>), devoid of the general [distinction into] homogeneous, heterogeneous, and internal difference, is the ultimate reality; and everything else is falsely imagined upon it by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and is illusory. In order to describe the impossibility of the statement of non-duality conveying the meaning intended by them, [the author] first restates their position:
'One only' —
thus. If the word 'tat' (that) is connected to the first half [of the verse] through the eternal relation with the [word] 'yat' (which),
[then] 'which <s>Upaniṣadic</s> statement' — 'that' is the syntactic connection.

children.text: yadvā uttarārdhe tacchadbaḥ prasiddhaparāmarśī na tu yacchabdanirdiṣṭapratinirdeśarūpaḥ /
children.translated_text: Alternatively, in the second half, the word 'tat' (that) is a reference to something well-known, not a correlative reference to what is indicated by the word 'yat'.
In 'that <s>Brahman</s>' (<s>tadbrahma</s>) here, the reading 'sat brahma' (Being is <s>Brahman</s>) is also possible.

The word 'advitīya' (without a second) qualifies the word 'sat' (Being) which denotes <s>Brahman</s>; [and] the intent of the <s>pūrvapakṣins</s> (opponents) is that it means the non-existence of anything other than <s>Brahman</s>. // 1 //

body.translated_text: Here, in the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s>, the essential nature and so forth of cognition (<s>saṃvid</s>) — which is of the nature of a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) and its result (<s>phala</s>), and which establishes the reality of the objects of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>) — is examined. This is the first [treatise] in the <s>Siddhitraya</s>, in the form of verse-commentary like the <s>Ślokavārtika</s> and <s>Ślokamālikā</s>. And the <s>Ātmasiddhi</s> and <s>Īśvarasiddhi</s> are like the <s>Tantravārtika</s>. Moreover, in the beginning, middle, and end, a large portion of the text is lost. And in the available portion of the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s>, abundant refutation of the <s>Advaitin</s> position is seen. For the <s>Advaitins</s>,
Here we ask: in the statement 'advitīya' (without a second), what compound is intended?
Is it a <s>tatpuruṣa</s> compound or a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound? Let it be stated. // 2 //

children.translated_text: 'Here' —
thus.
'In the statement of advitīya' — in the word 'advitīya.'
Alternatively, 'or is it a <s>bahuvrīhi</s>?' is the syntactic connection. // 2 //

body.translated_text: To refute this [Advaitin interpretation], the <s>siddhāntin</s> (proponent of the established view) proposes alternative analyses of the compound 'advitīya' —
In the former [i.e., <s>tatpuruṣa</s>], the meaning of the latter member is principally intended.
In that case, that <s>Brahman</s> [would be described as] other than the second, or similar [to the second]. // 3 //
Or it would be opposed to the second. In all three [cases], the other [entity] is not negated.

body.text: anyatve sadṛśatve vā dvitīyaṃ sidhyati dhruvam // 4 //
body.translated_text: Whether as other or as similar, the second is certainly established. // 4 //

body.text: advitīyapadasya tatpuruṣavṛttatve na dvitīyasya bādha ityāha

children.translated_text: 'In the former' —

children.text:
ityādinā ślokacatuṣṭayena /
tatpuruṣa iti prathamakalpe tāvaduttarapadārthaḥ prādhānyena vivakṣyate, uttarapadārthapradhānatvāttatpuruṣasyetyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so on, with four verses. In the first alternative — that it is a <s>tatpuruṣa</s> compound — the meaning of the latter member is principally intended, because a <s>tatpuruṣa</s> has the meaning of the latter member as primary — this is the meaning. [The word consists of:] 'na dvitīyam' = 'advitīyam.'
'In that case' —

children.text:
ti /
na dvitīyamadvitīyam /
nañtatpuruṣe cāropitatvasya pūrvapadārthatvaṃ tasya cottarapadārthaviśeṣaṇatvamiṣyate śābdikaiḥ /
āropaśca sadṛśādau /
tatphalitakathanaṃ tadanyādyarthe nañ iti /
children.translated_text: thus. 'Not second' = 'advitīya.' In a <s>nañ-tatpuruṣa</s> compound, grammarians accept that the superimposed [meaning] is the meaning of the prior member, and that [the prior member meaning] qualifies the meaning of the latter member. And superimposition is upon what is similar, etc. The statement of the resulting [meaning] is: 'the <s>nañ</s> is used in the sense of other, similar, etc.'
'The <s>nañ</s> combined [with a noun] is used in the sense of other, similar, or co-referential — for such is the way of meaning' —

children.text:
riti ca śābdikānāṃ paribhāṣā /
tathā cādvitīyapadenāropitadvitīyatvavadbrahmeti bodhe tatra dvitīyānyatvasya dvitīyasadṛśatvasya dvitīyaviruddhatvasya vā pratītiḥ phalati /
arthatraye 'pi brahmabhinnasya dvitīyapadārthasya na bādhaḥ /
dvitīyapratiyogikasya bhedasya sādṛśyasya vā pratibodhane pratiyogitayā dvitīyasiddherniṣpratyūhatvāditi bhāvaḥ // 3 //4 //
children.translated_text: so is the maxim of the grammarians. Accordingly, when the word 'advitīya' yields the understanding '<s>Brahman</s> possessing superimposed secondness,' then the cognition that arises is [one of]: otherness from the second, similarity to the second, or opposition to the second. In all three senses, there is no negation of the meaning of the word 'second,' which is different from <s>Brahman</s>. Because when the difference or similarity that has the second as counter-correlate is cognized, the second is established through its status as counter-correlate — and this [establishment] is unimpeded. This is the purport. // 3 // 4 //

body.translated_text: If the word 'advitīya' has a <s>tatpuruṣa</s> construction, the second is not negated — [the author] states [this] thus:

body.text: viruddhatve dvitīyena tṛtīyaṃ prathamaṃ tu vā /
body.translated_text: If [<s>Brahman</s> is described as] opposed to the second, the second [would make <s>Brahman</s>] third or first —
<s>Brahman</s> [so] arrives [at being first or third], because it is opposed to the second. // 5 //

body.text: nanvevamapi dvitīyaviruddhatve brahmaṇo bodhite kathaṃ na dvitīyasya bādha ityatrāha

children.translated_text: 'If [there is] opposition' —
thus.
The purport is this: 'secondness' here is of the nature of being that which completes the number two.
'Opposition to the second' means possessing a quality opposed to secondness.

children.text: sa ca dharmaḥ prathamatvaṃ niyamataḥ tṛtīyatvādi vā /
children.translated_text: And that quality is necessarily firstness, or thirdness, etc.
By this much alone, no negation of any second [entity occurs]. // 5 //

body.translated_text: 'But even so, if \'opposed to second\' is understood of <s>Brahman</s>, how is the second not negated?' — to this [the author] responds:
Therefore, all classes of entities — the first, third, and so on —
having been touched by the second in that way, remain undisturbed, un-negated. // 6 //

children.translated_text: 'Therefore' —

children.text:
iti /
dvitīyena - dvitvasaṅkhyāpūrakeṇa, tathā spṛṣṭvā - virodhasaṃbandhena sambadhya, svasthāḥ - svasvapramāṇādhīnasiddhikāḥ santaḥ, advitīyoktyābādhitāḥ prathamatṛtīyādyartharāśayo vartanta evetyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. 'By the second' means by that which completes the number two. 'Having been thus touched' means having been connected by the relation of opposition. 'Undisturbed' means remaining with their own existence dependent on their own means of valid knowledge. The meaning is: the classes of entities [designated as] first, third, etc. simply continue to exist, un-negated by the statement 'advitīya.'
The reading 'spṛṣṭā' [instead of 'spṛṣṭvā'] is also possible. // 6 //

body.translated_text: Accordingly [the author] says:
'But surely the <s>nañ</s> negates absolutely everything other than <s>Brahman</s>,
because the term 'second' is merely an indicator (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) of everything [other than <s>Brahman</s>].' // 7 //

children.translated_text: 'But surely the <s>nañ</s>' —

children.text:
ñiti /
ayamāśayaḥ-dvitīyapadaṃ na mukhyārthakam /
kintu bhedaprapañcamātralakṣakam /
children.translated_text: thus. The purport is: the word 'dvitīya' (second) is not used in its primary sense, but is merely an indicator of the entirety of differentiated plurality.
And the particle <s>nañ</s> denotes absolute non-existence (<s>atyantābhāva</s>).
'The non-existence of the second' = 'advitīya.'
'In the absence of [the primary] meaning, [there is] an <s>avyayībhāva</s> [compound].'
And thus, the negation of differentiated plurality is established by the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> statement 'advitīya' — this is [the opponent's contention]. // 7 //

body.translated_text: Here the <s>pūrvapakṣin</s> (opponent) objects:
'Not so. [This is] not a negation, for from this [word 'advitīya'], what is understood [of <s>Brahman</s>] is [merely its] difference from the second,

body.text: tato 'nyattadviruddhaṃ vā sadṛśaṃ vātra vakti saḥ // 8 //
body.translated_text: or what is other than that, opposed to that, or similar to that — this is what it says.' // 8 //

children.translated_text: 'Not so' —

children.text:
iti /
hirhetau /
yato 'smādadvitīyapadādbrahmapadasamānādhikaraṇāt dvitīyato bhinnatvādireva bodhyate brahmaṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. 'Hi' means 'because.' Since from this word 'advitīya,' which is co-referential (<s>samānādhikaraṇa</s>) with the word '<s>Brahma</s>,' only otherness from the second and such [meanings] are understood of <s>Brahman</s>,
and not merely the negation of plurality —
therefore the <s>avyayībhāva</s> [analysis] is not appropriate here. This is the purport.
Though this [<s>avyayībhāva</s> analysis] was not [explicitly] proposed [by the opponent], it is refuted here incidentally.
'Saḥ' — [i.e.,] the word 'advitīya.' // 8 //

body.translated_text: [The siddhāntin] refutes [the objection]:
'If what is intended is: \'That is <s>Brahman</s> which has no second whatsoever,\''
then the defining statements [beginning with] 'truth' and so on would become non-defining (<s>apalakṣaṇa</s>).' // 9 //

body.text:
anupapannaśca brahmabhinnasya sarvasya niṣedhaḥ /
tathā sati brahmalakṣaṇavākyānāmasaṅgatiprasaṅgādityāha

children.translated_text: 'The second' —
thus.

children.text: yatsaṃbandhino 'nyasya-yato bhinnasya sarvasyābhāvaḥ, tadbrahmetyarthakathane lakṣyavṛttyasādhāraṇadharmarūpasya lakṣaṇasyāpyasattvātsatyajñānādilakṣaṇavākyamapalakṣaṇaṃbhavediti bhāvaḥ // 9 //
children.translated_text: If the meaning expressed is 'That is <s>Brahman</s> in relation to which everything other [than it] is non-existent,' then, since the defining characteristic — which is of the nature of an uncommon property applying to the defined object — would also be non-existent, the defining statements such as 'truth, knowledge, etc.' would become non-defining (<s>apalakṣaṇa</s>). This is the purport. // 9 //

body.translated_text: Moreover, the negation of everything other than <s>Brahman</s> is untenable — because, in that case, the absurd consequence would follow that the statements defining <s>Brahman</s> [with attributes like 'truth, knowledge, infinite'] would become incoherent. [The author] states:
'In 'advitīya' — whose scope is merely the non-existence of the meaning of 'second' —
because the meaning of <s>nañ</s> resides in itself, there would be no syntactic connection with the word '<s>Brahman</s>.'' // 10 //

children.translated_text: 'In advitīya' —
thus. 'In advitīya' — in the word 'advitīya.' 'Because it resides in itself' — because it has its own meaning as primary. That is to say, because it does not qualify the meaning of another word.
It cannot have a qualifying syntactic connection with the word 'sat' which denotes <s>Brahman</s>.
For this [word 'advitīya'] should be co-referential with and a qualifier of that ['sat'].
That undesired consequence cannot be avoided.
And if that is so, the absurd consequence of a split sentence [follows]. This is the purport. // 10 //

body.translated_text: [The author] also states the non-connection of the <s>avyayībhāva</s> [compound] with the word 'sat' [= <s>Brahman</s>]:
'The absence of a second is not, in that case, a qualifier of <s>Brahman</s>;

body.text: viśeṣaṇe vā tadbrahma tṛtīyaṃ prathamaṃ tu vā // 11 //
body.translated_text: or if [it were] a qualifier, that <s>Brahman</s> [would become] third or first.' // 11 //

body.text:
nanu dvitīyābhāvo brahmasvarūpameva /
tadbrahmapadasāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ ghaṭata iti cettatrāha

children.translated_text: 'The second' —

children.text:
ti /
dvitīyābhāvo 'bhedena brahmaṇo na viśeṣaṇaṃ bhavitumarhati /
abhāvasya tucchatvādbrahmaṇaḥ satyatvāt satyatucchayoraikyāyogāditi pūrvārdhasyārthaḥ /
brahmaviśeṣaṇatve 'pi vadāmaḥ dvitīyaṃ pratīyogi prathamam /
tadabhāvatvaṃ dvitīyam /
tṛtīyaṃ ca viśeṣyaṃ brahma /
children.translated_text: thus. The absence of the second cannot be a qualifier of <s>Brahman</s> in the manner of non-difference [i.e., identity]. Because absence is vacuous (<s>tuccha</s>) while <s>Brahman</s> is real, and the identity of the real and the vacuous is impossible — this is the meaning of the first half. Even if [the absence] were a qualifier of <s>Brahman</s>, we say: the second is the first counter-correlate; its absence-ness is the second [thing]; and the third is <s>Brahman</s>, the qualificand.
Or, <s>Brahman</s> is the first;
the counter-correlate 'second' is the second [thing];

children.text: tṛtīyaṃ tadabhāvatvaviśeṣaṇamiti prathamatvaṃ tṛtīyatvaṃ vā brahmaṇo 'varjanīyamityuttarārdhārthaḥ /
children.translated_text: the qualifier 'absence-of-that' is the third [thing]. Thus firstness or thirdness of <s>Brahman</s> is unavoidable — this is the meaning of the second half.
Thus the untenability of the <s>avyayībhāva</s> alternative has also been stated. // 11 //

body.translated_text: 'But surely the absence of a second is the very nature (<s>svarūpa</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>; therefore its co-referentiality with the word '<s>Brahman</s>' is possible' — if so, to that [the author] says:
'All that was said before applies equally when the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> [analysis] is adopted.',

body.text: brahmaṇaḥ prathamā ye ca tṛtīyādyā jagatrtraye // 12 //
body.translated_text: 'Those that are first with respect to <s>Brahman</s>, and the third and other [entities] in the three worlds — // 12 //
because of being non-second with respect to <s>Brahman</s>, they remain undisturbed, un-negated.

body.text: kiñca tatra bahuvrīhau samāse saṃśrite sati // 13 //
body.translated_text: Moreover, when a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound is resorted to — // 13 //
the compound-meaning, [namely] the <s>nañ</s>-meaning [= absence], cannot have syntactic connection with another word-meaning.
If there were connection with another meaning, [only then] the genitive 'yasya' (of which) would be appropriate.' // 14 //

children.translated_text: 'All that was said' —

children.text:
iti /
bahuvrīhivṛtte 'pyadvitīyapadetatpuruṣa iva prathamatṛtīyādisarvasadbhāvo 'nivāryaḥ prasakta evetyarthaḥ /
tadevopapādayatyardhābhyāṃ
children.translated_text: thus. Even in the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> construction, the existence of the first, third, and all [other entities] — just as in the <s>tatpuruṣa</s> — is irresistible and simply follows. This is the meaning. [The author] establishes this very [point] with [the next] half-verses —
'Of <s>Brahman</s>' —
and
'<s>Brahman</s>' —

children.text:
ti ca /
nāsti dvitīyaṃ yasya tadbrahmetyatra pakṣe vigrahaḥ /
brahmaniṣṭhadvitvasaṅkhyāpūrakaṃ nāstītyarthaḥ /
tathā ca brahmaṇa eva dvitīyatvaṃ labhyeta /
tataśca brahmāpekṣayā prathamasya tṛtīyādeśca na bādho 'dvitīyaśrutyetyarthaḥ /
ādyasaṅkhyāpūrakatvaṃ prathamatvam , tritvādisaṅkhyāpūrakatvaṃ ca tṛtīyatvādīti bodhyam /
brahma pratyadvitīyatvāt-brahmāpekṣayā dvitīyatvābhāvāt /
tacca brahmāpekṣayā prathamatvāttṛtīyāditvādvā /
svasthā ityādi pūrvapadvyākhyeyam /
nanu bahuvrīhighaṭakasya dvitīyapadasya dvitvasaṅkhyāpūrakārthatvaṃ, dvitve ca yacchabdārthasya brahmaṇo niṣṭhatvasaṃbandhonānvayo nopeyate; yena prathamatṛtīyādiprasaktiḥ /
kintu dvitīyapadaṃ bhinnaparam /
bhede ca brahmapratiyogikatvasyānvayaḥ /
yato brahmaṇo bhinnaṃ nāsti tadbrahmādvitīyamiti dvitīyabādho 'dvitīyaśrutyā labhyata evetyatrāha
children.translated_text: thus. In the present alternative, the analysis is: 'That is <s>Brahman</s> which has no second.' The meaning is: that which completes the number two with respect to <s>Brahman</s> does not exist. And accordingly, secondness would pertain only to <s>Brahman</s> [itself]. Therefore, by the statement 'advitīya,' there is no negation of the first, third, etc. relative to <s>Brahman</s>. This is the meaning. One should understand that firstness is being that which completes the number one, and thirdness etc. is being that which completes the number three etc. 'Because of being non-second with respect to <s>Brahman</s>' — because of the absence of secondness relative to <s>Brahman</s>. And that [absence] is due to firstness relative to <s>Brahman</s> or to thirdness etc. 'Undisturbed' etc. should be explained as before. But [the opponent says:] of the word 'dvitīya' which is a component of the <s>bahuvrīhi</s>, the meaning is 'that which completes the number two'; and in the number two, we do not accept the connection of residence-relation with <s>Brahman</s> as the referent of 'yat' (which) — by which there would follow [the consequence of] first, third, etc. Rather, the word 'dvitīya' means 'other' (<s>bhinna</s>). And in the case of 'other,' the syntactic connection is of counter-correlateness to <s>Brahman</s>. Thus, '<s>Brahman</s> has nothing other than it — that <s>Brahman</s> is advitīya' — so the negation of the second is indeed obtained from the statement 'advitīya.' To this [the author] responds:
'Moreover' —

children.text:
ti /
anyapadārthapradhāno hi bahuvrīhiḥ /
tathā ca bahuvrīhivṛttapadopasthāpyadvitīyābhāvasyānyapadārthabrahmaviśeṣaṇatvaṃ vaktavyam /
tanna ghaṭate /
brahmabhinnasarvaśūnyavāde dvitīyābhāvasyāpi śūnyatayā brahmapadārthaviśeṣaṇatvāyogādityarthaḥ /
vṛttyarthasya bahuvrīhyarthasya, nañarthasya dvitīyābhāvasya /
kuto na padārthāntarānvayāsambhavaḥ ? tatrāha
children.translated_text: thus. For a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound has the meaning of another word-referent as primary. And accordingly, the absence of the second, which is presented by the <s>bahuvrīhi</s>-derived word, must be stated to be a qualifier of <s>Brahman</s>, which is the meaning of another word. That does not work. Because, in the doctrine that everything other than <s>Brahman</s> is void, the absence of the second too would be void, and so it cannot be a qualifier of the meaning of the word '<s>Brahman</s>.' This is the meaning. 'The compound-meaning' — the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> meaning. 'The <s>nañ</s>-meaning' — the absence of the second. Why is there no possibility of connection with another word-meaning? To that [the author] says:
'If there were' —

children.text:
ti /
yasyeti ṣaṣṭhī prakṛtyarthānviter'thāntarasaṃbandhe prāmāṇike sati saṅgacchate /
nirviśeṣe ca brahmaṇi prakṛtyarthe padārthāntarasaṃbandhasyāsatyatvāt ṣaṣṭhībahuvrīhiśca prakṛte na ghaṭata ityarthaḥ // 12 //13 //14 //
children.translated_text: thus. The genitive ('yasya' — of which) is appropriate when there is a genuine connection of the stem-meaning with another meaning. But since, in a qualifier-less (<s>nirviśeṣa</s>) <s>Brahman</s>, the connection of the stem-meaning with another word-meaning is unreal, the genitive <s>bahuvrīhi</s> does not work in this context. This is the meaning. // 12 // 13 // 14 //

body.translated_text: Now [the author] states the objection against the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> alternative:
'The non-existence of a second entity is neither <s>Brahman</s> nor a qualifier [of <s>Brahman</s>].',
'Because of being non-existent, for what is non-existent cannot be <s>Brahman</s>, nor can it be a qualifier.' // 15 //

body.text: rāhoḥ śira ityādāvabhede 'pi ṣaṣṭhyā dṛṣṭeryadabhinno dvitīyābhāvastadadvitīyaṃ brahmeti vivakṣāṃ pratikṣepati,

children.translated_text: In the second [verse],
thus.

children.text: asataḥ satpadārthābhedastadviśeṣaṇatvamapi na yujyate iti bhāvaḥ // 15 //
children.translated_text: Since a non-existent [thing] cannot be non-different from a real entity (<s>satpadārtha</s>), its being a qualifier of that [real entity] is also not logically tenable—this is the purport. // 15 //

body.translated_text: In [the expression] '<s>Rāhu</s>'s head' and the like, even though there is non-difference [between <s>Rāhu</s> and his head, the genitive is used], — lest this [example] suggest that the absence of the second, being non-different [from <s>Brahman</s>], could serve [as qualifier of <s>Brahman</s>] in 'that <s>Brahman</s> which is advitīya,' [the author] refutes [this] —
Therefore, the reality of the manifold world is not contradicted by the non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) scriptures;
it is established by the force of its own valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), and is also approved by scripture. // 16 //

children.translated_text: 'Therefore'
—thus.

children.text: nirdeṣapratyakṣādipramāṇasiddhaḥ śrutyāpi paramārthatvenānuvarṇito bhedaprapañcasadbhāvo nādvitīyaśrutibādhyaḥ, upapāditaprakāreṇādvitīyaśruteḥ brahmabhinnanāstitāpratipādanāsāmarthyādityarthaḥ // 16 //
children.translated_text: The reality of the differentiated manifold world, established by the indicated valid means of knowledge such as perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and the rest, and also commended by scripture as being ultimately real, is not contradicted by the 'non-duality' scripture, because, as has been demonstrated, the 'non-duality' scripture does not have the capacity to establish the non-existence of anything different from <s>Brahman</s>—this is the meaning. // 16 //

body.translated_text: He concludes the examination showing the untenable nature of the meaning of the 'non-duality' scripture as understood by the opponent:

children.translated_text: (Thus concludes the examination of the faults in the opponent's understanding of the meaning of the 'non-duality' scripture.)
Therefore, the meaning of the scripture 'Brahman is without a second' (<s>advitīya</s>) is stated [as follows]:

body.translated_text: A second worthy of being counted alongside [<s>Brahman</s>] did not exist, does not exist, and will not exist. // 17 //
Whether equal to or greater than It, one who could be counted as a second—
since this entire universe is but a fraction of Its sovereign splendor (<s>vibhavavyūha</s>), // 18 //
how could it attain the status of being designated by the word 'second'?
Just as the <s>Cola</s> king, the emperor, is 'without a second' on this earth today, // 19 //
such a statement is directed at excluding a king equal to him,
but does not negate his servants, sons, wives, and so forth. // 20 //
Likewise, the crores of <s>Brahmāṇḍas</s> (cosmic eggs) containing gods, demons, humans, and <s>Brahmā</s>—
for the Lord of all, who is untouched by afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), <s>karma</s>, and their results, // 21 //
the treasury of the sixfold divine attributes beginning with knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), whose splendor is inconceivable—
those [crores of Brahmāṇḍas] are [but] drops and spray from the ocean of the glory of <s>Viṣṇu</s>'s sovereign manifestation (<s>vibhūti</s>). // 22 //

children.translated_text: 'Therefore'
—thus. Since the meaning understood by the opponent is untenable, a different, well-fitting meaning is being presented by us—this is the purport.
'It is stated'
—this declaration is for the purpose of showing that the meaning being stated is astonishing as if unprecedented, and for the purpose of drawing attention. He states that very meaning:
'In the second [place]'

children.text:
ti /
prathamato brahmaṇo gaṇane kṛte tena saha gaṇanārhe dvitīyaḥ samo vādhiko vā padārthaḥ kālatraye 'pi nāstītyarthaḥ /
nanu vividhavicitrānantacidacitprapañce kathaṃ kasyacidapi brahmasamasyābhāvaḥ ? tatrāha
children.translated_text: —thus. When counting is done beginning with <s>Brahman</s>, no entity—whether equal to or greater than It—worthy of being counted alongside It as a second, exists in any of the three periods of time—this is the meaning. But in the manifold, variegated, infinite expanse of sentient and insentient [entities], how can there be an absence of anything equal to <s>Brahman</s>? In response he says:
'Since'

children.text:
iti /
asya paramātmano 'nantamahāvibhūtervibhūtyekadeśāṃśamātratvāccaturdaśabhuvanātmakabrahmāṇḍakoṭerapi tadantargatasyodumbaramaśakavatparicchinnasvarūpasvabhāvāderbhavabrahmāderapi na tena sāmyagandhaprasaṅga iti dvitīyavāgāspa datāṃ-dvitīyapadavācyatāṃ, brahmaṇā saha gaṇanāyogyatvam , kathaṃ tat-jagat pratipadyeta-prāpnuyādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: —thus. Because even crores of cosmic eggs (<s>brahmāṇḍas</s>) constituting fourteen worlds are but a fraction, a mere portion, of one section of the infinite, great sovereign manifestation (<s>vibhūti</s>) of this Supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>)—and because <s>Brahmā</s> and others contained within it are of a circumscribed nature and essence like a fly on a fig fruit—there is not even a hint of equality with Him; therefore, how could the universe attain the status of being designated by the word 'second' (<s>dvitīyavāgāspadatā</s>)—i.e., eligibility to be counted alongside <s>Brahman</s>? This is the meaning.
In our doctrine, it is intended that both usages (<s>vṛtti</s>) of the word 'advitīya' (without a second) are applicable.

children.text: tathā cānugṛhītaṃ śatadūṣaṇyāṃ śrīmadvedāntadeśikacaraṇaiḥasmatpakṣe tu vṛttidvayamapi samyak /
children.translated_text: And this has been favorably cited in the <s>Śatadūṣaṇī</s> by the revered feet of <s>Śrīmad Vedāntadeśika</s>: 'In our school, both usages are fully appropriate.
By the statement of the exclusion of a second, the foremost position [of <s>Brahman</s>] in enumeration is established.
By the statement of the absence of a second, the negation of [any entity] equal to It [is established].'

body.translated_text: What then is the meaning of the 'non-duality' scripture? In response he says:

body.text:
iti /
etadvyākurmahe-atiśayitavastugaṇanāprastāve brahmaṇa eva prathamaparigaṇanaṃ nyāyyam /
tasyaiva mukhyātiśayavattvāt /
mukhyasyaiva prathamaparigaṇanasya loke śāstre ca dṛṣṭeḥ /
kavikulagaṇanāprasaṅge kālidāsasyaiva hi prāthamyena gaṇanaṃ kavilokaprasiddham /
yathocyatepurākavīnāṃ gaṇanāprasaṅge kaniṣṭhikādhiṣṭhitakālidāsā iti /
śāstrakṛto jaiminerācāryasyāpi saṃmataṃ mukhyasya prathamaparigaṇanam /
tathā hi sūtrayāmāsa

children.translated_text: 'The primary [entity is to be enumerated first], due to prior injunction, as in worldly [practice]'

children.text:
diti /
evaṃ nañtatpuruṣe brahmaṇa evāgragaṇyatā sthitā /
tataḥ sarvādhitakatvasiddhiḥ /
tataścādhikaniṣedhaḥ phalati /
samasyaiva dvitīyagaṇanāyogyatvamityāśayamūlakaṃ capurā kavīnāmitiślokasyottarārdhaṃ paripaṭhyate adyāpi tattulyakaverabhāvādanāmikā sār'thavatī babhūvaiti /
tathā ca bahuvrīhivṛttyā samaniṣedhaḥ phalati brahmaṇa iti /
muktānāmapi bhogamātrasāmyamiti na brahmaṇā saha gaṇanaṃ mukhyaparigaṇanaprastāve yuktam /
tanmukhyaṃ vastu vastuto brahmaikameveti advitīyatvaṃ tasya pratitiṣṭhatīti ca bodhyam /
evamadvitīyaśruteḥ brahmaṇaḥ samābhyadhikarāhityapratipādanaparatvaṃ vyavasthāpitam /
children.translated_text: —thus. In this way, in the negative compound (<s>nañ-tatpuruṣa</s>), the foremost position of <s>Brahman</s> alone in enumeration is established. From that, the establishment of Its being superior to all follows. And from that, the negation of a superior [entity] bears fruit. The intention underlying 'among ancient poets' is that the second half of that very verse is also recited: 'Since even today there is no poet equal to him, the ring finger has become meaningful.' And thus, through the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound usage, the negation of an equal [to <s>Brahman</s>] also bears fruit. Even for liberated souls, there is merely equality of enjoyment—therefore, counting them alongside <s>Brahman</s> in the context of enumerating the primary [entity] is not appropriate. That primary entity is in reality <s>Brahman</s> alone—thus Its being 'without a second' is established. And this should be understood. Thus, the purport of the 'non-duality' scripture as establishing that <s>Brahman</s> has no equal or superior has been determined.
'There is none seen equal to It or greater than It'
—in accordance with this other <s>śruti</s> [passage],
'There is none equal to You, how then a greater? O You of incomparable power, even in the three worlds'

children.text:
ityupabṛṃhaṇānusārāccaidamarthyameva tasya nyāyyamiti hārdam /
athādvitīyapadasya samāntaraniṣedhaparatve laukikaprayogaṃ ca nidarśayati
children.translated_text: —in accordance with this corroborating [<s>smṛti</s>] text, this alone is the fitting essential meaning [of the 'non-duality' scripture]. Now he presents a worldly usage as an illustration for the purport of the word 'advitīya' (without a second) as negating an equal:
'Just as'

children.text:
ti /
colanṛpasyāsthānapaṇḍitaṃ vijityavādāhaverājāsanaṃ rājyārdhaṃ ca tatsamarpitamadhigatavanta ime paramācāryāḥ pūrvāśrame /
tatprasaṅgasmārakaścāyaṃ colanṛpaprastāvo 'tra /
yathā rājño 'dvitīyatvavarṇanaṃ rājavibhūtyāderniṣedhakaṃ na, kintu tatsamanṛpāntaraniṣedhakameva, evaṃ brahmaṇo 'dvitīyatvaśrutirna tadvibhūterniṣedhiketyāha
children.translated_text: —thus. These supreme preceptors [<s>Yāmuna</s>'s lineage], in their former stage of life (<s>pūrvāśrama</s>), having defeated a rival disputant, the court scholar of the <s>Cola</s> king, obtained the royal seat and half the kingdom bestowed by him. This mention of the <s>Cola</s> king here evokes that occasion. Just as the description of the king's being 'without a second' does not negate the king's retinue and the like but only negates another king equal to him—so he says, the non-duality scripture of <s>Brahman</s> does not negate Its sovereign manifestation:
'Likewise'

children.text:
ti /
atra yā ityapatitam /
yāḥ surāsuranarabrahmagarbhabrahmāṇḍakoṭayaḥ, tā veṣṇavamahāvibhūtyarṇavaviśīryamāṇa jalakaṇikāyamānāḥ tadadvitīyatvaśrutyā na bādhyanta iti yāvat /
aupaniṣadaṃ paraṃ tattvaṃ paraṃ brahma śrīmannārāyaṇa eveti ca viṣṇoriti nirdeśena jñāpitam // 17 //18 //19 //20 //21 //22 //
children.translated_text: —thus. Here the word 'which' (<s>yā</s>) is to be supplied. Those crores of <s>Brahmāṇḍas</s> containing gods, demons, humans, and <s>Brahmā</s>—appearing as drops of water scattering from the ocean of <s>Viṣṇu</s>'s great sovereign manifestation (<s>vibhūti</s>)—are not contradicted by the 'non-duality' scripture, in summary. And by the designation '<s>Viṣṇu</s>,' it is indicated that the supreme reality (<s>para tattva</s>) taught in the <s>Upaniṣads</s>, the supreme <s>Brahman</s>, is none other than <s>Śrīman Nārāyaṇa</s>. // 17-22 //

body.translated_text: —thus. We explain this: In the context of enumerating supreme entities, it is proper that <s>Brahman</s> alone be counted first—because It alone possesses primary supremacy; because the first enumeration of the primary [entity] is observed both in the world and in authoritative texts. In the context of enumerating the community of poets, it is well-known in the world of poets that <s>Kālidāsa</s> alone is counted first. As it is said: 'In the context of enumerating ancient poets, <s>Kālidāsa</s> is established on the little finger [i.e., counted first].' The author of the <s>Śāstra</s>, the master <s>Jaimini</s>, also approves the first enumeration of the primary [entity]. For he composed the <s>sūtra</s>:
Who indeed, by a mere snap of the fingers, could count all seven oceans,
and [at the same time] count the waves, foam, bubbles, and drops? // 23 //

body.text: yathaika eva savitā na dvitīyo nabhaḥsthale /
body.translated_text: Just as it is said, 'There is only one sun, no second, in the sky'—

body.text: ityuktā na hi sāvitrā niṣidhyante 'tra raśmayaḥ // 24 //
body.translated_text: the rays of the sun (<s>sāvitrā raśmayaḥ</s>) are certainly not negated thereby. // 24 //
Just as in the counting of primary countable entities, number (<s>saṅkhyā</s>) is itself not counted,
since number exists separately therein, like an entity different from the countable. // 25 //

children.translated_text: 'Who'

children.text:
iti /
tatsvarūpāntargatasya tena saha gaṇanāyoga ityatredaṃ nidarśanam , savitṛnidarśanaṃ ca /
guṇasya guṇinā saha gaṇanāyoga ityatra
children.translated_text: —thus. The illustration here is that what is contained within the very nature [of <s>Brahman</s>] cannot be counted alongside It; and the sun illustration [also serves this purpose]. Regarding [the point] that an attribute (<s>guṇa</s>) cannot be counted alongside the possessor of the attribute (<s>guṇin</s>):
'Just as in the primary [enumeration]'

children.text:
ti /
pṛthaksatī-saṅkhyeyādbhinnatvena sthitā /
yadvā apṛthaksatīticchedaḥ /
apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇabhūtetyarthaḥ /
saṅkhyeyānyapadārthavaditi tu vaidharmyadṛṣṭāntaḥ /
saṅkhyeyadravyagaṇanāyāṃ saṅkhyeyo 'nyaḥ padārtho yathā gaṇyate na tathā tadguṇabhūtā saṅkhyā tena saha gaṇyata ityarthaḥ /
yadvā saṅkhyeyatvenāprastutavastvantaravadityarthaḥ /
sādharmyadṛṣṭāntatvamidānīṃ ghaṭate // 23 //24 //25 //
children.translated_text: —thus. 'Existing separately' (<s>pṛthaksatī</s>)—established as different from the countable. Or, the reading is '<s>apṛthaksatī</s>'—meaning: being a qualifier that is non-separately established (<s>apṛthaksiddha</s>). 'Like an entity different from the countable' (<s>saṅkhyeyānyapadārthavat</s>) is an illustration by dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya dṛṣṭānta</s>): just as in counting countable substances, another entity that is countable is counted, but number, which is an attribute of that [substance], is not counted alongside it—this is the meaning. Or: just as something irrelevant—like an entity not under discussion—[is not counted among the countable]. This [reading] now fits as an illustration by similarity (<s>sādharmya dṛṣṭānta</s>). // 23-25 //

body.translated_text: To the objection, 'Even if they are not equal, let them be accepted as counted alongside [<s>Brahman</s>],' he responds:

body.text: tathā, pādo 'sya viśvā bhūtāni tripādasyāmṛtaṃ divi /
body.translated_text: Likewise, [the <s>śruti</s>:] 'One quarter of Him is all these beings; three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven'—
thus declaring, established the entire universe in the state of being thus [i.e., a portion of <s>Brahman</s>]. // 26 //

body.text: nanu sarvaṃ tadā śobhanam ; yadi brahmavibhūtitvādau pramāṇaṃ syādityatrāha

children.translated_text: 'Likewise'
—thus.
'One quarter of Him'
—thus.

children.text: yathā brahmaguṇatvaṃ sidhyejjagataḥ tathaiva brahmāṃśatvaṃ pratipādayacchrutijātaṃ sarvaṃ jagata brahmāpṛthaksiddhaprakāratve vyavārthāpayadityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Just as the world's being an attribute (<s>guṇatva</s>) of <s>Brahman</s> is established, so also the corpus of <s>śruti</s> [passages], establishing the world's being a portion (<s>aṃśatva</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>, has settled the entire universe in the mode of being a non-separately-established (<s>apṛthaksiddha</s>) attribute (<s>prakāra</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>—this is the meaning.

And attribute-ness (<s>guṇatva</s>), which is in the form of utter dependence (<s>atyantapāratantrya</s>), designated by the word 'being-thus' (<s>itthambhāva</s>), is precisely the nature of being a non-separately-established attribute.
By [the word] 'being-thus' (<s>itthambhāva</s>), portion-ness (<s>aṃśatva</s>) characterized as being a part of [<s>Brahman</s>'s] essential nature is not [meant];

rather, it is indicated that the world's being a portion of <s>Brahman</s> has the character of being an attribute (<s>prakāratā</s>) included within the essential nature of the qualified <s>Brahman</s> (<s>viśiṣṭa Brahman</s>)—this is made clear. // 26 //

body.translated_text: But [the opponent says:] 'All would be well, if there were a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for [the world's] being <s>Brahman</s>'s sovereign manifestation and so forth.' In response he says:

body.text: tathā, etāvānasya mahimā tato jyāyastaro hi saḥ /
body.translated_text: Likewise, [the <s>śruti</s> passages:] 'Such is His greatness, yet He is greater than that';
'Where one does not know anything else'—that is [<s>Brahman</s> called] <s>Bhūman</s> (the Infinite), the inner [controller];
'It manifestly causes fear in him'—and such other <s>śruti</s> passages are supreme. // 27 //
'For whom this entire universe, the whole <s>Brahmāṇḍa</s>, is like an atom compared to [Mount] <s>Meru</s>'—
such [<s>smṛti</s> passages] and all [similar statements] have as their purport the 'being-thus' (<s>itthambhāvatā</s>) of the entire [universe to <s>Brahman</s>]. // 28 //

children.translated_text: 'Likewise'
—thus.
'Such [is His greatness]'

children.text:
niti /
mahimā ityanena jagato vibhūtitvaṃ brahmaṇo 'tiśayāvahatvādguṇatvaṃ ca jñāyate /
children.translated_text: —thus. By [the word] 'greatness' (<s>mahimā</s>), the world's being a sovereign manifestation (<s>vibhūti</s>) [of <s>Brahman</s>] and its being an attribute (<s>guṇatva</s>) that conveys <s>Brahman</s>'s supremacy (<s>atiśaya</s>) is known.
'And the <s>Puruṣa</s> is greater than that'

children.text:
iti brahmaṇo jagadapekṣayātivailakṣaṇyaṃ ca /
ato na brahmasvarūpaikadeśatā mṛdaṃśateva tatpariṇāmaghaṭāderjagato yuktā /
ato 'pṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatayā viśiṣṭaikavastvekadeśatvarūpameva brahmāṃśatvaṃ jagato 'bhimatamiti bhāvaḥ /
sarvasya brahmasvarūpāntargatatve śrutimudāharati
children.translated_text: —this [indicates] the utter distinctness of <s>Brahman</s> in relation to the world. Therefore, the world's being a part of <s>Brahman</s>'s essential nature—like a pot being a part of clay through the latter's transformation—is not tenable. Hence, the intended meaning is that the world's being a 'portion' (<s>aṃśatva</s>) of <s>Brahman</s> is in the form of being a part of one qualified entity (<s>viśiṣṭaikavastu</s>), through the relationship of being a non-separately-established qualifier (<s>apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa</s>). He cites a <s>śruti</s> for the inclusion of everything within <s>Brahman</s>'s essential nature:
'Where'

children.text:
ti /
yatra viśiṣṭe brahmaṇi samanubhūyamāne 'nyatsvatantraṃ vastu na paśyati, sarvasya tadantarbhāvāt , sa bhūmetyarthaḥ /
sarvaprakārakaḥ sarvātmā paraṃ brahma paramapuruṣo nārāyaṇa eva bhūmā, anyaḥ sarvo 'pyalpaka iti proktaṃ bhavati /
svaniṣṭhaprañcadarśananindayā ca brahmaniṣṭhatvameva tasya gamyata ityāśayena śrutyantaramupādatte
children.translated_text: —thus. 'Where,' when the qualified <s>Brahman</s> is being experienced, one does not see any other independent entity—because everything is included within It—that is [called] <s>Bhūman</s> (the Infinite), this is the meaning. The supreme <s>Brahman</s>, the Supreme Person, <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> alone—who possesses all modes and is the Self of all—is <s>Bhūman</s>; everything else is limited—thus it is declared. And with the intention that, through the censure of seeing the manifold as self-dependent, the import is precisely [<s>Brahman</s>'s] being the ground [of everything], he adduces another <s>śruti</s>:
'An interval'
—thus.

children.text: yadā hyevaiṣa etasminnu daramantaraṃ kurute, atha tasya bhayaṃ bhavatī
children.translated_text: 'When indeed one makes even a small interval in this [<s>Brahman</s>], then fear arises for him'

children.text:
ti taittirīyopaniṣadi /
etasmin prapañce daramalpamapi antaramantarālaṃ brahmasaṃbandhavicchedaṃ yadā paśyati tadaivāsyaivaṃ jānataḥ saṃsārabhayamupasthitamagre bhavatītyarthaḥ /
paraprakriyācchāyayaivamatrārtho vivakṣito bhedamithyātvaṃ na sidhyatyetadvākyata iti bodhanāya /
paramātmani niṣṭhāśabditasya dhruvānusmaraṇasya pūrvavākyaprastutasyālpakālavicchede 'pi saṃsārabhayaprasaṅga eveti tu siddhāntisammator'thaḥ /
viṣṇumahāvibhūtyekadeśatve jagataḥ smṛtivākyaṃ
children.translated_text: —thus in the <s>Taittirīya Upaniṣad</s>. When one sees even a minute interval (<s>dara</s>)—a gap, a severance of the connection with <s>Brahman</s>—in this manifold world, then for one who knows thus, the fear of <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence) arises immediately—this is the meaning. By the shadow of the opponent's own system, the intended meaning here is thus explained [in order to show that]: the falsity of difference is not established by this passage—for the purpose of making this known. But the doctrinally approved meaning is: even a brief interruption of the steady remembrance (<s>dhruvānusmāraṇa</s>) of the Supreme Self, which was the topic of the preceding passage—even that entails the danger of <s>saṃsāra</s>. The <s>smṛti</s> passage for the world's being a portion of <s>Viṣṇu</s>'s great sovereign manifestation is:
'[Compared to Mount] <s>Meru</s>'

children.text:
rityādi /
ityādaya ityasyāgre smṛtayaśceti yojyam /
taditthambhāvatāparāḥ- brahmāpṛthaksiddhaprakāratvapratipādanatatparāḥ // 27 //28 //
children.translated_text: —and so forth. The word 'and so forth' (<s>ityādikāḥ</s>) should be connected with 'and the <s>smṛti</s> passages' ahead. 'Having as their purport the being-thus [of the world to <s>Brahman</s>]'—having as their purport the establishment of [the world's] being a non-separately-established attribute (<s>prakāra</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>. // 27-28 //

body.translated_text: Why is the world not simply a part of <s>Brahman</s>'s essential nature? In response he says:
The world of movable and immovable [entities] is a mere verbal elaboration (<s>vācārambhaṇamātra</s>),
being a product of modification (<s>vikāra</s>); the primordial cause alone (<s>mūlakāraṇa</s>) is the Real (<s>sat</s>). // 29 //

body.text: nanu virukteṣu vacaneṣu brahmavibhūtitvādau jagataḥ pratipādite 'pi vacanāntareṣu kāraṇamātrasya satyatvam anyasya sarvasyāsatyatvaṃ ca pratīyate iti tadanurodheneṣāṃ vyāvahārikaviṣayatvameva mantavyamiti cettatrāha

children.translated_text: '[Mere] verbal [elaboration]'

children.text:
ti /
vacanāntareṣvapi mithyātvaṃ nocyate bhedaprapañcasya, kintu brahmātmakatvena sattaiveti bhāvaḥ /
śrautakatipayapadaghaṭitaṃ śrautārthānuvādarūpaṃ
children.translated_text: —thus. Even in those other statements, the falsity of the differentiated manifold world is not stated; rather, [what is stated is] its reality precisely as having <s>Brahman</s> as its Self (<s>brahmātmakatva</s>)—this is the purport.
'A mere verbal elaboration'
—and so forth—this is composed of certain terms from <s>śruti</s> and restates the meaning of the <s>śruti</s>. The <s>śruti</s> passages evoked by the respective terms are intended.
'Modification is a mere verbal elaboration, a name; the clay alone is the real'
—thus in the <s>Chāndogya [Upaniṣad]</s>, sixth chapter. 'By speech'—

children.text:
iti tṛtīyā prayojanasya hetutvavivakṣayā /
ārambhaṇam-ālambhavam-spṛṣṭam /
ālambhaḥ sparśahiṃsayoḥ /
gṛhītamiti yāvat /
ārambhate ityārambhaṇaṃ-sṛṣṭamiti vā /
napuṃsakaikaśeṣaikavadbhāvau /
kintat ? vikāro nāmadheyaṃ ca /
kena spṛṣṭamityākāṅkṣāyāṃntvetha yathā somyaikena mṛtpiṇḍeneti pūrvaprakṛto mṛtpiṇḍo yogyatvātkartṛtayānveti /
ghaṭatvādyavasthārūpo vikāraḥ tattadavasthāyogaprayuktaṃ ghaṭādināma ca mṛtpiṇḍenaiva gṛhītaṃ vākpūrvakavyavahārāyeti phalitam /
evaṃ kāraṇadravyasyaiva nānāvasthābhāktvena nānākāryātmakatvātkāryāṇāṃ kāraṇānanyatvamityāha
children.translated_text:
Thus the third [interpretation takes] the purpose as [expressing] causality.
'<s>Ārambhaṇam</s>' means '<s>ālambhavam</s>'—'touched' [i.e., grasped].
'<s>Ālambha</s>' [means] contact or injury.
That is to say, 'grasped.'
'<s>Ārambhate</s>' means '<s>ārambhaṇam</s>'—'created,' as it were.
The neuter singular is by the rule of single remainder (<s>ekaśeṣa</s>) and uniform gender (<s>ekavadbhāva</s>).
What then? A modification and a name.
When the expectancy arises 'By what is it grasped?'—just as [in the Upaniṣad] 'O good one, by one lump of clay,' the previously mentioned lump of clay, being suitable, is connected as the agent.
The modification, which is the form of a state such as pot-ness, and the name 'pot' etc., which is applied to that state—both are grasped by the lump of clay alone, for the purpose of verbal conventional usage—this is the purport.
Thus, since the causal substance alone, through assuming various states, has the nature of various effects, the non-difference of effects from their cause is stated:
'Clay alone is real'

children.text:
iti /
atra sarvaṃ mṛṇmayaṃ viśeṣyam /
itiśabdaḥ prakāravācī /
sarvaṃ mṛṇmayaṃ mṛttikātvaprakāreṇaiva prāmāṇikam /
na tu mṛdanātmakatvenetyarthaḥ /
anena kāṇādābhimata upādānopādeyayoratyantabhedo nirastaḥ /
ekavijñānena sarvavijñānapratijñopapādanārthaṃ pravṛttatvādasya vākyasyopādānopādeyayorananyatva eva tātparyamuktadiśā /
na tu kāryamātrasya mithyātve /
tathā sati sarvasya jñātavyasyābhāvādeva sarvaṃ jñātaṃ syādityasaṅgatamāpadyeta /
samastapadatve parābhimate vāgārambhaṇamiti bhavet /
vācārambhaṇaśabdasya mithyārthakatvaṃ cāprasiddhameva parābhimatamiti bodhyam /
children.translated_text:
—thus.
Here, 'everything made of clay' is the qualificand.
The word '<s>iti</s>' expresses manner.
Everything made of clay is valid precisely in the manner of being clay; but not in the manner of being non-clay—this is the meaning.
By this, the absolute difference between material cause and effect accepted by the <s>Kaṇādas</s> (Vaiśeṣikas) is refuted.
Since this passage has commenced for the purpose of establishing the promise 'by knowing one, everything is known,' its purport is precisely the non-difference of material cause and effect—as indicated.
Not the falsity of the mere effect.
For if it were so, since everything to be known would be non-existent, everything would be known [trivially], and an absurd consequence would follow.
If the opponent takes it as a compound, it would be '<s>vāgārambhaṇam</s>' [beginning of speech].
And that the word '<s>vācārambhaṇa</s>' means 'having the sense of falsity' should be understood as itself an unestablished claim of the opponent.
'That is the real'
—this is a restatement in meaning of that [previous passage].
'Immutable' (<s>kūṭastha</s>)

children.text:
mityādiḥ /
upādānatve 'pi brahmaṇo nirvikāratvaṃ kūṭasthaśabdena vivakṣitam /
satsatyam-satataikarūpam /
nanu nirvikāratve kathamupādānatvam ? sarvacidaciccharīrakatvāt sūkṣmacidacidviśiṣṭatvenopādānatvaṃ brahmaṇa upapannameva /
so 'yaṃ śarīrātmabhāvo jagadbrahmaṇoḥ
children.translated_text:
—and so forth.
Even though <s>Brahman</s> is the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>), its changelessness is what is intended by the word '<s>kūṭastha</s>.'
'<s>Sat</s>' means '<s>satya</s>'—that which is eternally of one form.
But if it is changeless, how can it be the material cause? Because <s>Brahman</s> has all sentient and insentient entities as its body, its being the material cause is perfectly established through being qualified by subtle sentient and insentient [entities].
This very relationship of body and self between the world and <s>Brahman</s>
'Having being (<s>sat</s>) as their source'—'all this has that as its self (<s>ātman</s>)'

children.text:
iti nirdiṣṭaḥ /
nacaivaṃ svarūpapariṇāmābhāve mṛṇmayadṛṣṭāntāsaṅgatiḥ, kāryakāraṇayorananyatvamātre dṛṣṭāntasaṅgateḥ /
nanu cetanācetanaprapañcasya brahmānanyatvaṃ vā katham ? brahmātmakatvena brahmarūpatvenānanyatvopapatteḥ /
tadidameva prāmāṇikamiti cocyate
children.translated_text:
—thus it is stated.
Nor is there, in the absence of transformation of its own nature, any inconsistency with the example of clay, since the example is relevant only to the extent of non-difference between cause and effect.
But how can the non-difference of the sentient and insentient manifold from <s>Brahman</s> be maintained? Because non-difference is established through having <s>Brahman</s> as its self, through having the form of <s>Brahman</s>.
And it is said that precisely this is what is valid:
'All this has that as its self; that is the real'
—through syntactical connection as a single sentence.
And this meaning alone is consistent with the illustrative sentence—this should be reflected upon.

children.text: paravyākhyācchāyayā tu tadbrahma satyaṃ sadaikarūpamityartho varṇitaḥ /
children.translated_text: But following the shadow of the opponent's interpretation, the meaning has been described as: 'That <s>Brahman</s> is real—eternally of one form.'
In the verse, '<s>vācārambhaṇamātram</s>' means: it is produced entirely only for verbal conventional usage. // 29 //

body.translated_text: But [the opponent says:] 'Even if the aforesaid statements establish the world's being <s>Brahman</s>'s sovereign manifestation, in other statements only the reality of the cause and the unreality of everything else is understood; therefore, in accordance with those, these [former statements] should be taken as pertaining to conventional reality (<s>vyāvahārikaviṣaya</s>) alone.' In response he says:
The effect is non-different from its cause, like sparks from fire,
Through extensive illustrations of clay, iron, seed, and so forth. // 30 //

body.text: samānaprakaraṇeṣūpādānopādeyayoraikyasyaiva pratipādanācca na kāryasya mithyātvaṃ vācārambhaṇaśruterarthaḥ / kintu kāraṇātmakataiveti pratibodhayannāha

children.translated_text: 'Non-different'
—thus.

children.text: pāpakādvyucca ritānāṃ visphuliṅgānāmagnyaṃśatvenāgnyananyatvavadbrahmaṇa udbhūtasya prapañcasyāpi brahmāṃśabhūtasya brahmānanyatvameva vivakṣitam /
children.translated_text: Just as sparks that have sprung forth from fire, being portions of fire, are non-different from fire—so too the manifold that has arisen from <s>Brahman</s>, being a portion of <s>Brahman</s>, is intended to be non-different from <s>Brahman</s> alone.

children.text: idaṃ cānanyatvaṃ mṛdādidṛṣṭāntaiśca śrutiṣu nirūpitamiti yāvat // 30 //
children.translated_text: And this non-difference is also established in the <s>śrutis</s> through illustrations of clay and so forth—this much [is meant]. // 30 //

body.translated_text: Since in passages of the same context, it is the unity of material cause and effect alone that is taught, the meaning of the '<s>vācārambhaṇa</s>' <s>śruti</s> is not the falsity of the effect; rather, it is precisely the nature of being identical with the cause—thus informing, he says:
Fire could not burn straw, water could not submerge,
Nor could wind move, without the nourishment of that power. // 31 //

children.translated_text: 'Could not burn'
—thus.
This meaning is well-known in the <s>Kenopaniṣad</s>. // 31 //

body.translated_text:
The origin of effects as being of the nature of the cause has been stated.
That even what has the form of an <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory/explanatory passage) can be an indicator of purport—he says:
From the knowledge of one primary [reality], all would be known—
Thus, through Vedic statements and authoritative traditions rooted in them. // 32 //
This world, consisting of sentient and insentient, has its being through having <s>Brahman</s> as its self—
Thus is it established; the glory (<s>vibhūti</s>) of <s>Brahman</s> is not negated. // 33 //

children.translated_text: 'Did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard?'

children.text:
ti pratijñātamekavijñānena sarvavijñānaṃ brahmaṇa ekasyaiva pāramārthye ghaṭate /
natu tadbhinnānāṃ bahūnāṃ pāramārthye /
tatprapañcasyāpāramārthyamakāmenāpi svīkartavyamiti cettatrāha
children.translated_text: —The promise 'by knowing one, everything is known' is possible only if <s>Brahman</s> alone is ultimately real, not if the many things different from it are [also] ultimately real. Therefore, even unwillingly, one must accept the unreality of the manifold—if such [an objection is raised], to that he says:
'One' (<s>eka</s>)

children.text:
ti /
brahmaṇo nikhilajagadantarātmatvena nikhilajagatpradhānatayā nikhilasya ca taccharīratvena tatprakārataikasvarūpatayā tasmin jñāte tadanantargataṃ kimapi jñātavyaṃ mukhyaṃ nāvaśiṣyata iti ekavijñānena sarvavijñāvākyasyārtha iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text:
—thus.
Since <s>Brahman</s> is the inner self of the entire world, since it is primary to the entire world, and since the entire world, being its body, has a single essential nature as its mode—when it is known, no primary object of knowledge that is contained within it remains [unknown]. This is the meaning of the statement 'by knowing one, everything is known'—such is the purport.
'And so forth'

children.text:
ti /
niruktārthaparaiḥ śrutivacanaistanmūlopabṛṃhaṇasmṛtivacanaiśca brahmātmakatvena labdhasvarūpaḥ prapañca ityeva bodhyate /
na tu brahmaṇo vibhūtibhūtaḥ sa niṣidhyata ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text:
—thus.
Through <s>śruti</s> passages whose meanings have been explained, and through <s>smṛti</s> passages that elaborate on them as their foundation—one should understand that the manifold has its essential nature as obtained through having <s>Brahman</s> as its self. But it, being the glory (<s>vibhūti</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>, is not negated—this is the meaning.
'Having its being through <s>Brahman</s> as self' (<s>brahmātmanā ātmalābha</s>)

children.text:
iti /
ātmano lābho yasyeti bahuvrīhiḥ /
brahmābhinnāntarātmanā prayojyasvarūpalābhavānityarthaḥ /
brahmatātmalābho 'yamiti samastapāṭhaḥ saṃbhāvya /
tatra ca ātmano lābhaḥ ātmalābhaḥ-svarūpasattā brahmatmatayā-brahmatmakatvena ātmalābho yasyeti bahuvrīhiḥ /
brahmāvibhūtibhūtasya prapañcasya na niṣedhaḥ kṛtaḥ śāstreṣviti nirūpitametāvatā // 32 //33 //
children.translated_text:
—thus.
'Whose self-attainment is through the self'—this is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound.
The meaning is: having its essential nature obtained through <s>Brahman</s>, which is its non-different inner self.
Alternatively, considering the reading '<s>brahmātmātmalābho 'yam</s>' as a compound: therein, '<s>ātmalābha</s>' means self-attainment, i.e., the existence of its own nature; '<s>ātmalābha</s>' with '<s>brahmātmanā</s>' means: that whose self-attainment is through having <s>Brahman</s> as its self—this is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s>.
The manifold, which is the glory of <s>Brahman</s>, is not negated in the scriptures—this much has been established. // 32 // 33 //

body.translated_text: But [the opponent says:]
If that [manifold] were negated, then since everything would be false, of both worldly and Vedic [transactions],
The conventional usages would be destroyed; and likewise, even the cognition of <s>Brahman</s> would [be destroyed]. // 34 //

children.translated_text: 'If that were negated'

children.text:
iti /
prapañcaniṣedhe vivakṣite śāstravacanataḥ tattadarthaviśeṣapratipādanopādānādyarthāḥ sarve vyavahārā laukikā vaidikāśca lupyeran-aprāmāṇikā visaṃvādinaśca bhaveyuḥ, sarvasya mithyātvādityarthaḥ /
nanu bhedavyavahārāṇāmaprāmāṇikatvamiṣṭameveti cettatrāha
children.translated_text:
—thus.
If the negation of the manifold were intended, all conventional usages—both worldly and Vedic—which serve to teach specific meanings, adopt [entities], and so forth, would be destroyed—they would become unauthoritative and contradictory—since everything would be false. This is the meaning.
But if it is maintained that the inauthenticity of dualistic conventional usages is precisely what is accepted, to that he says:
'Likewise'
—thus.

children.text: brahmabhinnasarvamithyātve brahmaviṣayakadhiya aupaniṣadyā apivilopo 'satyatā prasajyata ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: If everything different from <s>Brahman</s> is false, then even the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> cognition pertaining to <s>Brahman</s> would suffer destruction, i.e., unreality—this is the meaning.
Because it would be produced from an unreal cause, it would be unreal, and because its object would be unreal—such is the purport. // 34 //

body.translated_text: Now, since the negation of the manifold is untenable, and since even those <s>śruti</s> passages that are superficially understood as having negation as their purport must be given a different interpretation—with this intent, he says:
Due to its being 'conventionally real,' even in its falsity there is no contradiction
With perception and the like—such is [their] view; [but this was] refuted even earlier. // 35 //

body.text: nanu paramārthadṛṣṭyā brahmabhinnasya sarvasya mithyātve 'pi tataḥ prāk avidyātaḥ pramāṇaprameyavyavahārādi nirūhyata iti cettatrāha

children.translated_text: 'Conventionally real' (<s>vyāvahārika</s>)
—thus.
This portion of the refutation has been lost [from the manuscript].

children.text: vyāvahārikasattayā pramāṇaprameyavyavahāropapādane vyāvahārikapramāṇabhāvena śrutyādinā janitā parabrahmabuddhirapi bhavatabhimatā vyāvahārikārthamātragocarā bhavet ; nirviśeṣabrahmamātrapāramārthyasyāpi vyavahāraikaśaraṇatvāt /
children.translated_text: If conventional activity of valid means and objects of knowledge is established through conventional existence, then the cognition of the Supreme <s>Brahman</s> generated by <s>śruti</s> and other [means]—which are, on their own view, merely conventionally valid—would also pertain only to a conventionally real object; since even the ultimate reality of <s>Brahman</s> alone depends solely on conventional [means of knowledge].
And thus, even the ultimate reality of <s>Brahman</s> alone could not be established, due to the absence of an ultimate-level proof.

children.text: etadviṣaye pūrvācāryaiḥ sūribhireva parākrāntaṃ nitarāmiti visamyate 'treti bodhyam // 35 //
children.translated_text: On this subject, the earlier masters (<s>pūrvācāryas</s>), who were scholars, have already thoroughly prevailed—this should be understood as the reason for brevity here. // 35 //

body.translated_text: But even if everything different from <s>Brahman</s> is false from the standpoint of ultimate reality, prior to that, from ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), the conventional activity of valid means and objects of knowledge is produced—if such [an objection is raised], to that he says:
Therefore, by the <s>Upaniṣad</s>-born cognition of <s>Brahman</s>'s non-duality, the world
Is not sublated, because it is the glory (<s>vibhūti</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>—this is established. // 36 //

children.translated_text: (Thus the description of the meaning of the 'non-dual' <s>śruti</s>, preceded by the establishment of the world as the glory of <s>Brahman</s>.)
He concludes the demonstration that the 'non-dual' <s>śruti</s> does not sublate the manifold:
'Therefore'

children.text:
ti /
brahmaṇo vibhūtitvācca jagadbrahmādvaitadhiyā na bādhyate /
savibhūtikasyaiva tasyādvitīyatvadhiya upaniṣatsiddhatvāt /
children.translated_text:
—thus.
Because the world is the glory of <s>Brahman</s>, it is not sublated by the cognition of <s>Brahman</s>'s non-duality; for the non-duality cognition pertains precisely to <s>Brahman</s> together with its glory, as established in the <s>Upaniṣads</s>.
The particle '<s>ca</s>' serves to aggregate additional reasons such as the establishment through unsublatted experience.
Or, '<s>ca</s>' has the sense of 'but.'
An equal or a superior [to <s>Brahman</s>] is sublated,
but not the world, which is [<s>Brahman</s>'s] glory—this is the meaning. // 36 //

body.text: nanu sattve prapañcasya nāstīti pratyayaḥ katham /
body.translated_text: But if the manifold exists, how can there be the cognition 'it does not exist'?

body.text: asattve vā kathaṃ tasminnastīti pratyayo bhavet // 37 //
body.translated_text: Or if it does not exist, how can there be the cognition 'it exists' regarding it? // 37 //

body.text:
prapañcasyādvitīyaśrutyā bādha iti parapakṣo nirastaḥ /
atha tasya sadasadanirvacanīyatvamapi parābhimataṃ nirasituṃ vicāramupakramate

children.translated_text: 'But if it exists'

children.text:
iti /
sattve prapañcasya nāstīti bādhaviṣayatvaṃ kathaṃ ghaṭatetyākṣepo mādhyamikādīnām /
atra pratīpakṣaḥ sāṅkhyādīnām
children.translated_text:
—thus.
If the manifold exists, how can being the object of sublation through the cognition 'it does not exist' be possible?—this is the objection of the <s>Mādhyamikas</s> and others.
Here, the counter-objection from the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> and others:
'If it does not exist'
—thus.

children.text: asattve sadbuddhibodhyatvaṃ pratipannaṃ tasya kathaṃ ghaṭeteti // 37 //
children.translated_text: If it does not exist, how could its being the object of the established cognition 'it exists' be possible? // 37 //

body.translated_text: The opponent's position that the manifold is sublated by the 'non-dual' <s>śruti</s> has been refuted. Now, to refute also the view accepted by the opponent that it is neither real nor unreal (indeterminable, <s>anirvacanīya</s>), he commences the investigation:
The simultaneous existence and non-existence of one thing is impossible due to mutual contradiction,
When the conflicting pair of 'existent' and 'non-existent' cognitions is obtained. // 38 //
Due to the absence of certainty regarding either meaning,
The <s>Jainas</s> have accepted the both-real-and-unreal nature of the manifold. // 39 //

children.translated_text: 'Both-real-and-unreal' (<s>sadasattva</s>)

—thus.
The contradictory pair is not fit to be accepted in a single [locus]—this much [is meant].
He states the occasion for investigation:
'Real and unreal' (<s>sadasat</s>)

children.text:
diti /
viruddhākāradvayaprasaṅge parasparavirodhādubhayasyānyatarasyākārasya vānirṇayāddhetorvicāraḥ prāptāvasara iti yāvat /
atravicāraḥ prakramyataiti śeṣapūraṇena vākyārtho vaktavyaḥ /
tatrādāvanaikāntyavādināṃ jainānāṃ matamāha
children.translated_text:
—thus.
When the encounter with two contradictory aspects arises, due to the impossibility of determining either one of the two, or both, by reason of their mutual contradiction—the investigation has found its occasion. This much [is meant].
'Here the investigation is commenced'—with this supplementation, the sentence-meaning should be stated.
Therein, he first states the view of the <s>Jainas</s>, the non-absolutists (<s>anekāntavādins</s>):
'Both-real-and-unreal' (<s>sadasattva</s>)

children.text:
iti /
pratīyamānatvādevaikasmin sadasattvayorna virodha ityabhimānaḥ /
yadvā jainamatānuvādaḥ
children.translated_text:
—thus.
Since both are experienced, there is no contradiction in both-existence-and-non-existence in a single [locus]—this is [their] presumption.
Alternatively, verses 38-39 are a restatement of the <s>Jaina</s> view:
'When the conflicting pair of sat and asat cognitions is obtained'
—beginning with this
'The <s>Jainas</s> have accepted'

children.text:
ityantena /
sadasattvayoḥ pratīyayormadhye ekasyaiva nirṇaye hetvabhāvādyathāpratīti prapañcasyobhayamevaiṣṭavyamiti janā āsthitā ityarthaḥ /
niścayābhāvahetuta ityanena niścayahetvabhāvo vivakṣitaḥ /
pāṭhāntaraṃ vā saṃbhāvyate // 38 //39 //
children.translated_text:
—ending with this.
Among the two cognitions of existence and non-existence that are experienced, since there is no reason for determining only one, both must be accepted for the manifold in accordance with experience—thus the <s>Jainas</s> are established. This is the meaning.
'Due to the absence of certainty as the reason'—by this, the absence of a reason for certainty is intended.
Alternatively, a variant reading may be considered. // 38 // 39 //

body.translated_text: But the <s>Jainas</s> say: on the strength of both 'exists' and 'does not exist' cognitions, both-existence-and-non-existence must be asserted. To that he says:
Giving priority to the attainment of existence, from the arising of the cognition 'does not exist,'
The <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> have accepted that the manifold always exists. // 40 //

children.translated_text: 'Giving priority to the attainment of existence'
—thus.
Since negation presupposes [prior] connection, since the negated must be subservient [to the affirmed], the cognition of existence is stronger.
Therefore, the manifold always has existence alone.
The cognition 'does not exist,' however, pertains [merely] to the absence of manifestation—this is their intent. // 40 //

body.translated_text: He states the <s>Kāpila</s> (<s>Sāṅkhya</s>) view, which holds absolute existence, contradicting the above:
In the difficulty of the conflicting pair obtained through cognitions of existence and non-existence,
For the sake of resolving the contradiction, by breaking into the aspects of existence and non-existence,
Some have declared the manifold to be indeterminable as either real or unreal. // 41 //

children.translated_text: 'Real and unreal' (<s>sadasat</s>)
—thus.

children.text: pratītibalātsattvāsattvarūpaviruddhadharmadvayāpattirūpasaṅkaṭe prasakte viruddhayoraikādhikaraṇyānupapattibalātsattvamasattvaṃ ca viruddhaṃ dharmadvayaṃ parityajya na sat nāpyasaditi sadasadanirvacaniyaṃ prapañca nirvacanti śāṅkarā ityarthaḥ // 41 //
children.translated_text: When the difficulty arises of the encounter with the contradictory pair of aspects—existence and non-existence—due to the force of experience, and since the co-location of contradictories is untenable, the <s>Śāṅkaras</s> (Advaitins), abandoning both the contradictory qualities of existence and non-existence, declare the manifold as indeterminable—neither real nor unreal (<s>sadasadanirvacanīya</s>). This is the meaning. // 41 //

body.translated_text: He states the view of the <s>Māyāvādins</s> (Advaitins), which opposes both [previous] views:
Through the distinction of existence and non-existence, according to differences of place, time, and the like,
Others, holding [that the existence and non-existence] of pots and the like [is established thus], have declared a system. (Verse 42)

children.translated_text: 'Existence and non-existence'
— thus.
'By distinction' — the instrumental is used in the sense of 'in this manner.'

children.text: vibhaktadeśakālādiviśeṣataḥ sattvamasattvaṃ ca pratītaṃ vyavasthitaṃ ghaṭāderghaṭata eveti bhāvo 'mīṣām // 42 //
children.translated_text: Through the particular distinctions of distinct place, time, and the like, the existence and non-existence of a pot and the like is recognized as established from the pot itself — such is the purport of these [thinkers]. (42)

body.translated_text: He states the position of the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others:
Thus, since from the clash of disputants a doubt has arisen,
A determination is made therein according to the view of the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>. (Verse 43)

children.translated_text: 'Thus' —
'From the clash of disputants' — from the dispute among disputants; that is to say, from the conflict of views.
From the arising of doubt due to the conflict, an investigation is being undertaken for the determination of the doubtful matter.

children.text: tatra pakṣāntarāṇāṃ sadoṣatvapratipādanapūrvakaṃ sopādhikasattvāsattvapakṣo mīmāṃsakābhimato nirṇīyate sadyuktyeti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therein, preceded by the demonstration of the faultiness of the alternative positions, the view approved by the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> — namely, the position of existence and non-existence with qualifications (<s>sopādhika</s>) — is determined as well-reasoned. Such is the purport.
'Is made' — the use of the present tense is due to the proximity [of the investigation].
And this is a thesis-statement intended to settle the understanding of the listener. (43)

body.translated_text: If non-existence in the essential nature of the pot, together with existence, were known [simultaneously],
Then there would indeed be existence and non-existence simultaneously in pots and the like. (Verse 44)
Since here the cognitions of the form 'this exists' and 'this does not exist'
Are not [cognitions of] 'it exists' and 'it does not exist' [absolutely], due to the differences of place, time, and condition. (Verse 45)
Therefore, existence and non-existence in pots and the like are established through the distinction of place and the like;
Since the <s>syādvāda</s> (the Jaina doctrine of 'maybe') has been refuted, it has no possibility here. (Verse 46)

children.translated_text: beginning with 'the essential nature of the pot'

children.translated_text: — by means of three verses. The meaning is this: Non-existence recognized in the essential nature of the pot — that is to say, the very cognition 'it does not exist' — if it were also to establish the existence of that [pot], or if the cognition were to establish both existence and non-existence without qualifications, then the combination of existence and non-existence would have to be accepted. But this is not so. Rather, cognitions establish existence through some particular distinction of place, time, condition, and the like, and non-existence only through the qualification of another place and the like. Therefore, since existence and non-existence are established in the pot and the like through differences of place and the like, the other doctrine — being vitiated by faults such as contradiction — has no possibility. Such is the meaning. The reading 'nirastasyādvādasya' (of the refuted <s>syādvāda</s>) is also possible. In that case, the meaning is: the <s>syādvāda</s> — the Jaina doctrine of non-absolutism saying 'maybe it exists, maybe it does not exist' — which has been refuted through self-contradiction, has no possibility. And here, the position of the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others, and the distinction from it in the established conclusion, was elaborated by the revered master <s>Nigamāntācārya</s> (<s>Yāmunācārya</s>) in the sixtieth debate of the <s>Śatadūṣaṇī</s>. As stated: 'We accept the position that the establishment of both [existence and non-existence] is through the difference of qualifications, since it is not far-fetched.' The difference of qualifications is as follows: existence through its own nature (<s>svātman</s>), non-existence through another nature (<s>anyātman</s>); existence at its own time, non-existence at another time; likewise, existence in its own place, non-existence in another place. Here, identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) or conjunction (<s>saṃsarga</s>) is designated as existence. Non-existence is designated of the very same entity in a form contrary to that. But in the sixth position, the very conjunction of contradictory properties in the entity is designated as the cause for the designation of non-existence. For a pot is said to exist as a pot-nature, but not to exist as a cloth-nature. Existing in its own place and time, it does not exist in a place and time opposed to its own. The elders approve of precisely this, because of the favorability to apprehension and because of its simplicity. Here is the analysis: Existence has either identity or some other relation as its defining characteristic. In 'this pot exists,' existence characterized by identity with pot-nature is cognized. In 'here and now the pot exists,' existence characterized by conjunction with this place and time is cognized. Likewise, in 'this cloth does not exist,' non-existence characterized by the absence of identity with cloth-nature — non-existence as cloth-nature — is cognized. And in 'there and then the pot does not exist,' non-existence characterized by the absence of conjunction with that place and time is cognized. Thus, the establishment of both existence and non-existence — which are of the form of presence and absence — in pots and the like, through the difference of place and the like, is one position. The alternative position is that even absence is itself a form of another positive entity. Just as 'this pot exists' — the existence of the pot cognized therein is just pot-ness, so that very same [pot-ness] is the object of cognition even in 'this cloth does not exist,' in the form of difference from cloth. Likewise, existence characterized by conjunction with one's own place and time also becomes the object of the cognition of non-existence in another place, through the absence of conjunction with the other place and the like. And thus it is established that a particular property (<s>dharmaviśeṣa</s>) of entities alone is the domain of the cognitions 'it exists' and 'it does not exist.' This is also approved by those who hold the established conclusion. (44)(45)(46)

body.translated_text: Therein, by refuting the position that combines absolute existence and absolute non-existence [simultaneously], the established conclusion is expounded
Objection: Spatial relation and the like are possible only for what [already] exists.
The existence of what is non-existent is not accepted as [arising] from spatial and temporal relation. (Verse 47)
Relation requires two substrata; therefore, the existence of what exists would always obtain.
That existence would come to the non-existent through causal factors [as] origination — this is extremely implausible. (Verse 48)
The manifold world, having a beginning and an end, is therefore placed within the domain of the existent.

body.text: uktaṃ ca - ādāvante ca yannāsti nāsti madhye 'pi tattathā iti /
body.translated_text: And it has been stated: 'That which does not exist at the beginning and at the end does not exist in the middle either.'
Therefore, let it be accepted that [the world], whose existence is certain, is always existent. (Verse 49)

children.translated_text: 'Objection: spatial relation and the like' —

pūrvamasato ghaṭādeḥ svadeśakālasaṃbandhena sattotpattyā durupapādā /

First, the production of existence of a pot and the like, which were previously non-existent, through relation with their own place and time — this is difficult to establish. Because a relation, being a conjunction produced by two relata, cannot arise when one of the relata does not exist. And thus: existence through spatial and temporal relation, and spatial and temporal relation through existence — this is mutual dependence (<s>anyonyāśraya</s>). Therefore, the existence of entities must always be maintained —
'The existence of what exists would always obtain' —

Rather, origination of what was previously non-existent through the operation of causal factors should be stated. To this he says:

children.translated_text: thus. The production of existence of what is non-existent, even through a hundred efforts, is difficult to establish — like [extracting] oil from sand. Moreover, if what is non-existent could originate [through causal factors], then since there is no distinction in the non-existence of [various things], from a stick, wheel, and the like, a cloth too would absurdly originate, just as a pot does. And through some operation, even horns of a hare might sometimes arise. It is with this consideration that this has been stated. If one objects that there is no over-extension because the specific material cause has a fixed capacity for producing specific effects — no, this will not do, because apart from the effect being contained [in the cause], the restriction of capacity too is difficult to explain. Therefore, it should be accepted that the effect, being already existent, is manifested through the operation of causal factors — he says:
'Having a beginning and an end' —

children.translated_text: thus. Appearance and disappearance alone are the beginning and end, i.e., origination and destruction — such is the purport. Here the corroborating citation is:
'At the beginning' —
thus.
'Therefore' —
thus. The meaning is: let it be accepted that what is ascertained as existent is always existent. (47)(48)(49)

body.translated_text: The proponent of the doctrine of permanent existence (<s>sattvaikāntyavādin</s>) — the <s>Sāṅkhya</s> philosopher (<s>Kāpila</s>) — stands opposed here, maintaining that he can establish both existence and non-existence without contradiction:
What is non-existent is always non-existent, because of the impossibility of being produced — like a sky-flower.
There is no distinction in non-existence between what was non-existent before and what is absolutely non-existent. (Verse 50)

children.translated_text: (Thus the establishment of the manifold world within the domain of existence.)
'Non-existent' —

janyayogāt - utpattyayogāt /
prāgatyantāsatoḥ - pūrvamasatotyantāsa taśca /
