children.translated_text: thus. 'Because of the impossibility of being produced' — because of the impossibility of origination. 'What was non-existent before and what is absolutely non-existent' — what was previously non-existent and what is eternally non-existent. Thus the <s>Sāṅkhya</s> (<s>Kāpila</s>) position has been presented. Here, the portion of the text that is devoted to the refutation of this <s>Sāṅkhya</s> position and to the presentation and refutation of other positions appears to be lost. For the convenience of the reader, the manner of refutation of the <s>Sāṅkhya</s> position is briefly indicated here. The substance (<s>dravya</s>) is indeed eternal. But the states — such as pot-ness, potsherd-ness, and the like — are adventitious. And the operation of causal factors serves precisely the purpose of the attainment of a particular state. It is because the substance exists that it can be the object of causal operation and can assume different states. And through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>), the fixed capacity of each causal system for each particular effect is established — so there is no over-extension. And the cognition of 'being produced,' 'being destroyed,' and the like, with regard to the substance in its specific state-form, is well-explained. But on the view that the causal system is merely a manifester [rather than a producer], the distinction between what the cause makes known and [what it produces] cannot be maintained. If manifestation differs from cognition, then origination through another means has already been admitted. Moreover, if manifestation is eternal, then the operation of causal factors is entirely pointless. If yet another manifestation [of the manifestation] is accepted, there is infinite regress. And if that [manifestation] itself is produced, then the doctrine of effect-in-cause (<s>satkāryavāda</s>) is contradicted. Since one admits the production of that very manifestation, it is fitting to admit the origination of that [effect] itself as it is apprehended. The <s>satkāryavāda</s> should be maintained in the sense that the existent substance alone assumes a different state as the effect-in-cause. And this is also established in the Vedāntic tradition.
The manifold differentiation [produced] by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is false.
And its falsity is understood from the <s>śruti</s> (scripture) [declaring <s>Brahman</s> to be] without a second.

children.text: tacca pratītibādhābhyāṃ sadasadvilakṣaṇatvasiddheḥ supratiṣṭhitamiti hi māyāvādināṃ matam /
children.translated_text: And that [falsity] is well-established through the proof that [the world] is different from both the existent and the non-existent, by means of cognition and sublation — such is the position of the <s>Māyāvādins</s> (Advaitins).
But that has been mostly refuted by the preceding and subsequent sections — this should be understood. (50)

body.translated_text: And as for what is heard regarding <s>Śvetaketu</s> — the [teaching] 'That thou art' (<s>tattvamasi</s>) —
In the sixth <s>prapāṭhaka</s> (chapter) [of the <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s>], how can it have its primary meaning? (Verse 51)

children.translated_text: is understood from the sentence '<s>tattvamasi</s>' ('That thou art').
In order to refute this doctrine of the Advaitins, he commences an investigation of the meaning of the sentence '<s>tattvamasi</s>':
'<s>Śvetaketu</s>' —

children.text:
iti /
upādāyasambodhya /
chāndogya ityādiḥ /
jīvabrahmaikye tattvamasivākyameva mukhyaṃ pramāṇamabhimanyate taiḥ /
asyāpi samānādhikaraṇavākyasya mukhyārthatvaṃ tanmate na saṃbhavatītyaha
children.translated_text: thus. 'Having addressed' — having instructed. '<s>Chāndogya</s>' and so forth is supplied. Those [Advaitins] consider the sentence '<s>tattvamasi</s>' itself as the primary authority for the identity of the individual self and <s>Brahman</s>. Even of this co-referential sentence (<s>samānādhikaraṇavākya</s>), he says that the primary meaning is not possible according to their view —
'Of that' —
and so on. (51)

body.translated_text: Now, [the Advaitins hold that] the knowledge of the identity of the individual self (<s>ātman</s>) with <s>Brahman</s> — which is mere undifferentiated consciousness — is alone the remover of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). And that the identity of the self with <s>Brahman</s>, which is mere undifferentiated consciousness,
The conscious being denoted by the word 'thou' (<s>tvam</s>) is afflicted by misery (<s>kārpaṇya</s>), grief (<s>śoka</s>), and suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>);
The omniscient one, of true resolve, is a boundless ocean of happiness;
He is the referent of the word 'that' (<s>tat</s>) — how can the identity of the two be [maintained]? It is like [equating] light and darkness. (Verse 52)

children.translated_text: 'Misery' —
thus.
'<s>Kārpaṇya</s>' — wretchedness, helplessness.
'<s>Śoka</s>' — the mental agitation born from reflecting on past suffering.
'<s>Duḥkha</s>' — characterized by the present experience of the undesirable.

children.text: samānavibhaktyā pratipannamaikyaṃ jīveśvarayorviruddhasvabhāvayorna ghaṭata iti mukhyārthāsaṃbhava evetyāśayaḥ // 52 //
children.translated_text: The identity of the individual self (<s>jīva</s>) and the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>), which is understood through co-referential [predication], is not feasible for [entities] of contradictory natures — thus, the impossibility of the primary meaning alone [is the import]. (52)

body.translated_text: [Whether] in the meaning of 'thou' (<s>tvam</s>) as the essential attribute, or in the peripheral [attribute] ..... (or in the differentiating [attribute] of the meaning of 'that'),
The co-reference of the words 'that' (<s>tat</s>) and 'thou' (<s>tvam</s>) in a [single] attribute is far removed. (Verse 53)

children.translated_text: 'In the meaning of thou' —
thus.
The attribute pertaining to the meaning of 'thou' is ignorance, suffering, and the like.
And the attribute pertaining to the meaning of 'that' is omniscience, being the cause of the universe, and the like.
And that [latter attribute] is accepted by the opponents as a peripheral definition (<s>taṭasthalakṣaṇa</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>.

Since these two attributes differentiate their respective substrata, the identity of the meanings of 'that' and 'thou' is very far removed — like [the identity of] a horse and a donkey. Such is the meaning. (53)

body.translated_text: Whether ignorance, omniscience, suffering, happiness, and the like
Are a qualifying attribute (<s>viśeṣaṇa</s>) of the consciousness-element (<s>ciddhātu</s>), or else an indicatory attribute (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>),
There would be a difference between the meanings of 'thou' and 'that' because of the transference of contradictory qualities. (Verse 54)

nanvajñatvādi sarvajñatvādi copalakṣaṇatayaivocyate, na tu viśeṣaṇatayā /
ubhayopalakṣitaṃ vastvekamevetyarthaḥ /
ato na virodha ityatrāha

children.translated_text: 'Ignorance' —
thus.
'Of the consciousness-element (<s>ciddhātu</s>)' — of the essence of consciousness.

children.text: upalakṣaṇatve 'pi ajñatvādinopalakṣyasya jīvabhāvasya sarvajñatvādinopalakṣyasyeśvarabhāvasya ca vaiyadhikaraṇyādeva tvantadarthayoraikyaṃ na sidhyatītyarthaḥ // 54 //
children.translated_text: Even if [the terms are taken as] indicative references (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>), the identity of the two indicated objects—the state of being a <s>jīva</s> (individual soul), indicated by ignorance and the like, and the state of being <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), indicated by omniscience and the like—is not established, precisely because of the difference of substrata (<s>vaiyadhikaraṇya</s>). This is the meaning. // 54 //

body.translated_text: Objection: Ignorance and the like, and omniscience and the like, are stated only as indicatory attributes (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>), not as qualifying attributes (<s>viśeṣaṇa</s>). The entity indicated by both is one and the same — such is the meaning. Therefore there is no contradiction. To this he says:
By the abandonment of one part of the denoted meaning, the position of consciousness as a single individual entity [is maintained],
the [identity expressed as] 'he is this one' (<s>so'yaṃ</s>) as in the case of a cow—that the meaning of the two words [<s>tat</s> and <s>tvam</s>] [is thus understood]—is inelegant. // 55 //

body.text:
nanu virodhānmukhyārthastyajyate /
cinmātre tu padadvayalakṣaṇopeyate, yathā so 'yaṃ raurityatra tattedantopalakṣite vastumātre lakṣaṇā padadvayasya tatheti śaṅkate

children.translated_text: 'of the denoted meaning'—

children.text:
ti /
vācyaikadeśasya pravṛttinimittabhedasya tyāgena viśeṣyamātre cinmātre padadvayasya vṛttiḥ jahadajahallakṣaṇayeti /
etatpratikṣipati
children.translated_text: By the abandonment of one part of the denoted meaning—that is, the difference in the grounds of application (<s>pravṛttinimitta</s>)—the application of the two words to the mere qualificand (<s>viśeṣya</s>), that is, mere consciousness, is through the secondary meaning that partially retains and partially abandons [the primary meaning] (<s>jahadajahallakṣaṇā</s>). He rejects this [saying:]
'this too is inelegant'—
thus.
'Inelegant' (<s>apeśala</s>) means 'not beautiful.'
The meaning is: when the contradiction can be resolved by the secondary meaning of a single word alone, the postulation of a secondary meaning for both words is not pleasing. // 55 //

body.translated_text: Objection: Since there is contradiction [in the primary meaning], the primary meaning is abandoned. In mere consciousness (<s>cinmātra</s>), the secondary meaning (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) of the two words is arrived at—just as in 'he is this [<s>Devadatta</s>]' (<s>so'yaṃ rauḥ</s>), where the secondary meaning of the two words applies to the mere entity indicated by 'that' and 'this.' He raises this objection [saying:]
Because of the applicability of contradictory pairs to even a single substrate through differences of place, time, and condition,
'he is this cow' (<s>so'yaṃ gauḥ</s>) is appropriate. // 56 //

children.translated_text: 'place, time'—

children.text:
ti /
tattā nāma taddeśakālayogitā /
idantaitaddeśakālayogitā /
tattāviśiṣṭe idantānvayasya bādhe 'pi ekasmin dharmiṇyubhayānvaye na virodhaḥ / deśadvayasaṃbandhaḥ paricchinnasya vastunaḥ kālabhedātparihriyate /
children.translated_text: thus. 'Thatness' (<s>tattā</s>) means the connection with that place and time. 'Thisness' (<s>idantā</s>) means the connection with this place and time. Even when the 'thisness' is contradicted in [something] qualified by 'thatness,' there is no contradiction in the applicability of both to a single substrate. The connection of a delimited entity with two places is resolved through the difference of time.
And the connection with two times is established precisely because of [the entity's] permanence.

children.text: prātipadikābhyāṃ deśadvayakāladvayasaṃbandhasya samānavibhaktyā tadāśrayadravyaikyasya ca pratipādane na virodhaleśo 'pi /
children.translated_text: In expressing the connection with two places and two times through the two nominal stems and the identity of the underlying substance through the same case-ending, there is not even a trace of contradiction.
In this very meaning lies the purport of the sentence 'he is this one' (<s>so'yam</s>).
Therefore, there is no secondary meaning of the two words in the illustrative example. This is the meaning. // 56 //

body.translated_text: He says that in the illustrative example too, there is no secondary meaning for the two words—
In the case of the self-luminous element of consciousness, when there is the conjunction of contradictory pairs,
there is nothing whatsoever in differences of place, time, condition, and so forth [that can serve] as a means of establishing [non-contradiction]. // 57 //

body.text: na tvevaṃ bhavatā vaktuṃ śakyata ityāha

children.translated_text: 'of the self-luminous'—
thus.

children.text: nirviśeṣe cinmātre viruddhadharmadvayasambandhasyāvirodhopapādakaṃ deśakālāvasthābhedādau kiñcidapi na ghaṭate /
children.translated_text: In undifferentiated mere consciousness (<s>nirviśeṣa cinmātra</s>), nothing whatsoever in the differences of place, time, or condition can serve as a means of establishing the non-contradiction of the connection of two contradictory properties.
Because its nature is self-luminous, even ignorance cannot be suspected as a means of establishing non-contradiction in it. This is the purport. // 57 //

body.translated_text: He says that such [a resolution] cannot, however, be stated by you—
In the self-luminous conscious self (<s>cidātman</s>) in which all dualities have been shaken off,
the <s>śāstra</s> (scripture) would be without an object, since there would be no delusion of the misery of duality. // 58 //

body.text: brahmaṇyavidyānvayāyogādevāvidyākṛtabhedadarśananirasanārthatvaṃ śāstrasya nirviśeṣacinmātra brahmātmaikyaviṣayatvaṃ ca parābhimataṃ na saṃbhavītyāha

children.translated_text: 'in which [all dualities] have been shaken off'—

children.text:
ti /
dvandvaśabdo bhedavācyatra /
ajñānenaiva bhedabhramo vaktavyaḥ /
na ca nirviśeṣe svaprakāśe ca tatprasaktiḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. The word 'pair' (<s>dvandva</s>) here means 'difference.' The delusion of difference is to be accounted for by ignorance alone. But its applicability to [something that is] undifferentiated and self-luminous is not [possible].
Since that which is to be negated is not established, the purport of <s>śāstra</s> in the unity-knowledge that is claimed to negate it cannot be maintained.
Therefore, the <s>ādhyātma-śāstra</s> (spiritual scripture) and the great statement (<s>mahāvākya</s>) 'that thou art' (<s>tattvamasi</s>) would become purposeless. This is the meaning.

By this, the [position] that the difference of the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> (internal organ) produced by <s>avidyā</s> alone is the limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) that creates the states of <s>jīva</s> and <s>Īśvara</s> in mere consciousness is also [refuted]—
because of the very impossibility of <s>avidyā</s> therein. This should be understood. // 58 //

body.translated_text: He says that the opponent's position—that the purpose of <s>śāstra</s> is to negate the perception of difference caused by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) in <s>Brahman</s>, and that the <s>śāstra</s> has as its object the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>Ātman</s> as undifferentiated mere consciousness—is not possible—
By this, [the attributes of] having true desires (<s>satyakāmatva</s>), being the cause of the world (<s>jagatkāraṇatā</s>), and the like

body.text: mā ... pare ( māyopādhau pare )'dhyastāḥ śokamohadayaḥ punaḥ // 59 //
body.translated_text: are superimposed on the Supreme through the limiting adjunct of <s>māyā</s>; while grief, delusion, and the like // 59 //
are [superimposed] on the <s>jīva</s> conditioned by the limiting adjunct of <s>avidyā</s>—the view that upon [their] destruction [the distinction] ceases—
this is the view of petty (<s>kṣudra</s>) knowers of <s>Brahman</s>, and has already been refuted previously. // 60 //

body.text: cinmātre brahmaṇyavidyānvayānupapattiparyālocanayā kaiścidadvaitibhiḥ kalpitaṃ māyāvidyopādhibhedaṃ tata eveśeśitavyabhedaṃ cāparamārthamupapādyamānaṃ nirasyati

children.translated_text: 'by this'—

children.text:
ti /
etena-nirdhūtatrividhabhede cinmātre māyāvidyopādhibhedāsiddhyaiva /
māyopādhau-māyopahitacinmātre pare-īśvare /
vināśeneti /
tattvamasivākyajanyaikyasākṣātkāreṇa māyāvidyopādhināśe tatkalpita īśajīvabhāvo 'pi nivṛtto nāvatiṣṭhata ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. 'By this'—by the very non-establishment of the difference of <s>māyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s> as limiting adjuncts when all threefold differences have been shaken off in mere consciousness. 'In the Supreme conditioned by <s>māyā</s>'—in <s>Īśvara</s> as mere consciousness overlaid by <s>māyā</s>. 'By destruction'—the meaning is: upon the destruction of the limiting adjuncts of <s>māyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s> through the direct realization of unity produced by the sentence '<s>tattvamasi</s>' (that thou art), the distinction of Lord and <s>jīva</s> fabricated by those [adjuncts] also ceases and does not remain.
'has already been refuted previously'—

children.text:
iti /
etaddūṣaṇabhāgo viluptaḥ /
aparamārthatvenābhimatayostayoḥ kalpakābhāvādasiddhireva /
svataḥkalpanāyāmātmāśrayaḥ /
brahmaṇa eva tatkalpakatve brahmasvarūpasya nityatvāttayornityatvaprasaktiḥ /
aikyajñānena nivṛttyupagame 'pi tasya kṣaṇikatvādeva punarapi brahmasvarūpabalāttayoḥ kalpanāprasaṅgaḥ /
kiñca māyāyā bhrāntijanakatve duḥkhādijanakatve cāvidyāto vibhāgāsiddhiḥ /
tasyā yathārthabuddhijanakatve krīḍārasamātraparikaratve cāpuruṣārthatvāyogāttannirasanānupapattiḥ /
anādibhāvarūpāyāstasyā jñānamātrato nirasanāyogaścetyādi dūṣaṇamanusandheyam /
avidyāyā eva bahusaṃmatatvānmāyāvidyopādhibhedavādino 'mī kṣudrā brahmavido 'dvaitiṣviti ca bodhyam // 59 //60 //
children.translated_text: thus. This portion of the refutation is lost [from the manuscript]. The non-establishment itself [of the two limiting adjuncts] is due to the absence of a fabricator of those two [adjuncts] that are admitted as unreal. In the case of self-fabrication, there is the fallacy of self-dependence (<s>ātmāśraya</s>). If <s>Brahman</s> itself is the fabricator, then since the nature of <s>Brahman</s> is eternal, there would be the unwanted consequence of the eternity of those two. Even if the cessation [of the limiting adjuncts] is accepted through the knowledge of unity, since that [knowledge] is momentary, there would again be the unwanted consequence of the fabrication of those two by the very nature of <s>Brahman</s>. Furthermore, if <s>māyā</s> produces delusion and suffering, then the distinction from <s>avidyā</s> is not established. If it produces true knowledge and serves merely as a playful accessory, then since there would be no unfitness for human purposes, the negation of it would not be possible. And since it is beginningless and of the nature of a positive entity, the negation of it merely through knowledge is not possible—such refutations should be considered. Since <s>avidyā</s> alone is widely accepted, these proponents of the distinction between <s>māyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s> as limiting adjuncts are 'petty knowers of <s>Brahman</s>' among the <s>Advaitins</s>—this too should be understood. // 59 // 60 //

body.translated_text: He rejects the position fabricated by certain <s>Advaitins</s>—through the consideration of the impossibility of <s>avidyā</s>'s connection with <s>Brahman</s> as mere consciousness—[namely,] the difference of <s>māyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s> as limiting adjuncts, and thereby the difference of Lord and the lorded-over, established as unreal—
Whether the limiting adjuncts of <s>māyā</s>, <s>avidyā</s>, and so forth [are connected] with the essence of consciousness or with [<s>Brahman</s> as] qualified—
in the former case, there is a confusion of all [attributes], due to the non-distinction of the Supreme and the <s>jīva</s>. // 61 //
In the latter case too, likewise; even if consciousness is qualified,
the essence of consciousness is indeed without difference. Through the limiting adjuncts of <s>māyā</s>, <s>avidyā</s>, and so forth,
[it appears] as if differentiated and deluded, and [you consider it] qualified. // 62 //

children.translated_text: 'with the essence of consciousness'—

children.text:
iti /
kiṃ cinmātremāyāvidyādyupādhayaḥ saṃbandhante, uta viśiṣṭe /
niraṃśe cinmātre māyāvidyāsambandhe tatprayuktasvabhāvabhedā ekasminneva prasajyante iti jīveśvarasvabhāvasāṅkaryaprasaṅgaḥ /
viśiṣṭe cet kiṃ tadviśeṣaṇam ? māyāvidyā ceti cedātmāśrayaḥ, jīvatveśvaratve iti cedanyonyāśrayaḥ, anyattu viśeṣaṇaṃ durvacameva /
kiñca māyayāvidyayā vā saṃvitsvarūpasya cchedāsambhavādekameva tattadupahitaṃ bhavedgaganamiva maṭhāntavartighaṭena maṭhena copahitam /
tathā ca hastapādādyavacchinnasukhaduḥkhabhoga ekasyaiva yathā jīvasya, tathā tattadupādhiprayuktaiśvaryaduḥkhādibhoga ekasyaiva brahmaṇaḥ prasajyata iti jīvaparasvabhāvāvyavasthitirevetyarthaḥ // 61 //62 //
children.translated_text: thus. Do the limiting adjuncts of <s>māyā</s>, <s>avidyā</s>, and so forth connect with mere consciousness, or with [consciousness as] qualified? If the connection of <s>māyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s> is with partless mere consciousness, then the differences of nature produced by those would occur in one and the same [entity]—hence the unwanted consequence of a confusion of the natures of <s>jīva</s> and <s>Īśvara</s>. If [they connect] with the qualified, then what is that qualifier? If it be <s>māyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s>, there is the fallacy of self-dependence (<s>ātmāśraya</s>). If it be <s>jīva</s>-hood and <s>Īśvara</s>-hood, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (<s>anyonyāśraya</s>). Any other qualifier is simply impossible to state. Furthermore, since the cutting of the essence of consciousness by <s>māyā</s> or <s>avidyā</s> is impossible, it would be one and the same [consciousness] conditioned by those respective [adjuncts]—like space conditioned by a pot within a chamber and by the chamber itself. And just as the experience of pleasure and pain delimited by hands, feet, and so forth belongs to one and the same <s>jīva</s>, so the experience of lordship, suffering, and so forth produced by those respective limiting adjuncts would belong to one and the same <s>Brahman</s>—thus, the non-establishment of the distinction between the natures of <s>jīva</s> and the Supreme [follows]. This is the meaning. // 61 // 62 //

body.translated_text: It has been stated that the acceptance of the difference of limiting adjuncts is impossible. By [granting] that acceptance, another objection is also stated—

body.text: taṭasthāvasthitā dharmāḥ svarūpaṃ na spṛśanti kim /
body.translated_text: Do not the properties that stand as extraneous (<s>taṭastha</s>) fail to touch the essence?
It is not the case that by cutting the head of the staff-bearer, <s>Devadatta</s> is not harmed. // 63 //

children.translated_text: 'extraneous' (<s>taṭastha</s>)—

children.text:
ti /
māyayāvidyayā vopahitaṃ taṭasthamityucyate brahma /
tanniṣṭhasya sārvajñyāderajñatvādeśca daṇḍena kuṇḍalena vopahite kādācitkadaṇḍādiviśeṣaṇavattayā taṭasthaśabdite devadatte vartamānasya sukhasya duḥkhasya ca devadattātmanīva brahmaṇi sambandho durvāra eveti bhāvaḥ /
tatrānanditvaprasaṅgasya sahyatvātkathañcihuḥkhitvasyāsahyasya prasaṅge nidarśanamāha
children.translated_text: thus. <s>Brahman</s> conditioned by <s>māyā</s> or <s>avidyā</s> is said to be 'extraneous' (<s>taṭastha</s>). The omniscience and the like that belong to that [conditioned <s>Brahman</s>], as well as the ignorance and the like—their connection with <s>Brahman</s> is inescapable, just as the pleasure and suffering present in <s>Devadatta</s> who is designated as 'extraneous' through occasional qualifying attributes like a staff or earrings [belong to <s>Devadatta</s> himself]. This is the purport. Since the consequence of non-bliss is tolerable, he gives an illustration for the intolerable consequence of being somehow a sufferer—
'it is not the case'—
thus.
Even with the difference of limiting adjuncts, the consequence of the co-presence of contradictories is inescapable.
Without a real difference of entities, establishment [of distinct attributes] through a merely fabricated difference of loci is difficult to achieve.
And thus, the fabrication of the difference of <s>māyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s> as limiting adjuncts is established as pointless. // 63 //

body.translated_text: Objection: Since the acceptance of the difference of conditioned loci avoids the confusion of the natures of <s>jīva</s> and <s>Īśvara</s> in <s>Brahman</s>—to this he says:
By the exclusion of the non-conscious portion, the residual singularity of consciousness—
that this is the meaning of '<s>tattvamasi</s>' (that thou art) and the like—is also not beautiful [i.e., unacceptable]. // 64 //

children.translated_text: (Thus, the demonstration of the impossibility in the opponent's position that '<s>tattvamasi</s>' has the purport of the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>Ātman</s>.)

He says that by this, the [position] that the meaning of the '<s>tattvamasi</s>' sentence is the unity of mere consciousness as the qualificand, through the abandonment of the difference of qualifiers in the form of the limiting adjuncts of <s>māyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s>, is also rejected—
'of the non-conscious portion'—
thus.
The secondary meaning of the two words, and the falling into defects in <s>Brahman</s> [alone]—this much has been stated. // 64 //

body.translated_text: In the absence of [anything] non-<s>Brahman</s> and non-self, the inner consciousness remains.
The two words '<s>tat</s>' (that) and '<s>tvam</s>' (thou) have as their scope the identity of <s>jīva</s> and the Supreme.
That identity, [even understood as] primary meaning, is also dependent on two real entities. // 65 //

children.translated_text: 'in the absence of non-<s>Brahman</s>'—

children.text:
ti /
brahmabhinnasyānātmatve tattvaṃpadadvayalakṣyārtha eka pratyaktatvaṃ cinmātramava śiṣyate /
tatra ca samānādhikaraṇavākyārthasya tādātmyasyanupapattirityarthaḥ /
atrottarārdhaṃ viluptamityūhyate /
tacca
children.translated_text: thus. When what is other than <s>Brahman</s> is non-self, the one remaining thing—inner consciousness, mere consciousness—is the object indicated by the secondary meaning of the two words '<s>tat</s>' and '<s>tvam</s>.' And in that [single entity], the impossibility of <s>tādātmya</s> (identity), which is the meaning of the co-referential sentence, [follows]. This is the meaning. Here, the latter half [of the verse] is surmised to be lost [from the manuscript]. And that would be:

children.text: ekaśeṣe tu tādātmyaṃ cinmātre naiva sambhavet
children.translated_text: 'In the case of a single remainder, <s>tādātmya</s> (identity) would simply not be possible in mere consciousness'—
this would be [the reading]. He elaborates the very impossibility of <s>tādātmya</s> when only a single [entity] remains—
'<s>tat tvam</s>' (that [and] thou)—

children.text:
iti /
samānādhikaraṇamiti śeṣaḥ /
tasya mukhyavṛttiryatra tat tanmukhyavṛtti /
children.translated_text: thus. 'Co-referential' should be supplied. That in which its primary meaning [applies] is 'that which has primary meaning' (<s>tanmukhyavṛtti</s>).
'dependent on two entities'—

children.text:
iti /
bhedasamānādhikaraṇābhedasya tādātmyasyātyantāyābhede 'sambhava iti bhāvaḥ /
atra yādavaprakāśaprakriyayā bhāṭṭaprakriyayā vā nirūpyate tādātmyamiti bodhyam /
siddhānte tu
children.translated_text: thus. <s>Tādātmya</s> (identity), which is [a relation] of non-difference co-referential with difference, is impossible in absolute non-difference. This is the purport. Here it should be understood that <s>tādātmya</s> is analyzed either according to the method of <s>Yādavaprakāśa</s> or the method of the <s>Bhāṭṭas</s>. But in the established doctrine [of <s>Viśiṣṭādvaita</s>],
'dependent on two entities'—
the meaning of this is: dependent on a single entity possessing a difference of properties that are the grounds of application (<s>pravṛttinimitta</s>).

children.text: dharmadvārakabhedaviśiṣṭasvarūpābheda eva ca tādātmyaṃ matamiti vivekaḥ // 65 //
children.translated_text: And <s>tādātmya</s> (identity) is held [in our doctrine] to be precisely the non-difference of essence that is qualified by a difference through the gateway of properties. This is the distinction. // 65 //

body.translated_text: Now he establishes the impossibility even of <s>tādātmya</s> (identity)—which is the meaning of co-referential predication (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>)—in the opponent's position—
But as for the alternative of difference-and-non-difference (<s>bhedābheda</s>) that has been raised by you—
when the relation is unreal—in the case of entities that are [both] non-different and different—it is meaningless. // 66 //

body.text:
nanu bhedābhedastādātmyamiti na saṃbhavati /
bhedābhedayorabhede 'tyantabhede 'pi bhedābhedasyāsiddheḥ /
bhedābhede vā tatrāpi tathetyanavastheti cettatrāha

children.translated_text: 'difference-and-non-difference'—

children.text:
ti /
ayaṃ vikalpanaprakāro nopalabhyamānagranthabhāge 'sti /
tadbhāgo viluptaḥ syādvā /
bhinnayostādātmyamutābhinnayoḥ /
ādye ghaṭaḥ paṭa iti prasajyate /
antye ghaṭo ghaṭa itīti vā bhedābhedavikalpo bodhyaḥ /
abhedābhedinaḥ-bhedābhedibhinnasya, atyantabhinnasyātyantābhinnasya vā bandhe - tādātmyasambandhe asati-aprāmāṇike sati bhavatkṛto 'yaṃ vikalpo 'pārtha ityarthaḥ /
na hi ghaṭo ghaṭa iti vā ghaṭaḥ paṭa iti vā sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ dṛṣṭam /
kintu nīlo ghaṭa ityeva /
children.translated_text: thus. This mode of argumentation does not exist in the available portion of the text. That portion may be lost. [The alternative is:] Is the <s>tādātmya</s> of [entities that are] different, or of [entities that are] non-different? In the first case, the consequence is 'a pot is a cloth.' In the second, 'a pot is a pot'—thus should the alternative of difference-and-non-difference be understood. 'Of one that is [both] non-different and different'—of one that is other than [the entity characterized by] difference-and-non-difference, [that is,] of one that is absolutely different or absolutely non-different—when the relation, that is, the <s>tādātmya</s> connection, is 'unreal'—that is, not established by a means of valid knowledge—the alternative made by you is meaningless. This is the meaning. For neither co-referentiality in the form 'a pot is a pot' nor 'a pot is a cloth' is observed. Rather, [it is seen only as] 'the blue pot.'
Therefore, <s>tādātmya</s> (identity) should be sought precisely in difference-and-non-difference.
The difference between difference and non-difference is simply difference [itself].

children.text: na ca bhede tayorvirodhādekatra samāveśo na ghaṭata iti vācyam , nīlaghaṭayoḥ pratītatvādeva tayorvirodhābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: Nor should it be said that since there is contradiction between the two, their co-presence in one [entity] is not possible—for from the very fact that blue and pot are cognized together, their non-contradiction [is established].

children.text: dharmato bhedaḥ svarūpato 'bheda iti vāvirodha iti bhāvaḥ // 66 //
children.translated_text: Difference in respect of properties (<s>dharma</s>) and non-difference in respect of essence (<s>svarūpa</s>)—thus there is no contradiction. This is the purport. // 66 //

body.translated_text: Objection: Difference-and-non-difference cannot be <s>tādātmya</s> (identity). For if difference and non-difference are themselves non-different, or if [they are] absolutely different, difference-and-non-difference is not established. Or if [there is] difference-and-non-difference in that too, then [there is] infinite regress. To this he says:
Non-difference, however, destroys the difference of the entities that are its substrates.
Difference is the mutual non-selfhood of entities. Thus of these two, // 67 //
Having accepted the very natures [of difference and non-difference],

children.translated_text: 'non-difference'—

children.text:
iti ślokadvayena /
bhedamardītiiti kvacitpāṭhaḥ /
tatra itiśabdasya evamityanenānvayaḥ ityevamiti /
bhedamardī-atyantabhedanirāsakaḥ /
etayoḥ-bhedābhedayoḥ svarūpaṃ svarūpabhedamupagamyaiva bhedo 'bhedo veti vikalpakoṭyorbādhanaṃ dūṣaṇaṃ kriyate /
tenasvābhyugamena, vāgbādhā-bhavaduktadūṣaṇavacanoparodhaḥ /
prasajyata iti śeṣaḥ /
tvaṃ ca svābhyupagamaviruddhavacanatvena nigṛhyasa ityarthaḥ // 67 //68 //
children.translated_text: —thus in two verses. 'The crusher of difference' (<s>bhedamardī</s>)—this is found in some readings. There, the word '<s>iti</s>' is construed with '<s>evam</s>' (thus). 'The crusher of difference'—one who completely negates difference. Of these two—difference and non-difference—the refutation is made by accepting their essential nature: [the question is] whether there is difference of essential nature or non-difference, and [the opponent's] own position is refuted in both alternatives. 'By his own admission'—'a contradiction of your own stated refutation'—this is to be supplied. 'It follows'—is to be added. And you are defeated by reason of making statements contradicting your own position—this is the meaning. // 67-68 //

body.translated_text: he who postulates difference-and-non-difference between them [i.e., between difference and non-difference themselves] also [incurs] self-contradiction—thus he says:
The conceptual construction regarding the difference and non-difference, the relation, and the existence and non-existence [of these]—
is refuted by perceptual experience and amounts to nothing but a drying of the throat. // 69 //

children.translated_text: 'Difference and non-difference'
—thus.
Does the [relation of] difference-cum-non-difference have a connection with the substratum (<s>dharmin</s>) or not?
In the first case, for that connection too, yet another connection must be stated.
And for that too, likewise—hence an infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>).

children.text: antye asambaddhasya viśiṣṭabuddhinirvāhakatvaṃ tasya na syāditi vikalpanamapi kaṇṭhaśoṣaṇamātraphalakaṃ pratyakṣānubhavabādhitaṃ cetyarthaḥ // 69 //
children.translated_text: In the latter case—since something unconnected cannot give rise to a qualified cognition—the conceptual construction [about its existence and non-existence] too yields nothing but the drying of the throat and is contradicted by perceptual experience—this is the meaning. // 69 //

body.translated_text: The cognition 'blue' with respect to a blue [thing]—the very same cognition 'blue' arises in a blue lotus;
'This is a blue lotus'—thus it shines directly for us. // 70 //

children.translated_text: 'Blue'
—thus.

children.text: nīlarūpavati ghaṭādau nīlabuddhiryathā nīlasamavāyāvagāhinī viditā nāpalapyā, evaṃ nīlamutpalamiti viditāprasiddhā nīlatādātmyamatirapi nāpalapyā /
children.translated_text: Just as in a pot and so forth possessing the form of blue, the cognition 'blue,' which apprehends the inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) of blue, is well-known and not to be denied; so too the cognition of identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) [expressed as] 'a blue lotus' is well-known and established and not to be denied.

The infinite regress is to be avoided either by [accepting] a self-sustaining and other-sustaining <s>samādhi</s> [i.e., a self-sufficient relation] or by an intrinsic relation (<s>svarūpasambandha</s>)—this is the purport. // 70 //

body.translated_text: Just as, even when the contact-relation (<s>saṃyoga</s>) is well-known, within the domain of perception,
there is the delusion of imposing conceptual constructions such as 'Is there difference or non-difference [between them]?' // 71 //
Likewise, regarding the identity-relation (<s>tādātmya</s>), which is grounded in <s>śruti</s> and perception,
the delusion of such fallacious reasoning is warded off by the rod of <s>śruti</s>. // 72 //

children.translated_text: 'Just as'

children.text:
ti /
saṃyoge bhedābhedāditustarko yathā-bhinnayoḥ saṃyoga utābhinnayoḥ /
ādye himavadvindhyayorapi saṃyogaprasaṅgaḥ /
antye svenaiva svasya saḥ /
saṃyogo dharmiṇo bhinno na vā /
bhede tasyāpi sambandhāntaraṃ tasyāpi tathetyanavasthā /
abhede saṃyoga eva na sidhyatītyādiḥ /
sphuṭapratipanne saṃyoge dustarkatanmūlavikalpanādi yathā bhramalakṣaṇaṃ kaṇṭhaśoṣaṇamātram , pratyakṣaparāhataṃ ca ; evaṃ nīlotpalāditādātmye pratyakṣe jīvabrahmatādātmye ca śāstrasiddhe dustarkavikalpanādi pratyakṣaśāstradaṇḍanivāritamiti bhāvaḥ /
śrutidaṇḍeneti prakṛtatattvamasivākyārthābhiprāyeṇoktam // 71 //72 //
children.translated_text: —thus. The fallacious reasoning regarding contact [is as follows]: Is contact [a relation] between different things or between non-different things? In the first case, there would be the absurd consequence of contact between the <s>Himālaya</s> and <s>Vindhya</s> [mountains, which are different but not in contact]. In the latter case, it would be contact of a thing with itself. Is contact different from the substratum or not? If different, then for that [connection] too, another relation [is needed], and for that too likewise—hence infinite regress. If non-different, then contact itself is not established—and so forth. Just as in the case of clearly perceived contact, fallacious reasoning and the conceptual constructions based on it are mere delusion, a mere drying of the throat, and are contradicted by perception; so too, regarding the identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) [perceived in] 'blue lotus' and the like, and regarding the identity of the individual self (<s>jīva</s>) and <s>Brahman</s> established by scripture—fallacious conceptual constructions are warded off by the rod of perception and scripture—this is the purport. The phrase 'by the rod of <s>śruti</s>' is said with reference to the meaning of the '<s>tattvamasi</s>' ('That thou art') statement presently under discussion. // 71-72 //

body.translated_text: He elaborates that the fallacious reasonings advanced by those hostile to the identity-relation are defeated by perception and authoritative scripture:
The <s>śruti</s>, which is indicative [of reality] and authorless (<s>apauruṣeya</s>), with great emphasis,
has repeatedly declared the identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) of <s>Brahman</s> and the individual self (<s>jīva</s>), saying '<s>tattvam</s>' ('That thou art'). // 73 //

children.translated_text: 'Indicative'
—thus.

children.text: pravṛttinimittarūpadharmabhedena dharmisvarūpābhedena ca tādātmyaṃ tattvamasītyādau tvamādiśabdānāṃ tattaccharīrakabrahmaparyantatayā nirūpaṇīyam , tadādipadānāṃ brahmātmakaparatayā vā /
children.translated_text: The identity [expressed] in '<s>tattvamasi</s>' ('That thou art') and the like is to be determined through the difference of attributes (<s>dharma</s>) that serve as the grounds of designation, and through the non-difference of the essential nature of the substratum (<s>dharmin</s>)—[such that] the words '<s>tvam</s>' ('thou') and the like are to be construed as ultimately referring to <s>Brahman</s> as the inner self (<s>śarīraka</s>) of the respective [entities]; or, the words '<s>tat</s>' ('that') and the like are to be construed as having <s>Brahman</s> as their ultimate referent.
But in the view of <s>Yādavaprakāśa</s>, the distinction is that both difference and non-difference pertain to the very essential natures of <s>jīva</s> and <s>Brahman</s>. // 73 //

body.translated_text: He states that there is also the indicative mark of import (<s>tātparyaliṅga</s>) in the form of repetition (<s>abhyāsa</s>) for the identity of the individual self and the Supreme:
The liberated self (<s>muktātman</s>), immersed in the lake of <s>Brahman</s>'s bliss, thrives in happiness.
And since at the stage of the fruit there would be no [surviving] enjoyer of the fruit, liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) would not serve human purposes (<s>puruṣārtha</s>).

body.text: ekaśeṣe hi ciddhātoḥ kasya mokṣaḥ phalaṃ bhavet // 74 //
body.translated_text: For if only bare consciousness (<s>cit</s>) remains, whose liberation would the fruit be? // 74 //

children.translated_text: (Thus the description of the impossibility of the meaning of co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) in the opponent's view.)

children.text:
etāvatā paramate prātipadikayoriva samānavibhakterapi na mukhyārthateti vyavasthāpitam /
yadyapi abhedamātrasya samānavibhaktyarthatvaṃ sambhavati /
tathāpi pravṛttinimittadharmabhedaprahāṇānna sāmānādhikaraṇyamukhyārthatā paramata iti bodhyam /
atha cinmātrapariśeṣe 'pi na yuktaḥ /
tathā sati mokṣasyāpuruṣārthatāprasakterityāha
children.translated_text: By this much, it has been established that, in the opponent's view, even when there is the same case-ending (as between two co-referential terms), there is no primary meaning—just as between two crude word-stems (<s>prātipadika</s>). Although mere non-difference can be the meaning of the same case-ending, nevertheless, since the difference of attributes serving as grounds of designation is not abandoned, co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) does not yield its primary meaning in the opponent's view—this should be understood. Now, even in the residual [view of] bare consciousness, it is not tenable, because there would be the absurd consequence that liberation would not serve human purposes. He says:
'<s>Brahman</s>'s [bliss]'
—thus.

children.text: eṣa brahma praviṣṭo 'smi grīṣme śītamiva hradam
children.translated_text: 'I have entered <s>Brahman</s>, as [one enters] a cool lake in summer'

children.text:
itivacanānusāreṇa brahmānandasya hradatvarūpaṇam , sakalasaṃsāratāpakleśaharatvānniratiśayāhlādakaratvācca tasya /
brahmānandaṃ hṛdantaḥstha
children.translated_text: —in accordance with this statement, the bliss of <s>Brahman</s> is described as a lake, because it removes the affliction and heat of all <s>saṃsāra</s> and because it causes unsurpassed delight. 'The bliss of <s>Brahman</s> [dwelling] within the heart'

children.text:
iti pūrvamudritapāṭhastu na samīcīnaḥ /
muktātmāparicchinnabrahmānandasāgare nimagno nityapravṛddhasukho varīvartitarāmiti śāstramaryādā /
paramaphale mokṣe bhoktṛtvāvasthāpannasya svasya vilayaṃ cejjānīyānnābhilaṣyettāmityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: —this previously printed reading is not correct. The standard of scripture is that the liberated self, immersed in the limitless ocean of <s>Brahman</s>'s bliss, revels supremely in ever-increasing happiness. If, upon [attaining] the supreme fruit of liberation, one were to know that one's own self—which has arrived at the state of being an enjoyer—is annihilated, one would not desire that [liberation]—this is the meaning.

children.text: ekaśeṣe-nirviśeṣacinmā trapariśeṣe, kasya-brahmaṇo jīvasya vā mokṣaḥ phalam ? na brahmaṇaḥ, nityamuktatvāt , nāpi jīvasya, tasyaiva tadā vilayāditi bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'If only [consciousness] remains'—if only qualityless, bare consciousness remains: whose—<s>Brahman</s>'s or the <s>jīva</s>'s—would liberation be a fruit? Not <s>Brahman</s>'s, because It is eternally liberated. Nor the <s>jīva</s>'s, because the <s>jīva</s> itself would be dissolved at that point—this is the purport.

children.text: cinmātrameva brahma jīvasya svarūpamiti cettarhi brahmaṇa evāvidyājīvabhāvādi vaktavyam /
children.translated_text: If one objects that bare consciousness alone is <s>Brahman</s> and is also the essential nature of the <s>jīva</s>, then ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), the status of being a <s>jīva</s>, and so forth must be predicated of <s>Brahman</s> itself.
And that is contradicted by <s>śruti</s> and reasoning—this should be reflected upon.

Thus the collection of refutations has been stated against [the view that] the meaning of '<s>tattvamasi</s>' is the identity of qualityless bare consciousness, arrived at by abandoning the conceptual alternatives of <s>jīva</s>-hood, lordship, and so forth, imagined by ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). // 74 //

body.translated_text: Furthermore, what consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>) transforms into the form of the manifold world?
To begin with, it is not the cognition of a pot, since the world is seen even when that [cognition] is absent. // 75 //

body.text: na hi tasyāmajātāyāṃ naṣṭāyāṃ vākhilaṃ jagat /
body.translated_text: For when that [pot-cognition] has not arisen or has perished, it cannot be said that the entire universe
does not exist, because there would be contradiction with perception in the state of liberation.
Nor is it some other consciousness, because other [things] are perceived even when that [consciousness] is destroyed. // 76 //

children.translated_text: 'Furthermore'

children.text:
tyādinā /
vivartate ayathākāreṇa bhāsate /
darśanāt - bhedaprapañcasya dṛṣṭeḥ /
adhiṣṭhānamantarā'ropyapratītyayogānna ghaṭapaṭādidhiyāmāgamāpāyinīnāṃ prapañcabhramādhiṣṭhānatvaṃ sambhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
jagat - bhedaprapañcaḥ /
tadbhānamiti yāvat /
children.translated_text: —and so forth. 'Transforms' (<s>vivartate</s>)—appears in a form other than its own. 'Since it is seen'—since the differentiated manifold is perceived. Without a substratum, the arising of a superimposed cognition is not possible; therefore, the cognitions of pots, cloths, and the like, which come and go, cannot serve as the substratum of the illusion of the manifold—this is the purport. 'The world'—the differentiated manifold. That is to say, its appearance.
'Nor'

children.text:
ti /
paṭajñānanāśe 'pi anyeṣāṃ ghaṭādibhedānāmupalambhānna paṭajñānāderapi prapañcādhyāsādhiṣṭhānatvaṃ saṃbhavatītyarthaḥ /
saṃvideva prapañcabhramādhiṣṭhānamiti pareṣāṃ matam /
tatra ghaṭapaṭādisaṃvidāṃ nādhiṣṭhānatvaṃ sambhavatītyuktaṃ bhavati // 75 //76 //
children.translated_text: —thus. Even when the cognition of a cloth perishes, since other [objects] such as pots and so forth are perceived, the cognition of a cloth and the like cannot serve as the substratum of the superimposition of the manifold—this is the meaning. The opponents hold that consciousness itself is the substratum of the illusion of the manifold. Against this, it has been stated that the particular cognitions of pots, cloths, and so forth cannot serve as the substratum. // 75-76 //

body.translated_text: Now, by examining the essential nature of the substratum of the illusion of the manifold and its cause, he brings out the inconsistency in the opponent's view as well:
But [the opponent says:] 'Consciousness is one and undifferentiated—there is no cognition of difference in it;

body.text: ghaṭādayo hi bhidyante na tu sā cit prakāśanāt // 77 //
body.translated_text: for pots and the like are differentiated, but that consciousness is not, because it illuminates [everything].' // 77 //
If [the objection is:] 'The cognition of a pot does not shine at the time of the cognition of a cloth'—

body.text: naivaṃ, ghaṭo hi nābhāti sā sphuratyeva tu sphuṭam // 78 //
body.translated_text: no, it is not so; for the pot does not shine [at that time], but that [consciousness] indeed shines clearly. // 78 //
If [the objection is:] 'But the consciousness delimited by the pot does not shine [at that time]'—
then by the term 'delimited by that [pot],' is it that very [consciousness] that is referred to, or something else?
If it is that very [consciousness], it does shine. If it is something else—we do not assert its shining. // 79 //

children.translated_text: 'But'

children.text:
iti /
akhaṇḍā saṃvidekā nityāvibhvī ca /
ghaṭādīnāmevānyajñāneṣvabhāsamānānāṃ bhedaḥ /
saṃvidastu sarvajñāneṣu prakāśamānatvādekatvameva /
tasyāṃ bhedabuddhistvaupādhikaviṣayā na yathārthasaṃvitsvarūpabhedaviṣayā /
saiva prapañcabhramādhiṣṭhānaṃ bhavati /
ghaṭabuddhiḥ paṭajñānakāle na bhāsate, kintu paṭadhīreveti cet , maivam /
tadā ghaṭa eva na bhāsate /
jñānaṃ tu bhāsata eva /
nanu ghaṭaviṣayakatvaviśiṣṭasaṃvidaḥ paṭajñāne 'bhānamiti cet , maivam /
ghaṭaviṣayakatvarūpaṃ ghaṭavyāvṛttattvamapi saṃvitsvarūpameva /
ataḥ paṭajñāne tasya bhānameva /
ghaṭaḥ paraṃ na bhāsate /
tasyātiriktatve tu paṭajñāne tadabhāne 'pi saṃvidobhānamakṣatameveti samuditāśayaḥ // 77 //78 //79 //
children.translated_text: —thus. Consciousness is partless, one, eternal, and all-pervading. It is only pots and the like—which do not appear in other cognitions—that are differentiated. But consciousness, because it shines in all cognitions, has unity alone. The cognition of difference in it is directed at adventitious limiting conditions (<s>upādhi</s>), not at a real difference in the nature of consciousness itself. That very [consciousness] can serve as the substratum of the illusion of the manifold. [If the objection is:] 'The cognition of a pot does not shine at the time of the cognition of a cloth; rather, only the cognition of a cloth [shines]'—no, it is not so. At that time, the pot itself does not shine; but knowledge (consciousness) indeed shines. [If the objection continues:] 'But the consciousness qualified as having the pot as its object does not appear in the cognition of a cloth'—no, it is not so. The nature of being delimited by the pot—the very nature of being distinct from the pot—is itself the nature of consciousness. Therefore, it does shine in the cognition of a cloth. Only the pot does not shine. But if [the pot-delimitation is] something additional [to consciousness], then even when it does not appear in the cognition of a cloth, the shining of consciousness remains unimpaired—this is the combined purport. // 77-79 //

body.translated_text: Here is the opponent's objection:

body.text: kiñcāsyāḥ svaprakāśāyā nīrūpāyā na hi svataḥ /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, for this [consciousness] which is self-luminous (<s>svaprakāśa</s>) and formless (<s>nīrūpa</s>), not by itself,
apart from the diversity of objects, is there the delusion of apprehending diversity [in it]. // 80 //

body.text: nanu saṃvidibhedābhāve ghaṭajñānamidaṃ, paṭajñānaṃ tat , ekamutpannamaparaṃ vinaṣṭamityādyanupapannaṃ bhavedityatrāha

children.translated_text: 'Furthermore'
—thus. 'Formless' (<s>nīrūpā</s>)—without form, without qualification, that is to say. 'The delusion of apprehending diversity'—the delusion of being qualified by an unreal form of diversity.
'Self-luminous' (<s>svaprakāśa</s>)—this contains the reason [for the argument].

children.text: saṃvinna nānā svaprakāśatvāt , yannānā tadasvaprakāśaṃ yathā ghaṭādīti /
children.translated_text: Consciousness is not diverse, because it is self-luminous; whatever is diverse is not self-luminous, like a pot and the like.
Even the perception of diversity in consciousness is merely a delusion conditioned by the difference of objects.
But there is no real difference in it—this is the purport. // 80 //

body.translated_text: But if there is no difference in consciousness, then [the distinctions like] 'this is the cognition of a pot,' 'that is the cognition of a cloth,' 'one has arisen, another has perished'—all these would be untenable. To this he says:

body.text: na vastu vastudharmo vā na pratyakṣo na laiṅgikaḥ /
body.translated_text: It is not a substance, not a property of a substance, not perceived, not inferred—
even the difference of knowable objects such as pots is merely of the nature of delusion. // 81 //

body.text:
nanūpādhibhedenaiva bhedo 'pi tatra vāstavo bhavet /
sāṃsargikasya dharmasya tatra tatrodayadarśanādityatrāha

children.translated_text: 'Not'

children.text:
ti /
viṣayabhedasyaivāvāstavikatvāttatprayuktaṃ saṃvinnānātvamapyavāstavikameveti bhāvaḥ /
bhedasya cāvāstavikatvaṃ durnirūpatvāt /
tathāhi-bhedo na tāvadvastusvarūpam /
pratiyogigrahāpekṣagrahasya bhedasya tadanapekṣagrahasvarūpatvāyogāt /
nāpi vastudharmo 'yam /
bhedasya dharmibhedo dharmāntaram /
tasyāpi svadharmibhedo dharmāntaram , evamuparyapi /
evaṃ ghaṭasya paṭabhedo dharmaḥ, paṭabhedabhedo 'pi tathā, evaṃ tadbhedo 'pīti cānavasthāprasakteḥ /
evaṃ svarūpato durnirūpasya pramāṇato 'pi durnirūpatvam /
yathā-pratyakṣaṃ tāvanna bhedagrāhi, kṣaṇikasya tasya svarūpapratiyogigrahaṇapūrvakabhedagrahaṇaparyantāvasthānābhāvādviramya vyāpārāyogācca /
yugapadeva tritayaṃ gṛhṇāti cet , samūhālambanavadupaśleṣaviśeṣāsiddhiḥ /
pratyakṣeṇa bhedagrahaṇābhāvādeva tanmūlāvinābhāvagrahādhīnodayamanumānamapi na bhede pramāṇaṃ bhavediti hṛdayam /
nanu tarhi bhedagrahaḥ katham ? tatrāha
children.translated_text: —thus. Since the difference of objects itself is unreal, the diversity of consciousness caused by it is also unreal—this is the purport. And the unreality of difference is because it is difficult to determine [its nature]. For: First, difference is not the essential nature of a substance, because difference, whose apprehension depends on the apprehension of its counter-correlate (<s>pratiyogin</s>), cannot have the nature of that which is apprehended without dependence [on anything else]. Nor is it a property of a substance. For the [pot's] difference from the cloth is a property; [but then] the difference of that [property] from its substratum is another property; and the difference of that too is yet another—and thus the absurd consequence of infinite regress. Thus: the pot's difference from the cloth is a property; the difference of that difference is likewise; the difference of that too—and so on infinitely. Thus, what is difficult to determine by its essential nature is also difficult to determine by valid means of knowledge. Namely: perception does not apprehend difference, because the momentary [perception] cannot persist long enough to first apprehend the essential nature and the counter-correlate and then apprehend the difference [between them], and because, having ceased, it cannot resume its function. If [it is claimed that perception] apprehends all three simultaneously, then [the response is:] as with a collective apprehension (<s>samūhālambana</s>), the specific relation of contact (<s>upaśleṣa</s>) is not established. Since perception does not apprehend difference, inference too—whose arising depends on the apprehension of invariable concomitance, which itself is based on [perception]—cannot serve as a valid means of knowledge for difference. This is the essential point. But then how is difference apprehended? To that he says:
'Merely of the nature of delusion'

body.translated_text: But [the objection is:] 'Even through the difference of limiting conditions, the difference in it [consciousness] would be real, since the arising of a relational property (<s>sāṃsargikadharma</s>) is seen here and there.' To this he says:
Since [this is so], the arising of the apprehension of difference in cognition is dependent on that [delusion];
how then could there be any possibility of its being ultimately real? // 82 //

children.translated_text: 'Since'
—thus. The claim that diversity in consciousness is intrinsic is far removed [from reality].
Even the diversity conditioned by limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>) does not [truly] exist,
because of the absence of [real] difference in the limiting adjuncts themselves.

Rather, [diversity in consciousness is] merely a delusion dependent on the difference of non-ultimate limiting adjuncts rooted in the defect of beginningless ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>)—this is the meaning.
Thus it has been stated that the cognition of difference in knowledge based on the difference of objects is not in accordance with reality. // 82 //

body.text: kiñca svayaṃprakāśasya svato vā parato 'pi vā /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, of that which is self-luminous (<s>svayaṃprakāśa</s>), could prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) and so forth be established either by itself or by another?
By itself, to begin with, it is not tenable. // 83 //
Because, when it [consciousness] exists, the non-existence would be contradicted by [its very] existence;
Because that which illuminates its own cause could not [exist] even when it itself is absent;
And because consciousness, being of no other object [than itself], is not [established] by another either. // 84 //

children.translated_text: 'Moreover' (<s>kiñca</s>)

children.text:
ti /
saṃvidaḥ prāgabhāvaḥ pradhvaṃsābhāvo vā kiṃ tayaiva gṛhyate ? uta saṃvidantareṇeti vikalpya prathamaṃ kalpa pratikṣipati
children.translated_text:
—thus.
Is the prior non-existence or the posterior non-existence of cognition (<s>saṃvid</s>) apprehended by that very cognition itself? Or by another cognition?—Posing this dilemma, he first rejects the first alternative:
'By itself' (<s>svataḥ</s>)

children.text:
iti /
svena satā svābhāvo gṛhyata ? utāsatā ? ādyandūṣayati
children.translated_text:
—thus.
Is its own non-existence apprehended by itself as existent? Or as non-existent? He refutes the first:
'In itself' (<s>svasmin</s>)

—thus.
He refutes the latter:
'Its own ground being absent' (<s>svanimitte</s>)

children.text:
ti /
svādhīnasya prakāśasya svasya grāhakasyābhāve 'sambhavādityarthaḥ /
parata iti kalpaṃ dūṣayati
children.translated_text:
—thus.
Because it is impossible when there is an absence of its own apprehender, i.e., of the illumination dependent on itself—this is the meaning.
He refutes the alternative 'by another' (<s>parataḥ</s>):
'Non-different' (<s>ananye</s>)

children.text:
ti /
pratiyoginamullikhya hyabhāvo grāhyaḥ /
jñānasya jñānāntaragocaratvābhāvānna jñānāntareṇāpi tatprāgabhāvagrahaṇaṃ sambhavatītyarthaḥ /
saṃvinnānātvopagame 'pi na tatprāgabhāvagrahasambhava ityabhyupagamya vādaḥ kṛtaḥ /
natvadvaitināmabhimataṃ vastutaḥ tannānātvamiti bodhyam // 83 //84 //
children.translated_text:
—thus.
For a non-existence must be apprehended with reference to its counter-positive (<s>pratiyogin</s>).
Since cognition does not come within the scope of another cognition, the apprehension of its prior non-existence by another cognition is also not possible—this is the meaning.
Even granting the plurality of cognitions (<s>saṃvit</s>), the impossibility of apprehending its prior non-existence has been argued by way of concession.
But it should be understood that in reality, the non-dualists do not accept the plurality of cognition. // 83 // 84 //

body.translated_text: Now, to demonstrate that even the cognition of difference based on origination and the like is not veridical regarding it, he states the impossibility of origination and the like:
Moreover, since what is cognized is different [from cognition], there can be no possibility of it being a property of consciousness,
Like form and the like; therefore, consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>) is non-dual, self-luminous. // 85 //

children.translated_text: 'Moreover' (<s>kiñca</s>)

children.text:
ti /
bhedo na cito vedyatvādrūpādivadityanumānamatra vivakṣitam /
children.translated_text:
—thus.
The inference intended here is: Difference is not a property of consciousness, because it is cognizable, like form and the like.
'Therefore' (<s>ataḥ</s>)
—thus.

Since difference is difficult to establish and cannot be a property of consciousness, consciousness is devoid of all difference—whether of the same class (<s>sajātīya</s>), of a different class (<s>vijātīya</s>), or internal (<s>svagata</s>); and since it is self-luminous, it is distinguished from the void (<s>tuccha</s>)—such is the purport. // 85 //

body.translated_text: He states the proof for the absence of plurality in consciousness:
Therefore, whatever conceptualization and idle talk has been [made] resorting to difference in that [consciousness],
This is a sport of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)—so the knowers of <s>Brahman</s> know. // 86 //

children.translated_text: (Thus the recapitulation of the opponent's establishment of the unity of consciousness.)
'Therefore' (<s>ataḥ</s>)
—thus.

children.text: yato nirbhedatvaṃ saṃvidaḥ, ataḥ kiṃ ghaṭasaṃvidadhiṣṭhānamāhosvitpaṭa- saṃvidityādivikalpajalpanaṃ yat , so 'yaṃ saṃvidbhedāvalambī vikalpādivādaḥ saṃvitsvarūpayāthātmyājñānakārya ityadvaitino manyanta ityarthaḥ // 86 //
children.translated_text: Since consciousness is without difference, whatever conceptual talk such as 'Is this the cognition of a pot, or the cognition of a cloth?' and so forth, which depends on differences in consciousness—this discourse of conceptualization and the like, which relies on differentiation of consciousness, is the product of ignorance of the true nature of consciousness—so the Advaitins hold. This is the meaning. // 86 //

body.translated_text: Alas! This teaching about <s>Brahman</s> looks well among the faithful;
We are unfaithful, we who demand reasoning. // 87 //

children.translated_text: 'Alas!' (<s>hanta</s>)
—thus.
'Alas' expresses distress at the opponents' delusion.

children.text: śraddhāmātraśaraṇeṣu vineyabuddhiṣu nirūpaṇāsamartheṣu bhavadabhimato 'yaṃ brahmopadeśaḥ śobhate nāma /
children.translated_text: This teaching of <s>Brahman</s> of yours may look well among the faithful, who are of obedient intellect, who take refuge in faith alone, and who are incapable of critical examination;

children.text: yuktivimarśakā vayaṃ tu nātra bhavadīye brahmopadeśe śraddhālavaḥ /
children.translated_text: But we, who are investigators through reasoning, are not faithful regarding this teaching of <s>Brahman</s> of yours.

children.text: ato 'smān rañjayituṃ satpramāṇatarkā evopādeyāḥ, na tu śuṣkopadeśā iti bhāvaḥ // 87 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, to convince us, valid proofs and reasoning alone should be employed, not dry teachings—such is the purport. // 87 //

body.translated_text: He commences to refute the recapitulated opponent's view:
Pertaining to each individual knower, mutually distinct,
Cognitions shine directly, like pleasure and pain. // 88 //

children.translated_text: 'Pertaining to each knower' (<s>pratipramātṛ</s>)
—thus.

children.text: puruṣabhedena, ekasminnapi puruṣe viṣayabhedena, ekasminneva viṣaye kālabhedena karaṇabhedena ca dhiyo nānā pratyātmamadhyakṣasiddhāḥ sukhaduḥkhādivadityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Cognitions are diverse—by difference of persons, by difference of objects even in a single person, and by difference of time and instrument even regarding a single object—each directly established in one's own awareness, like pleasure and pain. This is the meaning.
If the plurality of cognition were denied, then by the same logic, the plurality of pleasure and pain too would be subject to denial.
If that is accepted, it contradicts experience—such is the purport. // 88 //

body.translated_text: First, he says that the plurality of consciousness is established by experience and not fit to be denied by sophistical arguments:
For the difference [of cognition] that is manifested through its relata—such as conjunction, desire, and the like—

body.text: na hi bhedaḥ svato nāsti nāpratyakṣaśca sammataḥ // 89 //
body.translated_text: We hold that it is neither intrinsically non-existent nor non-perceptible. // 89 //

body.text: nanu yathā nirbhede 'pyākāśe sambandhivyaṅgyo bhedo ghaṭākāśo 'yamayaṃ tu maṭhākāśa iti pratīyate, evaṃ saṃvidyapi viṣayāśrayavyaṅgyo bhedo na vāstava iti cettatrāha

children.translated_text: 'The relata' (<s>sambandhin</s>)
—thus.

children.text: yathā bhūtalaghaṭasaṃyogo 'yam , sa tu kuḍyamusalasaṃyoga iti sambandhibhedenaiva vyāvṛttatayā pratīyamānaḥ saṃyogabhedo vāstava eva sambandhijanyatvāttasya, yathā vā caitrasya ghaṭecchā, maitrasya paṭecchetyevaṃ sambandhibhedena bhinnatayā pratīyamānā bhinnabhinnaivecchā tattatpuruṣīyā tadā tadā jāyamānā, evaṃ viṣayāśrayabhedena pratīyamīnaḥ saṃvidbhedo 'pi vāstavika eva kālādibhedena jāyamāna iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Just as the conjunction of a pot with the ground, 'This is the conjunction with the pot, but that is the conjunction with the wall and pestle'—the difference of conjunction, being apprehended as distinct precisely through the difference of relata, is real indeed, because it is produced by the relata; or just as <s>Caitra</s>'s desire for a pot and <s>Maitra</s>'s desire for a cloth—thus desire, being apprehended as different through the difference of relata, is indeed different, being that of each respective person and arising at each respective time—so too, the difference of consciousness, being apprehended through difference of objects and substrata, is real indeed, arising through difference of time and the like. Such is the purport.

children.text: siddhānte tattatpuruṣe vartamānasya dharmabhutajñānasyaikatve nityatve 'pi tattadarthaprakāśanārthaprasaraṇāvasthābhedaviśiṣṭaveṣeṇa nānātvamanityatvaṃ ca saṃmataṃ, prakṛternityaikatve 'pi tatpariṇāmabhedānāmivetyavadheyamatra // 89 //
children.translated_text: In the [Viśiṣṭādvaita] established doctrine, even though the attributive cognition (<s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s>) existing in each person is one and eternal, its plurality and non-eternality are accepted in the form of being qualified by different states of expansion for illuminating different objects—just as <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), though eternal and one, has different modifications. This should be noted here. // 89 //

body.translated_text: But just as in space, which is undivided, a difference manifested through relata is apprehended—'This is the space of the pot, this is the space of the hall'—similarly, even in consciousness, the difference manifested through objects and substrata is not real—if so objected, to that he says:
If consciousness itself were accepted as all-pervading and eternal,

body.text: tataḥ sarvaṃ sadā bhāyāt , na vā kiñcitkadācana // 90 //
body.translated_text: Then either everything would always shine, or nothing would shine at any time. // 90 //

children.translated_text: 'If' (<s>yadi</s>)
—and so forth.

children.text: nityavibhunaḥ prakāśakasyaikasya jñānasya sarvaviṣayasambandhe samāne sadā sarvārthasya bhānaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: If a single cognition that is eternal and all-pervading is equally related to all objects, then the absurd consequence follows that all objects would always be cognized.

children.text: prakāśakajñānasambandhe 'pyabhāne tu kasyacidapi kadāpi bhānaṃ na syāt /
children.translated_text: But if, even when related to the illuminating cognition, some object is not cognized, then nothing would ever be cognized at any time;
Because no other cause is possible beyond the relation with illuminating cognition—this is the meaning. // 90 //

body.translated_text: Having thus established the plurality of consciousness from the force of apprehension, he also states the counter-evidence against its unity:
At that time, the arrangement [that] cognition [is produced] by the proximity or non-proximity of the object
Cannot hold, because consciousness is held to be all-pervading like space. // 91 //

children.translated_text: 'At that time' (<s>tadānīm</s>)
—thus.
'<s>Sannidhītarat</s>' means: the condition of proximity and non-proximity.
The arrangement whereby objects are cognized or not cognized based on the proximity or non-proximity of cognition is difficult to establish.
Because cognition is always related to everything, like space—this is the meaning.

children.text: siddhānte tu saṅkocavikāsābhyāṃ jñānasya viṣayabhede sannidhyasannidhī vyavasthite iti bodhyam // 91 //
children.translated_text: But in the [Viśiṣṭādvaita] established doctrine, through contraction and expansion, the proximity and non-proximity of cognition with respect to different objects is well-established. This should be understood. // 91 //

body.translated_text: Nor [can the arrangement be] through difference of instruments, because for what is eternal, those [instruments] do not exist.
Nor through the intrinsic plurality [of consciousness], because its unity has been accepted [by you]. // 92 //

body.text: etatkaraṇajanyaṃ jñānametamevārthaṃ gṛhṇātītyevaṃ karaṇabhedenāpi vyavasthā durvacā bhavadbhirityāha

children.translated_text: 'Nor' (<s>nāpi</s>)

children.text:
ti /
nityatve jñānasya karaṇāsambhavāditi yāvat /
arthabhedena jñānabhedo 'pi durvacaḥ saṃvidadvaitavādibhirityāha
children.translated_text:
—thus.
Because if cognition is eternal, instruments are impossible—this much [is meant].
The difference of cognition through difference of objects is also difficult to maintain for the proponents of non-duality of consciousness, he says:
'Nor' (<s>na ca</s>)

body.translated_text: 'This cognition, born of this instrument, apprehends this very object'—even such an arrangement through difference of instruments is difficult to maintain on your part, he says:
And then, a deaf or blind person and the like would apprehend sound and the like;
And the distinction between teacher and pupil and the like would become groundless. // 93 //

children.translated_text: (Thus the establishment of the plurality of consciousness through the refutation of the unity-of-consciousness doctrine.)
He also brings out the absurd consequence of the breakdown of worldly and Vedic conventions on the theory of unity of illuminating consciousness:
'And then' (<s>tataśca</s>)
—thus.

children.text: nanu prakāśakasya caitanyasyaikatve 'pi cakṣurādiprasṛtayā'ntarakaraṇavṛttyā viṣayasambaddhayāvidyāvaraṇanivartana eva caitanyaṃ taṃ tamarthaṃ prakāśayatīti vyavasthā ghaṭata iti cet ; naitatsādhu ; vṛtterjaḍāyā avidyāvaraṇanivartakatvāyogāt /
children.translated_text: But even if consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) as the illuminator is one, the arrangement is possible because consciousness illuminates each object only when the ignorance-veil is removed by the mental modification (<s>antaḥkaraṇavṛtti</s>) that has gone forth through the eye and the like and become connected with the object—if so objected: this is not sound, because the mental modification, being inert (<s>jaḍa</s>), cannot be the remover of the ignorance-veil.
And if it could, then let that [modification] itself be the illuminator of objects;
What need is there for consciousness as a hidden agent?—this is elaborated elsewhere.
Therefore, the difference of cognition through the difference of object and subject must be accepted—such is the purport. // 93 //

body.text: nanu naḥ saṃvido bhinnaṃ sarvaṃ nāma na kiñcana /
body.translated_text: But [the Advaitin says:] for us, nothing at all is different from consciousness;
Therefore, [the charge] 'everything would always shine' is groundlessly leveled. // 94 //

children.translated_text: 'But' (<s>nanu</s>)
—thus.

children.text: saṃvidbhinnasya sarvasya virahādevāsmanmate sarvaṃ sadā bhāyāditya sthānaṃ'nuyogo bhavatāmityarthaḥ // 94 //
children.translated_text: Since in our view, everything other than consciousness is absent, the charge 'everything would always shine' has no foothold against us—this is the meaning. // 94 //

body.translated_text: The opponent raises the absurd consequence of everything always shining, which was brought out by the established view:

body.text: idamākhyāhi bhoḥ kiṃ nu nīlādirna prakāśate /
body.translated_text: Tell us this, sir: is it that blue and the like do not shine at all,

body.text: prakāśamāno nīlādiḥ saṃvido vā na bhidyate // 95 //
body.translated_text: Or that blue and the like, while shining, are not different from consciousness? // 95 //

children.translated_text: 'This' (<s>idam</s>)
—thus.

children.text: kiṃ nīlādipratītireva nāstītyucyate, uta nīlādeḥ saṃvidabhinnatvena tatpratītiḥ saṃvitpratītirevābhimanyata ityarthaḥ // 95 //
children.translated_text: Is it being said that the cognition of blue and the like simply does not exist? Or is it that, because blue and the like are non-different from consciousness, their cognition is considered to be the cognition of consciousness itself?—this is the meaning. // 95 //

body.translated_text: The proponent of the established view responds:
In the first [case], the maintenance of worldly and Vedic [conventions], which is graced by experience, [would be destroyed],
Since nothing—no word, no meaning of words, and the like—would appear. // 96 //

children.translated_text: 'In the first' (<s>ādau</s>)

children.text:
viti /
nānāpratītinihnive nānāpadapadārthapratītinirvāhyaḥ sarvo laukiko vaidikaśca vyavahāraḥ pratītisubhagaḥ-abādhitānubhavasiddhaḥ samyaṅ nirvyūḍho bhavedbhavadbhirityupālambhaḥ /
children.translated_text:
—thus.
If the diverse cognitions are denied, the entire worldly and Vedic activity, which depends on diverse cognitions of words and their meanings—which is graced by experience, i.e., established through uncontradicted experience—could it be properly carried out by you?—this is the reproach.
'How?'
—thus the sentence should be completed. // 96 //

body.translated_text: He says the first alternative is untenable:
In the second [case], the non-duality of consciousness, which is your position, would be contradicted.
If this manifold of diverse forms is of the nature of consciousness,
Then consciousness too, having that as its nature, would be subject to plurality. // 97 //

children.translated_text: 'In the second' (<s>dvitīye</s>)
—thus.

If the diverse manifold that is apprehended is identical with consciousness, then the plurality of consciousness would follow—and thus the abandonment of the accepted non-duality of consciousness. This is the meaning.
In stating this, the inner point is that there is a self-contradiction [in the opponent's position]. // 97 //

body.translated_text: He refutes the second [alternative]:
Nor [can it be said that] because it is a sport of <s>avidyā</s>, the difference need not be determined [as real or unreal];
For that [<s>avidyā</s>], untouched by reasoning, becomes like a lac ornament [that melts]. // 98 //

children.translated_text: 'Nor' (<s>naca</s>)

children.text:
ti /
nīlādibhideti viśeṣyamadhyāhāryamatra /
bhinnatvenābhinnatvena vā nirūpayitumaśakyatvaṃ ca tasyā avidyāvilāsatvāt bhedābhedayoranirūpaṇaṃ yasyā bhedābhedānirūpaṇā /
āvidyāsya nīlādibhedasya mithyātvāt mithyārthe ca durghaṭatvasya bhūṣaṇatvādbhedābhedānirūpaṇopapattiḥ /
upapattyananuvartitvādeva ca sarvaṃ sadā bhāyādityādyāpatterapyanavakāśa iti hṛdayam /
pariharati
children.translated_text:
—thus.
The implicit qualificand here is 'the differentiation such as blue and the like.'
The inability to determine it as either different or non-different, because it is a sport of <s>avidyā</s>—'<s>bhedābhedānirūpaṇā</s>' means: that whose determination as either different or non-different is impossible.
Since this differentiation of blue and the like that belongs to <s>avidyā</s> is false, and since being difficult to explain is an ornament of what is false, the impossibility of determining difference or non-difference is plausible.
And precisely because it does not conform to [logical] plausibility, there is no room for the objection 'everything would always shine' and the like—such is the inner meaning.
He refutes:
'For that' (<s>sā hi</s>)

—thus.
A product of lac is '<s>jātuṣa</s>'.
'<s>Trapujatunoḥ ṣuk</s>'
—[by the grammatical rule,] the suffix <s>aṇ</s> and <s>ṣuk</s> augment [apply].

children.text: avidyā hi nyāyānalaspṛṣṭā jātuṣavanna jīvituṃ prabhavati /
children.translated_text: <s>Avidyā</s>, when touched by the fire of reasoning, cannot survive, like [an ornament made of] lac.
Its being a sport of that [<s>avidyā</s>] will not be established at all—such is the intent. // 98 //

body.translated_text: Here the opponent raises an objection:
For indeed, if this <s>avidyā</s> is held to be the absence of knowledge,
Then, having a nature that is without any real character, it determines nothing. // 99 //
If <s>avidyā</s> is something other [than mere absence of knowledge], then [your] claim that 'difference is indeterminable' is fine;
[But then] the dilemma of whether it is [identical with] the thing, or different from it, or something else, does not apply to it;
And that it is something other than knowledge—this is a well-spoken statement [i.e., ironic]! // 100 //

children.translated_text: 'For indeed' (<s>tathāhi</s>)

children.text:
tyādinā /
atra vikalpaḥ-kiṃ vidyābhāvo 'vidyā, uta vidyābhinnaṃ bhāvāntaramiti /
ādye dūṣaṇamāha
children.translated_text:
—and so forth.
Here the dilemma is: Is <s>avidyā</s> the absence of knowledge, or is it a positive entity different from knowledge? He states the refutation of the first:
'Without any real character' (<s>nirupākhya</s>)

children.text:
ti /
nirupākhyasvabhāvatvaṃ śūnyasvarūpatvam /
tathā ca svayamevālabdhasattāvidyā kathaṃ prapañcavyavasthāpikā bhavedityākūtam /
kalpāntaramanūdyadūṣayati
children.translated_text:
—thus.
'Having a nature without any real character' means having an empty nature.
And thus, <s>avidyā</s>, which has itself not attained existence, how could it be the establisher of the manifold?—such is the intent.
He restates and refutes the alternative:
'Something other' (<s>arthāntaram</s>)

children.text:
iti /
sādhvī-upapattyasahā, bhedānirūpaṇā-bhinnatvenābhinnatvena vāśakyanirūpaṇā cāvidyār'thāntaraṃ cedityanvayaḥ /
atra svavāgvirodhamāha
children.translated_text:
—thus.
'<s>Sādhvī</s>' means: incapable of being sustained [by reasoning].
'<s>Bhedānirūpaṇā</s>' means: that which cannot be determined as either different or non-different.
The syntactical connection is: 'And if <s>avidyā</s> is something other [than mere absence].'
Here he states the self-contradiction in [the opponent's] own words:
'Whether it is the thing or something other' (<s>arthānarthāntara</s>)

children.text:
ti /
suvyāhṛtamiti viparītalākṣaṇikam /
arthānarthāntaratvādivikalpo 'syā na yujyataiti vacanaṃvidyātor'thāntaramasāviti ca vacanaṃ mitho viruddhamiti yāvat // 99 //100 //
children.translated_text:
—thus.
'Well-spoken' is used in the sense of the opposite [i.e., ironically].
The statement 'the dilemma of whether it is the thing or something other does not apply to it' and the statement 'it is something other than knowledge' are mutually contradictory—this much [is meant]. // 99 // 100 //

body.translated_text: He elaborates the vulnerability of <s>avidyā</s> to reasoning:
But even if its status as something other is attributed [only] as imagined by delusion,
Alas! In that case, [your] <s>avidyā</s> itself would, in ultimate reality, be knowledge! // 101 //

children.translated_text: 'But' (<s>atha</s>)
—thus.
If the difference [between vidyā and avidyā] cannot be established, then what you accept as knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>) itself would be ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) — such is the purport. (101)

body.translated_text: If even the positive-entity status of <s>avidyā</s> is merely imagined, to that he says:

body.text: kiñca śuddhājaḍā saṃvit , avidyeyaṃ tu nedṛśī /
body.translated_text: Moreover, consciousness (<s>saṃvit</s>) is pure and non-inert, but this <s>avidyā</s> is not of such a nature;
By what reason, then, is it not established as something entirely different from that [consciousness]? (Verse 102)

children.translated_text: 'Moreover' —
thus.

children.text: tathā ca śuddhājaḍasaṃvidapekṣayā vikārāspadāśuddhajaḍāvidyāyā bheda eva paramārthataḥ kuto na nirūpyata ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus, in relation to pure, non-inert consciousness, the difference of <s>avidyā</s> — which is the locus of modification, impure, and inert — is indeed ultimate. Why is it not established [as different]? Such is the meaning.

children.text: tathā ca paramārthāvidyāvilāso bhedaḥ sarvo 'pi saṃvida ekasyā eva sakalārthaprakāśakatve sarvadā bhāseteti doṣastadavastha iti bhāvaḥ // 102 //
children.translated_text: And thus, all differentiation — being a sport of <s>avidyā</s>, which is ultimately [real] — would always shine forth, since consciousness alone, being one, illuminates all objects. The fault remains as before — such is the purport. (102)

body.translated_text: He says that <s>avidyā</s> deserves to be established as actually different [from consciousness]:
Moreover, this <s>avidyā</s> of yours, whose nature is that of an absence and the like —

body.text: sā vidyā kiṃ nu saṃvittirvedyaṃ vā veditāthavā // 103 //
body.translated_text: Is the <s>vidyā</s> [that is its counterpositive] consciousness (<s>saṃvitti</s>), or the known (<s>vedya</s>), or the knower (<s>veditṛ</s>)? (Verse 103)

children.translated_text: 'Moreover this' —
thus.
Let <s>avidyā</s> be of the nature of the absence of <s>vidyā</s>, or of a nature not different from <s>vidyā</s>.

children.text: tatra pratiyogibhūtā vidyā kiṃrūpeti vikalpanaṃ vimarśanārtham // 103 //
children.translated_text: Therein, the question 'what is the nature of the <s>vidyā</s> that is the counterpositive?' is posed for the purpose of critical examination. (103)

body.translated_text: Having refuted the indescribability (<s>anirvacanīyatva</s>) of <s>avidyā</s> through both its identity with and difference from [consciousness], he also states the impossibility of its essential nature:
If [vidyā] has the nature of the known or the knower, then <s>avidyā</s> is not removed by either of these.
For apart from knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>) is not removed by anything else.
If [you say] it is consciousness (<s>saṃvit</s>) itself — then, because of its [eternal] existence, [avidyā] is impossible. (Verse 104)
