children.translated_text: thus. 'Caused by that'—prompted by the difference of <s>jīvas</s>. 'Unlike dream behavior'—unlike practical transactions involving dream-objects. The purport is this: just as the unreality of dream-object transactions is ascertained only in the dream itself [i.e., upon waking], from subsequent sublation, and [is known] only at the time of [waking] practical activity—so too, the transactions prompted by the difference of <s>jīvas</s> are not sublated at that very time [of practical activity]. Rather, from the very perception of the reality of benefit and harm done by other <s>jīvas</s>, from the earliest sage (<s>prājña</s>) down to cowherds and boys, activity and engagement in accordance with that [perception of plurality] is seen to continue up to the dissolution [of the world]. And because the difference of <s>jīvas</s> is not sublated at the time of practical activity, even according to the opponent's own framework, it has merely conventional reality (<s>vyāvahārikatva</s>), not phenomenal unreality (<s>prātibhāsikatva</s>). And the inference 'the difference of <s>jīvas</s> is false because it is merely apparent, like the difference of persons in a dream' is vitiated (<s>sopādhika</s>) by its non-sublation at the time of practical activity. Accordingly, the <s>sūtra</s> [states:]
'And because of dissimilarity, [it is] not like a dream'—
and so on. // 148 //

body.translated_text: He says that the appearance of multiple <s>jīvas</s> is not refuted at the very time of practical transaction, as silver-in-nacre and the like [are]:
Therefore, even the oneness [of the <s>jīva</s> extracted] by reasoning is overturned by reasoning.
The mental states inferred from the differences of activity are contradictory [to oneness].
Other embodied beings too, each having a self like one's own self, cannot be denied. // 149 //

children.translated_text: 'Therefore'—

children.text:
ti /
tena-jīvabhedasya vyavahārakālābādhena /
sarve jīvā ahameva jīvatvādahamiva, sarvāṇi śarīrāṇi mayaivātmavanti śarīratvāt maccharīravaditi jīvaikyayuktirjīvabhedasādhakayuktiparāhatetyarthaḥ /
jīvabhedayukteḥ prābalyaṃ ca vyavahārābhādhyaviṣayatvādupalambhānuguṇyācceti bodhyam /
nanu kā sā jīvanānātvayuktiḥ ? tāmāha
children.translated_text: thus. 'By that'—by the non-sublation of the difference of <s>jīvas</s> at the time of practical transaction. The reasoning for the oneness of <s>jīvas</s>—'All <s>jīvas</s> are myself, because they are <s>jīvas</s>, like myself; all bodies are ensouled by me alone, because they are bodies, like my body'—is overturned by the reasoning that proves the difference of <s>jīvas</s>. This is the meaning. And the greater strength of the reasoning for <s>jīva</s>-plurality should be understood as due to its having as its object that which is not sublated in practical experience, and its conformity with perception.
Now, what is that reasoning for the plurality of <s>jīvas</s>? He states it:
'[from] the difference of activity'—

children.text: tattaddehagatavilakṣaṇapravṛttibhedānumitāḥ tattadanuguṇaviruddhajñānasaṅkalpaprayatnavanto 'nye dehino 'pi sa sa svātmeva svaśarīrapravṛttyanuguṇajñānādimān pratyātmasiddho na nihnotu śakyante ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. Inferred from the differences of distinctive activities in each body—[namely,] other embodied beings too, possessing cognitions, volitions, and efforts that are in accordance with and contradictory to [those activities], each having a self just like one's own self—established as possessing cognition and the like in accordance with one's own bodily activity, [each] proven for oneself—cannot be denied. This is the meaning.
The word '<s>mativṛtti</s>' (mental states) also implicitly indicates volition (<s>saṅkalpa</s>).

children.text: paraśarīrāṇisātmakāni ceṣṭāvattvāt svaśarīravaditi sātmakatve 'numite tadātmanāṃ svātmabhedaḥ pariśeṣāt sidhyati, paraśarīrapravṛttihetubhūtasaṅkalpaprayatnasya svāsamavetatve sati guṇatvātsvabhinnasamavetatvānumānāt /
children.translated_text: When it is inferred that other bodies are ensouled—because they possess purposeful movement, like one's own body—then the difference of those [other] souls from one's own soul is established by the method of residue (<s>pariśeṣa</s>), from the inference that the volition and effort that are the causes of the activity of other bodies are not co-inherent with oneself, and, being qualities, must inhere in something different from oneself.

children.text: svāsamavetatvaṃ ca tasya svasya tadā bhinnasaṅkalpapravṛttimattvādeva suniśceyamiti bodhyam // 149 //
children.translated_text: And the non-co-inherence of those [volitions and efforts] with oneself is easily ascertained from the very fact that one possesses different volitions and activities at that time. This should be understood. // 149 //

body.translated_text: By the very reason stated, he also refutes the extraction of oneness by reasoning:
Just as fires and the like that are inferred are different from those that are observed,

body.text: pratyakṣaṃ te (kṣyante)tathānyebhyo jīvebhyo na pṛthak katham // 150 //
body.translated_text: so too [other selves] are perceived [to be different]—how could they not be distinct from other <s>jīvas</s>? // 150 //

children.translated_text: 'Just as'—
thus.

children.text: ānumānāḥ anumānaprayojakāḥ sapakṣadṛṣṭāḥ vahnayo 'numeyātparvatīyavahneryathā bhinnāḥ vyāptigrahaṇakāle 'dhyakṣitāḥ, tathānumeyebhyaḥ paradehasthātmabhyaḥ śarīrapravṛtticetanasahkalpaprayatnapūrvakatvavyāptigrahakāle gṛhītaṃ tvadīyātmasvarūpaṃ tvaccharīrapravṛttihetusaṅkalpādimadbhinnatvena kuto na pratyakṣam ? api tu pratyakṣameveti yāvat /
children.translated_text: Just as fires that serve as the basis for inference—fires observed in homogeneous instances (<s>sapakṣa</s>) at the time of grasping the invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>)—are different from the fire to be inferred, such as the fire on the mountain, so too: at the time of grasping the concomitance 'purposeful bodily activity is preceded by conscious volition and effort,' the nature of your own self, grasped as possessing the volition and the like that cause the activity of your own body—how is it not directly perceived as different from the other selves located in other bodies, who are the objects to be inferred? Indeed, it is directly perceived [as different].
The reasoning for the oneness of <s>jīvas</s>, like the reasoning for the oneness of fires, is both useless and contradicted by experience. This is the essential point. // 150 //

body.translated_text: He presents an illustration for the difference of the other selves—which are to be proved—from one's own self, which serves as the paradigmatic case (<s>nidarśana</s>):
And if other conscious beings are not inferred from the distinctive features of [their] activity,
all practical transactions, both worldly and Vedic, would be undermined. // 151 //

children.translated_text: 'And if not'—
thus.

children.text: paradeheṣu parātmanaśceṣṭāviśeṣairanukūlapratikūlodāsīnānūhitvaiva hi tattadanuguṇā vyavahārāḥ dṛṣṭā loke, jīvabhedaprayuktā eva cādhikāryanadhikārivibhāgādivyavahārāḥ śāstrīyā dṛṣṭāḥ /
children.translated_text: It is observed in the world that practical transactions appropriate to favorable, unfavorable, and indifferent [others] are [undertaken] precisely through inferring other selves in other bodies from the distinctive features of their activity. And scriptural transactions too—such as the distinction between qualified and unqualified persons—are seen to be prompted by the difference of <s>jīvas</s>.
The obstruction of those [transactions] would follow from not accepting the difference of <s>jīvas</s>. This is the purport. // 151 //

body.translated_text: The positive argument for other selves has been stated. He also states the negative consequence (<s>bādhaka</s>) of not accepting it:
Nor can the differentiation of knower and knowable [be explained] through the difference of limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>),
because that [consequence] would apply even within one's own body, through the difference of head, hands, and so forth. // 152 //

body.text:
nanu saṃvinmātramekameva nānopādhiyogānnānājīvatayā bhāti /
aupādhikajīvabhedaprayukta eva vyavahārabhedaḥ, svabhāvāsaṅkaraśca /
upādhibhedo 'pi kalpita tavetyāśaṅkāmanūtyā pariharati

children.translated_text: 'Nor through <s>upādhi</s>-based'—
thus.
The mention of the differentiation of the knowable is incidental, for the sake of illustration.

If the establishment [of distinct selves] through <s>upādhi</s>-based difference is accepted, then through the <s>upādhi</s>-difference of head, hands, and feet as well, there would be the consequence of the difference of consciousness delimited by each of those.

children.text: tathā ca pāde me vedanā, śirasi sukhamityādipratisandhānānupattiriti yāvat // 152 //
children.translated_text: And thus, the connection (<s>pratisandhāna</s>) of '[there is] pain in my foot, happiness in my head' and the like would be impossible. This is the upshot. // 152 //

body.translated_text: Objection: Mere consciousness (<s>saṃvinmātra</s>) is one alone; through the connection with various limiting adjuncts, it appears as multiple <s>jīvas</s>. The difference of practical transactions is prompted by the <s>upādhi</s>-based difference of <s>jīvas</s>, and there is no confusion of essential natures. And even the difference of <s>upādhis</s> is fabricated [by you]. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it:
Just as, there, when sensation arises in the head, hands, feet, and so forth,
there is connection [of experience] in the case of oneness [of the self], so it would be the case everywhere for you. // 153 //

children.translated_text: 'Just as'—

children.text:
ti /
tathetyaniṣṭasamuccayārthaḥ /
yatheti vā syāt /
vastutaḥ sarvaśarīreṣu cita aikyātsarvagatasukhādipratisandhānaprasaṅga ityarthaḥ /
na ca śarīrabhedasyai vātmabhedakatvam , nanu karacaraṇādibhedasyeti vācyam , saubharyādau śarīrabhede 'pi pratisandhānasya dṛṣṭatvāttasyāpi bhedakatvāyogāt /
children.translated_text: thus. 'Just as' (<s>tathā</s>) is in the sense of conjoining an unwanted consequence. Or it may be 'just as' (<s>yathā</s>). In reality, since consciousness is one across all bodies, the consequence would be the connection of pleasure and the like occurring everywhere. This is the meaning. Nor should the difference of bodies alone be adduced as the differentiator of selves—objection: 'but [what about] the difference of hands, feet, and so forth?'—because even when there is a difference of bodies, as in the case of <s>Saubhari</s> and others, since the connection [of experience] is observed, [body-difference] too cannot serve as a differentiator.
Nor is the arrangement [valid] that only the body dependent on the <s>karma</s> of each individual person delimits the experience for each.
For even the simultaneous connection of <s>Saubhari</s> and others with multiple bodies is produced by his own <s>karma</s>.

children.text: natvasmadādestatheti vācyam , aupādhikātmabhedavāde pratikarmavyavasthāyā api durghaṭatvāt ; upādhestadīyatvaṃ tatkarmaṇā, upādhivyavasthayaiva ca tatkarmavyavasthitiriti parasparāśrayācceti dik /
children.translated_text: Nor should it be said that 'this is not so for us and others,' because even in the theory of <s>upādhi</s>-based differentiation of selves, the arrangement of individual <s>karma</s> is also difficult to establish—since the <s>upādhi</s>'s belonging to that [self] depends on that <s>karma</s>, and the arrangement of that <s>karma</s> itself depends on the arrangement of <s>upādhis</s>, [there is] mutual dependence (<s>parasparāśraya</s>). This is but an indication.
Therefore, the confusion of experiences and the like must be avoided by a real difference of <s>jīvas</s> alone. This is the purport. // 153 //

body.translated_text: Objection: Even with the difference of <s>upādhis</s>, the connection [of experience] is due to the non-difference of consciousness. To this he says:
Due to the distress of dying, the sufferings of hell, the ordeal of birth,
and the long time elapsed, experiences of previous births are not within the range of memory. // 154 //

body.text: nanu śarīrabhede 'pyātmaikyātpratisandhāne janmāntare 'nubhūtasyāpi janmāntare pratisandhānaṃ syādityatrāha

children.translated_text: 'Due to dying'—

children.text:
diti /
prabaladuḥkhānubhavasya saṃskārapramoṣakatvaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ loke prabalajvarādyarditasyādhītavismaraṇādinā /
children.translated_text: —thus. It is observed in the world that intense suffering-experience destroys impressions (<s>saṃskāras</s>)—as when one afflicted by severe fever and the like forgets what was studied.

children.text: janmabhede ca maraṇanarakagarbhavāsajanmakālaprabhavakleśabāhulyena saṃskāravināśātpūrvajanmānubhūtasmaraṇaṃ janmāntare ca jāyata ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: And in different births, due to the destruction of impressions by the abundance of afflictions arising at the time of death, passage through hell, residence in the womb, and birth—the memory of experiences from previous births does not arise in the next birth. This is the meaning.
Intending that even the passage of a long time can destroy impressions, the phrase 'long elapsed [time]' is used.

children.text: jīvanādṛṣṭabalāttu saṃskāraviśeṣasyāvinaṣṭatvaṃ jātamātra udbhūtatvaṃ ca kalpyate /
children.translated_text: But through the <s>jīva</s>'s unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), the non-destruction of particular impressions and their manifestation immediately upon birth is to be postulated.

For some, however, through an excess of merit, due to the non-destruction of impressions, even non-forgetfulness of previous births and the like is accepted in both worldly [convention] and authoritative scripture—this should be understood. // 154 //

body.translated_text: Objection: Even with the difference of bodies, since the self is one, [there would be] connection [of experience]; and even what was experienced in another birth would be connected in [yet] another birth. To this he says:
Among [experiences] such as happiness and suffering that arise simultaneously ...... [the difference is] evident;
there being a non-mixture of substrata in that case, how could there be the delusion of a single identity? // 155 //

children.translated_text: (Thus the refutation of the single-self doctrine posited by a single <s>avidyā</s>.)
'Simultaneously'
—thus.

children.text: ekakṣaṇa eva jāyamāneṣu nānāsukhaduḥkhānubhaveṣu kāladairghyādisaṃskārapramoṣakavirahe 'pi asmaraṇādi ātmanāmasaṅkarāt anakyādeva vyavasthāpyam /
children.translated_text: Among the diverse experiences of happiness and suffering arising at a single moment, even in the absence of the destroyers of impressions such as the passage of long time, the non-remembering and the like is to be explained precisely by the non-mixture of [distinct] selves.

children.text: tathā caikātmyadhiyo bhrāntirūpāyā api nodayāvasaraḥ, ātmabhedasyaiva sphuṭapratibhānāditibhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus, even for the cognition of unity [of selves], which is a form of error, there is no occasion for its arising—because the difference of selves is clearly apparent from the very beginning. This is the purport.
The refutations of the single-self doctrine posited by a single <s>avidyā</s> have been elaborated. // 155 //

body.translated_text: Nor, by multiple <s>jīvas</s> imagined by individual <s>avidyās</s>,
each seeing only their own respective [projected world], can this worldly activity be accounted for. // 156 //
They, being unaware of the affairs of others, each seeing only their own respective dream—
how could they carry on that [worldly activity] which is founded on association and the like requiring a single [shared world]? // 157 //

children.translated_text: 'Nor'

children.text:
ti /
avidyākalpitāścito nānājīṃvabhedāḥ /
te ca svasvāvidyākalpitaṃ padārthajātaṃ paśyanti pṛthak pṛthak svapna iva /
vyāvahārikā anye jīvā anyena na jñāyante /
svena dṛśyā jīvāstu svāpnavatprātibhāsikā evetyetatpakṣasāraḥ /
atra cānyaṃ jīvaṃ tadguṇadoṣādi vā vyāvahārikamanyo jīvastathābhūto na jānāti cettarhi tatsamāgamādiprasaṅgābhāvāt sahānubhūtayaikasādhyo 'nuvṛtto lokavyavahāraḥ kathaṃ nirvartyetetyarthaḥ /
svāvidyākalpitameva paśyantītyuktyā paravārtānabhijñatvaṃ-vyāvahārikajīvāntaravṛttānabhijñatvaṃ sidhyati /
na hi te jīvāntarāvidyākalpitāḥ /
kintu mūlāvidyākalpitā eva /
lokavyavahāro 'pi prātibhāsika eveti cettarhi ekajīvavādonmeṣaḥ /
tatra ca doṣa ukta eveti hārdam // 156 //157 //
children.translated_text: —thus. The multiple <s>jīva</s>-distinctions imagined by <s>avidyā</s> from consciousness—they each see the collection of objects imagined by their own respective <s>avidyā</s>, separately, as in a dream. The other <s>jīvas</s>, which are conventionally real (<s>vyāvahārika</s>), are not known by another [<s>jīva</s>]. But the <s>jīvas</s> seen by oneself are merely phenomenal (<s>prātibhāsika</s>), like those in a dream—this is the essence of this position. Here, if one <s>jīva</s>, being conventionally real, does not know another <s>jīva</s> or its qualities and defects and so forth as they truly are, then since there would be no occasion for association and the like with them, how could the continuous worldly activity—which requires shared experience—be carried out? This is the meaning. By saying 'they see only what is imagined by their own <s>avidyā</s>,' the unawareness of the affairs of others—i.e., unawareness of what pertains to other conventionally real <s>jīvas</s>—is established. For those [other <s>jīvas</s>] are not imagined by the <s>avidyā</s> of one's own [individual <s>jīva</s>]; rather, they are imagined by the root <s>avidyā</s> alone. If even worldly activity is merely phenomenal, then the single-self doctrine resurfaces—and the fault of that has already been stated. This is the essential point. // 156-157 //

body.translated_text: He refutes the multiple-selves-imagined-by-multiple-<s>avidyās</s> doctrine as well:
Furthermore, the self-luminosity, all-pervasiveness, unity, and eternality
accepted by you would establish consciousness as having a second, [thereby contradicting its non-duality]. // 158 //

body.text:
saṃvinmātre 'vidyākalpito meyamātṛbheda iti paramataṃ vistareṇa pratikṣiptametāvatā /
atha saṃvidi parābhimataṃ nirviśeṣatvaṃ pratikṣipati

children.translated_text: 'Furthermore'
—and so forth.
After the word 'your' (<s>te</s>), '[as] accepted' (<s>matām</s>) should be supplied.

children.text: bhavadabhimataireva dharmaiḥ saviśeṣatvaṃ saṃvidaḥ prasajyata iti bhāvaḥ // 158 //
children.translated_text: The purport is: by the very attributes accepted by you, the qualified nature (<s>saviśeṣatva</s>) of consciousness follows. // 158 //

body.translated_text: The opponent's view—that in bare consciousness, the difference between the knowable and the knower is imagined by <s>avidyā</s>—has been extensively refuted by this much. Now he refutes the qualitylessness (<s>nirviśeṣatva</s>) of consciousness as accepted by the opponent:

body.text: saṃvideva na te dharmāḥ, siddhāyāmapi saṃvidi /
body.translated_text: 'Those [attributes] are not [different from] consciousness'—[you say]; but even when consciousness is established,
there is dispute about those [attributes]; and because those having that nature are different [from consciousness]. // 159 //

body.text: svarūpābhedātteṣāṃ na saṃvidaḥ sadharmatvamiti śaṅkāmanūdya nirācaṣṭe

children.translated_text: '[Those are] consciousness itself'
—thus.

children.text: sampratipanne 'pi saṃvitsvarūpe tannityatvavibhutvaikatvasvaprakāśatvādau bauddhanaiyāyikamīmāṃsakādīnāṃ vivādāt svarūpabhedācca teṣāṃ dharmāṇāṃ saṃvitto na saṃpratipannasaṃvidabhinnatvaṃ teṣāṃ yujyata ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Even when the essential nature of consciousness is accepted, since there is dispute among <s>Buddhists</s>, <s>Naiyāyikas</s>, <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, and others regarding its eternality, all-pervasiveness, unity, self-luminosity, and so forth, and since those attributes are essentially different [from each other], their non-difference from the universally accepted consciousness cannot be maintained—this is the meaning.
And the essential difference [of these attributes] has been demonstrated in the <s>Ātmasiddhi</s>—this should be recalled. // 159 //

body.translated_text: He restates and refutes the objection that those attributes, being non-different from consciousness's own nature, do not make consciousness qualified:
Nor are those [attributes] established through error, so that they would not contradict non-duality;
for those qualities are established by the <s>Vedānta</s> passages that reveal reality. // 160 //

children.translated_text: 'Nor [are] those'

children.text:
iti /
tavāpi tattvedamparaśrutyantasiddhāste dharmāssaṃvido nityatvādaya ityeva matam /
tattaiḥ saviśeṣatvaṃ durvāram /
teṣāṃ bādhe tulyanayena saṃvido 'pi bādhaḥ syāditi dyotyate
children.translated_text: —thus. Even in your own view, those attributes of consciousness—eternality and so forth—are established by the <s>śruti</s> passages ending with '<s>tat tvam</s>' ('That thou art'). Therefore, the qualified nature [of consciousness] through them is unavoidable. If those [attributes] were sublated, then by the same logic, consciousness itself would be sublated too—this is indicated
by 'which reveal reality'
and so forth. // 160 //

body.translated_text: But even so, since those [attributes] are not ultimately real, the absence of an ultimate second [to <s>Brahman</s>] is well-preserved—if one objects thus, he responds:
If [you say that] bliss, self-luminosity, eternality, greatness, and so forth
are desired [to be] the very essential nature of <s>Brahman</s>—even there, let this be examined. // 161 //

children.translated_text: 'Bliss' (<s>ānanda</s>)
—thus. The word '<s>ānanda</s>' (bliss) has a predominantly substantive meaning.
'Greatness' (<s>mahimā</s>)—all-pervasiveness.
By the word 'and so forth' (<s>ādi</s>), unity and the like are to be included.
'<s>Atha</s>' has the meaning 'if.'
Because indeclinable words have multiple meanings. // 161 //

body.translated_text: Since the opponent holds that those attributes are non-different from <s>Brahman</s>'s essential nature, he states a refutation through yet another approach:
Whatever is designated by the word '<s>Brahman</s>'—is it that alone, [or are] happiness and the rest [something additional]?

body.text: athavā tasya te, yadvā ta eva brahmasaṃjñinaḥ // 162 //
body.translated_text: Or are they [attributes] of It? Or are they themselves called '<s>Brahman</s>'? // 162 //

children.translated_text: '<s>Brahman</s>'
—thus.

children.text: kimānandatvādayo brahmasvarūpamātram , uta tanniṣṭhā dharmāḥ, āhosvitteṣāmeva pratyekaṃ brahmasaṃjñā, samuditānāṃ veti vikalpaḥ // 162 //
children.translated_text: Are bliss-nature and so forth merely the essential nature of <s>Brahman</s>? Or are they attributes residing in It? Or does each of them individually bear the designation '<s>Brahman</s>'? Or does their aggregate?—this is the dilemma. // 162 //

body.translated_text: He presents the alternatives regarding the opponent's view:
In the first [alternative], the co-listing (<s>sahapāṭha</s>) of those respective terms would be purposeless, both in the <s>Vedas</s> and in the world;
and there would be the [defect of] non-difference discussed earlier, and [<s>Brahman</s> would have to be] the cause of the origination of the world and the like. // 163 //
For indeed, having accepted <s>Brahman</s>, the disputants' disputes are about those [attributes];
in the second [alternative], by those very [attributes], the 'having a second' of <s>Brahman</s> [follows]. // 164 //

children.translated_text: 'In the first'
—thus. In [the case of] utter non-difference, since [the co-listing] would have no additional meaning,
in [statements like] '<s>ānando brahma</s>' ('Bliss is <s>Brahman</s>'), '<s>satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma</s>' ('<s>Brahman</s> is truth, knowledge, infinite')—

children.text:
sahapāṭhasyānarthakyaṃ prasajyate /
na hi ghaṭaḥ kalaśa iti sahapāṭhaḥ /
brahmasvarūpaikyāsambhavaṃ ca teṣu dharmeṣu smārayati
children.translated_text: the co-listing would become purposeless. For there is no co-listing like 'the pot is the water-jar' [which would be tautologous]. He also reminds [us of] the impossibility of the identity of <s>Brahman</s>'s essential nature with those attributes:
'As discussed earlier'

children.text:
ti /
dvitīye kalpe tu brahmaṇaḥ saviśeṣatvaprasaṅga ityāha
children.translated_text: —thus. In the second alternative, the absurd consequence of <s>Brahman</s> having qualifications [follows]—he says:
'In the second'
—thus. 'That very [consequence]'—which contradicts what you accept. // 163-164 //

body.translated_text: In the third [alternative], <s>Brahman</s> would be fragmented, since [each attribute] would be nothing but that [one attribute] at every step;
or alternatively, the aggregate would be <s>Brahman</s>, like a grove is [an aggregate of] trees. // 165 //

children.translated_text: 'In the third'

children.text:
iti /
pratyekaśo brahmatvamityatra nānā brahma prasajyate satyaṃ brahma, jñānaṃ brahma, anantaṃ brahma, ānando brahmeti ; khaṇḍo muṇḍaḥ pūrṇaśṛṅgogaurityatrevetyarthaḥ /
tanmātratvāt-tattanmātrasvarūpatvādbrahmaṇaḥ /
satyatvādisamudāyo brahmetyatra doṣamāha
children.translated_text: —thus. If each one individually is <s>Brahman</s>, then many <s>Brahmans</s> would result: 'Truth is <s>Brahman</s>,' 'Knowledge is <s>Brahman</s>,' 'The Infinite is <s>Brahman</s>,' 'Bliss is <s>Brahman</s>'—just like [the absurdity of saying] '<s>Khaṇḍa</s> [is a cow], <s>Muṇḍa</s> [is a cow], and Full-Horned [is a cow]' [when each is merely a part of the description]—this is the meaning. 'Because of being nothing but that'—because <s>Brahman</s> would have as its sole nature that particular [attribute alone]. He states the fault of the aggregate [sub-alternative]:
'The aggregate of those'
—thus.
The printed reading '<s>vināśavat</s>' is incorrect.

children.text: taruvṛndasya vanatvavatsatyādisamudāyasya brahmatve, samudāyasya samudāyyananyatve pratyekapakṣoktadūṣaṇānativṛttiḥ, atiriktatve sāṃśatvaṃ guṇatvaṃ ca prasajyate brahmaṇa iti bhāvaḥ // 165 //
children.translated_text: If the aggregate of truth and so forth is <s>Brahman</s>—like a collection of trees being a grove—then if the aggregate is non-different from its parts, the refutation stated for the individual alternative is not overcome; if it is something additional, then <s>Brahman</s> would have parts and attributes—this is the purport. // 165 //

body.translated_text: In the third [alternative], he refutes both the individual and aggregate sub-alternatives, [starting with] the individual:
Intensity (<s>prakarṣa</s>) and illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>), though different, both reside in the sun;

body.text: tena na kvāpi vākyārtho vibhāgo 'sti nidarśanam // 166 //
body.translated_text: therefore, nowhere [in any statement] is there an illustration of an 'undivided' sentence-meaning. // 166 //

body.text: nanu satyādivākyamakhaṇḍārthaparaṃ svarūpalakṣaṇavākyatvāt , divā divi prakṛṣṭaprakāśaḥ sūryaḥ, niśi ca tathābhūtaścandra itivaditi nirviśeṣabrahmasiddhirityatrāha

children.translated_text: 'Intensity'
—thus.

children.text: dṛṣṭānto 'pi na kevalaravyādisvarūpamātraparaḥ, kintu ravyādivyapadeśagocarārthasyāsādhāraṇākārapradarśanapara iti nirviśeṣādvaitarūpo 'khaṇḍaḥ samānādhikaraṇavākyārtho nidarśanabhūto naivāstītibhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Even the illustration is not directed solely at the mere essential nature of the sun and the like; rather, it is directed at showing the distinctive form of the object designated by the terms 'sun' and the like. Therefore, an 'undivided' co-referential sentence-meaning of the form of qualityless non-dual [<s>Brahman</s>] that could serve as an illustration simply does not exist—this is the purport.
'Nowhere' (<s>kvāpi</s>)—in any co-referential sentence whatsoever.
'Undivided' (<s>avibhāga</s>)—without partition. // 166 //

body.translated_text: But [the opponent says:] 'The statements about truth and so forth convey an undivided meaning, because they are statements defining essential nature—just as [the statement] "The sun is the supreme illumination in the sky by day, and the moon [is so] at night"—thus the qualityless <s>Brahman</s> is established.' To this he says:

children.translated_text: If, by the exclusion of insentience, suffering, and the like, the words 'knowledge,' 'bliss,' and so forth
function [merely as exclusions] with reference to one and the same [<s>Brahman</s>], there would be no 'having a second' for the existent [<s>Brahman</s>]. // 167 //
'Insentience' (<s>jāḍya</s>)

children.text:
ti /
jñānādipadaṃ na jñānatvādiviśeṣaṃ pratipādayati /
kintu jaḍatvādyapohameva /
children.translated_text: —thus. The word 'knowledge' and the like does not convey a specific qualification such as being-knowledge; rather, [it conveys] merely the exclusion (<s>apoha</s>) of insentience and the like.
And exclusion is merely negation—an absence—which is the essential nature of the substrate itself. Therefore, there is no absurd consequence of <s>Brahman</s> being qualified.
And the meaningfulness of the terms is [maintained] through making known the exclusion of the respective counter-correlates such as insentience and the like—this is the intent of the objector.
The word 'not' (<s>na</s>) [at the beginning of the next verse] should be connected with the preceding one.
This verse restates the opponent's position. // 167 //

body.translated_text: Here the opponent objects:

body.text: apohāḥ kiṃ na santyeva, santo vā, nobhaye 'pi vā /
body.translated_text: Are those exclusions (<s>apoha</s>) simply non-existent, or do they exist, or are they neither?
If they exist, the existent [<s>Brahman</s>] would have a second; if otherwise, [it would] have the nature of insentience and the like. // 168 //

children.translated_text: 'The exclusions'

children.text:
iti /
nobhaye-na santo nāpyasantaḥ, sadasadvilakṣaṇā iti yāvat /
apohānāṃ sattve doṣamāha
children.translated_text: —thus. 'Neither'—neither existent nor non-existent; that is to say, different from both existent and non-existent. He states the fault if the exclusions exist:
'If they exist'

children.text:
iti /
apohānāṃ sattve taiḥ sataḥ sadvitīyatā syādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: —thus. If the exclusions exist, then [<s>Brahman</s>], being existent, would have a second through them—this is the meaning.
The refutation in case of non-existence: 'having the nature of insentience and the like.'
If the exclusions of insentience and the like are absent, the absurd consequence of insentience and the like [for <s>Brahman</s>] follows—this is the point.
The printed reading '<s>sattvasatsadvitīyaḥ svājjaḍādyātmakatetare</s>'
is incorrect. // 168 //

body.translated_text: He presents the alternatives and states the fault:
The statement of [something] different from both existent and non-existent has already been refuted earlier.

body.text: tathātve ca ghaṭādibhyo brahmāpi na viśiṣyate // 169 //
body.translated_text: And if that were the case, even <s>Brahman</s> would not be distinguished from pots and the like. // 169 //

children.translated_text: 'Both existent and non-existent'

children.text:
diti /
sadvyatireke 'sattvam , asadvyatireke ca sattvaṃ vyavasthitamiti sadasadbhinnatvaṃ kasyāpi na sambhavatīti pūrvamevoktamityarthaḥ /
dūṣaṇāntaramāha
children.translated_text: —thus. If [something is] different from the existent, it would be non-existent; and if different from the non-existent, it would be existent—thus being different from both existent and non-existent is not possible for anything—this has already been stated. This is the meaning. He states another refutation:
'If that were the case'
—thus.

children.text: apohānāṃ brahmasvarūpatve sadasadvilakṣaṇatve ca brahmaṇaḥ sadasadvilakṣaṇatvaṃ prasajyate prapañcasyeveti bhāvaḥ // 169 //
children.translated_text: If the exclusions are [held to be] <s>Brahman</s>'s own nature, and if they are different from both existent and non-existent, then the absurd consequence of <s>Brahman</s> itself being different from both existent and non-existent would follow—just like the manifold world [which the opponent claims is <s>anirvacanīya</s>]. This is the purport. // 169 //

body.translated_text: He refutes the third [alternative]:
Furthermore, without conveying a positive content contrary to the excludable—insentience and the like—
those [attributes] would not at all be excluded, just as with terms synonymous with that very [insentience]. // 170 //

children.translated_text: 'Furthermore'
—thus.

children.text: jaḍādivyāvartakadharmabodhanamantarā jaḍādivyāvṛttirna pratipādayituṃ śakyate satyādipadairjaḍādiparyāyapadairiveti vyāvartakadharmabodhakatvamavarjanīyam /
children.translated_text: Without the cognition of a property that differentiates from insentience and the like, the exclusion of insentience and the like cannot be conveyed by words like 'truth' and the like—just as by words synonymous with insentience itself. Therefore, the cognition of a differentiating property is unavoidable.
And thus, the qualified nature (<s>saviśeṣatva</s>) of <s>Brahman</s> through those attributes is inescapable—this is the meaning.
'Those respective [things]'—insentience and the like. 'Would be excluded'—would be differentiated. // 170 //

body.translated_text: He states another refutation:
When [you say that], with respect to the counter-correlate that is perceived, there is merely the cognition of another entity—
that itself is the absence [you intend]; and here too, by those [existing exclusions], the existent [<s>Brahman</s>] would have a second. // 171 //

children.translated_text: (Thus, by the establishment of [<s>Brahman</s>'s] qualified nature, the qualitylessness of consciousness is refuted.)

children.text:
nanu vyāvartakadharmavattvaṃ na bodhyate /
kintu jaḍādivyāvṛttirūpatvameva bodhyate jñānādipadairbrahmaṇaḥ /
tanna jaḍatvādiprasaṅga iti cettatrāha
children.translated_text: But [the opponent says:] 'It is not the possession of a differentiating property that is conveyed; rather, what the words 'knowledge' and the like convey about <s>Brahman</s> is merely the nature of exclusion from insentience and the like. Therefore, there is no absurd consequence of insentience and the like.' To this he responds:
'With respect to the counter-correlate'

children.text:
ti /
yogye pratiyoginyanupalabhyamāne 'dhikaraṇamātrajñānameva tadabhāva iti jñānaviśeṣarūpatvādabhāvasya jñānaviśeṣarūpaiḥ satyādipadalakṣyārthairabhāvairbhāvarūpaiḥ saviśeṣatā brahmaṇaḥ prasajyata ityarthaḥ /
abhāvasya jñānaviśeṣarūpatvamiti mataviśeṣeṇedam /
yadvā bhāvāntaramātradhīriti upalabhyamānaṃ bhāvāntaramityarthe paryavasannam /
yogye pratiyoginyanupalabhyamāne tatrādhikaraṇe yadbhāvāntaramupalabhyate tadeva pratiyogivyapekṣayābhāvavyapadeśabhāgiti adhikaraṇavṛttidharmāntararūpatvādabhāvānāṃ taiḥ saviśeṣatvaṃ prasajyata iti bhāvaḥ /
dvavye 'bhāvo dharmarūpaḥ /
dharmasya tu svaparanirvāhakatvena svarūpamevābhāvaḥ, sati sambhave dharmāntaraṃ veti yathopalambhaṃ vyavasthā /
yasmin pratīyamāne itarāropo na ghaṭate, tasyaiva tadabhāvarūpatvam /
satsvarūpe pratīyamāna eva bhedānāmadhyāsācca tatra tasyaiva netarābhāvarūpatvaṃ sambhavi /
na cāvidyayāviśadaṃ bhāsamāne sati bhedabhramaḥ /
avidyānivṛtau viśadaṃ bhāsamāne tu na sa iti viśadasvarūpasyābhāvarūpatvaṃ sambhavatīti vācyam /
vaiśadyasya svarūpatve pūrvamapyavidyādibhedāropāyogāt /
svarūpātiriktatve tu tasyaivābhāvarūpatvaṃ na svarūpasyeti prasaṅgāt /
kiñca nirviśeṣe svaprakāśe vastuni viśādāviśadabhānameva durvacam /
saviśeṣe tu katipayākāreṇa bhānamaviśadam , sarvākārabhānaṃ viśadamiti viśeṣaḥ /
kiñca brahmaṇo dravyatve sadharmakatvam , adravyatve tu kasyaciddharmarūpatvaṃ prasajyate /
children.translated_text:
—thus.
When a suitable counter-positive is not apprehended, the mere cognition of the substratum itself constitutes [the cognition of] the absence of that [counter-positive]. Since absence has the form of a specific cognition, <s>Brahman</s> would become qualified by absences that are of the form of specific cognitions and that are denoted by the words 'being' (<s>satya</s>) and the like through indication—and those absences are themselves positive entities. This is the meaning.
That absence has the form of a specific cognition—this is according to one particular doctrinal position.
Alternatively, 'mere cognition of a positive entity' reaches [the meaning of] 'a positive entity that is apprehended.' When a suitable counter-positive is not apprehended, whatever positive entity is apprehended at that substratum—that very entity, with reference to the counter-positive, receives the designation of 'absence.' Therefore, since absences have the form of properties other [than the counter-positive] existing in the substratum, <s>Brahman</s> would become qualified by them—such is the purport.
In the case of a substance, absence is in the form of a property. But for a property itself, its own nature itself is [its] absence [of its counter-positive], since it serves to establish both itself and the other. When there is possibility, another property [may serve]; otherwise [its own nature]—the arrangement follows apprehension.
That upon whose apprehension, the superimposition of the other is not possible—that alone has the form of the absence of that [other].
Since, when the nature of being (<s>sat</s>) is apprehended, differences are [also] superimposed upon it [by the opponent], that very [being] alone does not have the form of the absence of the other.
Nor should one say that when [<s>Brahman</s>] shines indistinctly due to <s>avidyā</s>, there is the illusion of difference, but when <s>avidyā</s> ceases and [<s>Brahman</s>] shines distinctly, that [illusion] does not [occur]—and thus the distinct nature alone could be the form of [the relevant] absence. For if distinctness is the own-nature [of <s>Brahman</s>], then even previously, the superimposition of difference and the like due to <s>avidyā</s> would be impossible. If distinctness is other than the own-nature, then it is that [distinctness] alone that would have the form of absence, not the own-nature [of <s>Brahman</s>]—this is the consequence.
Moreover, in a qualificationless, self-luminous entity, the very distinction between shining distinctly and shining indistinctly is difficult to maintain. But in a qualified entity, shining through only some aspects is 'indistinct,' while shining through all aspects is 'distinct'—this is the distinction.
Furthermore, if <s>Brahman</s> is a substance, it follows that it has properties; if it is not a substance, the consequence follows that it is a property of something else.
And that it could be different from both substance and non-substance is impossible—and so forth should be considered here.

By the word 'even' (<s>api</s>) in 'here too,' [it is indicated that] even if the words 'being' (<s>satya</s>) and the like have exclusion (<s>apoha</s>) as their indicated meaning, the establishment of [<s>Brahman</s>'s] being qualificationless does not follow.
The very laborious effort of fabricating an [alternative] definition reveals that [<s>Brahman</s>] is qualified—this is indicated.
Thus, the indeterminability as real or unreal of even the exclusion-natured [properties of] being (<s>satya</s>) and the like has been refuted. // 171 //

body.translated_text: From where is the separation of the distinctions of elements and elemental compounds from both the real and the unreal
Ascertained? Is it from perception and the like, or from scripture? // 172 //

children.translated_text: The means of valid knowledge—perception and the like—each ascertain their respective objects as they are;

children.text: vyavacchindanti jāyanta iti yā (tā) vat svasākṣikam // 173 //
children.translated_text: That [they] arise [in this way] is directly self-witnessed. // 173 //

body.text: atha prapañcasyāpi prasaṅgātsadasadanirvacanīyatvaṃ paramataṃ nirasyati bhūte tyādinā /
body.translated_text: Now, since the indeterminability as real or unreal would, by extension, apply to the manifold as well, he refutes the opponent's view beginning with 'elements' and so forth.

children.text:
pratyakṣādīnī ti /
svasvaprameyaṃ yathāyathaṃ tattadasādhāraṇākārato vijātīyasajātīyāntaravyattamavagamayanti pratyakṣādīnīti prasiddham /
tadasādhāraṇākāreṇa sadbhāva eva vastūnāṃ pramāṇānitāni , na tu sadasadanirvacanīyatva iti bhāvaḥ // 172 // 173 //
children.translated_text:
'Perception and the like'—thus.
The means of valid knowledge such as perception and the like make known each of their respective objects of knowledge as they are—distinguished from what is of a different class and what is of the same class and from internal [varieties], through their respective distinctive aspects. This is well-known.
Through those distinctive aspects, those [means of knowledge] prove the existence (<s>sadbhāva</s>) alone of things, not their indeterminability as real or unreal—such is the purport. // 172 // 173 //

body.text: yathāgrataḥ sthite nīle nīlimānyakathā na, dhīḥ /
body.translated_text: Just as, when blue is present before [one], the cognition 'this is blue' is not of another kind—the cognition

body.text: ekākārā , na hi tathā sphaṭike dhavake matiḥ // 174 //
body.translated_text: Is of a single aspect; but the cognition regarding crystal or white [objects] is not like that. // 174 //
Just as the cognition 'sweet' regarding milk is not the same as the cognition 'astringent' regarding neem;
And all conventional usages, both worldly and Vedic, are determinate. // 175 //

children.text:
etadevopapādayati yatheti /
nīle nīlamatiḥ , sphaṭike dhavalamatiśca naikaviṣayā , kintu parasparavyāvṛttaguṇaviṣayaiva ; tathā kṣīre madhuradhīḥ , nimbe kaṣāyadhīśca /
tathā cārthabhedālambanatvaṃ jñānānāṃ sthitamiti bhāvaḥ /
nīle nīlabuddhirekākārā ekaviṣayā /
tatra nīle na nīlānyaguṇaprasaṅgaḥ /
dhavalamatistu tato bhidyate bhinnākāretyarthaḥ /
naivetyasyāgre tādṛgiti ākṣipyate /
naivamiti vā pāṭhaḥ syāt /
tattadvastvasādhāraṇākārabhede 'bādhitapratītimuktvā vyavahāramapi tādṛśamupanyasyati pramāṇatayā vyavahārā iti /
abādhitapratyakṣādipramāṇatanmūlavyavahārabalādvastūnāṃ tattadasādhāraṇākāreṇa sattvamevopeyamiti bhāvaḥ // 174 // 175 //
children.translated_text:
He substantiates this very [point] with 'just as.'
The cognition 'blue' regarding blue, and the cognition 'white' regarding crystal, are not of one object, but pertain precisely to mutually distinct qualities. Likewise, the cognition 'sweet' regarding milk and the cognition 'astringent' regarding neem [are distinct].
Thus, the fact that cognitions take distinct objects as their basis is established—such is the purport.
The cognition of blue regarding blue is of a single aspect—it pertains to one object.
There, in [the case of] blue, there is no absurd consequence of a quality other than blue [being attributed].
But the cognition of white differs from it, being of a different aspect—this is the meaning.
Before 'not like that' (<s>naiva</s>), 'of such kind' (<s>tādṛk</s>) is to be supplied.
Alternatively, the reading may be '<s>naivam</s>.'
Having spoken of experience regarding the distinctiveness of aspects unique to each thing, which is uncontradicted, he also adduces conventional usage of the same kind as proof—'conventional usages' and so forth.
Through the force of uncontradicted perception and other valid means, and of the conventional usages rooted in them, the existence of things through their respective distinctive aspects alone must be accepted—such is the purport. // 174 // 175 //

body.text: satyaṃ pratītirastyasyā mūlaṃ nāstīti cenna tat /
body.translated_text: True, the experience exists; but [the claim] that it has no foundation—this is not so;

body.text: sā cedasti tasyā mūlaṃ kalpyatāṃ kāryabhūtayā // 176 //
body.translated_text: If it exists, let the foundation be inferred from the [experience] as its effect. // 176 //

children.text:
śaṅkātrānūdyate satyamiti /
pariharati na ta diti /
sāghu iti śeṣaḥ /
kāryabalāttadanuguṇaṃ mūlamabādhitapratītīnāṃ yathārthyavyavasthāpakamanumīyatāmiti bhāvaḥ // 176 //
children.translated_text:
The objection is restated with 'true' (<s>satyam</s>).
He refutes with 'not so' (<s>na tat</s>).
'It is sound'—this is to be supplied.
From the force of the effect, a foundation consistent with the veridical character of the uncontradicted experiences should be inferred—such is the purport. // 176 //

body.translated_text: It is established that the sense-organ, the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>), and the like [serve as valid instruments], from their conformity to the existence [of things].
Because neither simultaneity nor sequence is possible for determination and apprehension; // 177 //

body.text: aikyāyogācca bhedo na pratyakṣa iti yo bhramaḥ /
body.translated_text: And because unity is impossible—that difference is not perceptible—this is a delusion;
That [delusion] is due to the failure to grasp the distinction between difference and mutual non-existence (<s>itaretarābhāva</s>). // 178 //

children.text:
aduṣṭendriyādereva mitiyāthārthye hetutvamanvayavyatirekasiddhaṃ nāpalapyaṃ cetyāha kḷpta miti /
vastubhedo nirduṣṭendriyarūpeṇa pratyakṣapramāṇenaiva gṛhyate iti yāvat /
atra śaṅkate yaugapadye ti /
vyavacchedo bhedagrahaṇam /
vidhānaṃ svarūpagrahaṇam /
prātyakṣikapramiteryugapadevādhikaraṇatanniṣṭhabhedobhayagrāhitvaṃ na sambhavati , adhikaraṇagrahaṇasya pratiyogigraṇanairapekṣyāt , bhedagrahaṇasya tu tatsāpekṣatvāt /
prathamamadhikaraṇasvarūpaṃ gṛhītvāthaṃ bhedaṃ gṛhṇātīti kramo 'pi na sambhavati , pramiteḥ kṣaṇikatvādviramya vyāpārāyogādvā /
svarūpabhedayostadgrahaṇayoścaikyamapi na sambhavati /
ataḥ svarūpagrahasyaiva pratyakṣapramitirūpatvam , bhedagrahasya tu bhrāntilakṣaṇatvameveti bhāvaḥ /
śaṅkāṃ pratikṣipatīmām itī tyādinā /
bhedo 'nyonyābhāvaḥ , itaretarābhāvaḥ - anyasminnanyasya saṃsargābhāvaḥ /
yadvā bhedaḥ - saṃsārgābhāvabhedaḥ prāgabhāvādiḥ /
itarerābhāvaḥ - bhedaḥ /
tayoḥ svarūpayāthātmyājñānaprayukto niruktavidhaḥ pareṣāṃ bhrama ityarthaḥ // 177 // 178 //
children.translated_text:
That the [cognitive] instrument of an unimpaired sense-organ and the like alone is the cause of the veridicality of cognition is established through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>) and should not be denied—he says with 'it is established.'
The meaning is: the difference of objects is apprehended by perception as a valid means of knowledge, through the unimpaired sense-organ and the like.
Here the opponent raises an objection with 'simultaneity' and so forth.
'Determination' (<s>vyavaccheda</s>) means the apprehension of difference. 'Apprehension' (<s>vidhāna</s>) means the apprehension of own-nature.
It is not possible for perceptual cognition to apprehend both the substratum and the difference existing in the substratum simultaneously—because the apprehension of the substratum does not require [the apprehension of] the counter-positive, while the apprehension of difference does require it.
Sequential [apprehension], where one first apprehends the own-nature of the substratum and then apprehends the difference, is also not possible—because cognition is momentary, or because it cannot re-engage after ceasing.
Nor is the unity of own-nature and difference, and of their respective apprehensions, possible.
Therefore, only the apprehension of own-nature has the character of perceptual cognition, while the apprehension of difference has the character of an illusion—such is the purport.
He refutes this objection with 'that' (<s>iti</s>) and so forth.
Difference is mutual non-existence (<s>anyonyābhāva</s>). '<s>Itaretarābhāva</s>' means: the absence of conjunction of one thing in another.
Alternatively, 'difference' means: the division of relational absence such as prior non-existence and the like. '<s>Itaretarābhāva</s>' means: difference.
The delusion of the opponents described above is caused by ignorance of the true nature of those two [i.e., difference and mutual non-existence]—this is the meaning. // 177 // 178 //

body.translated_text: The very own-nature of entities, shining through perception,
Would be the cause of the convention of difference, with reference to the counter-positive. // 179 //

children.text:
bhedasya yāthātmyaṃ tāvadāha svarūpameve ti /
svarūpaṃ - svāsādhāraṇākāraḥ
children.translated_text:
He first states the true nature of difference: 'the very own-nature' and so forth.
'Own-nature' means: one's distinctive aspect,

children.text: tadeva gṛhyamāṇāṃ pratiyogismaraṇasahakāreṇetarasmādbhedavyavahāranidānam , yathā kambugrīvādimattvameva ghaṭasya paṭādbheda iti bhāvaḥ // 179 //
children.translated_text: That very [own-nature], when apprehended, together with the recollection of the counter-positive, is the ground for the convention of difference from the other. Just as pot-ness—having a neck-like form and the like—is itself the difference of the pot from the cloth. Such is the purport. // 179 //
Just as the cognition of that [substratum] alone is the instrument for the convention 'does not exist' in various [cases],
Or just as the distinction of short and long, in a single [object] of six aṅgulas. // 180 //

children.text:
atra nidarśanaṃ yatheti /
yathā bhūtalasvarūpajñānameva ghaṭādyanupalambhe sati tattatsmaraṇasahakāri ghaṭādiśūnyatāvyavahārasādhanaṃ matamabhāvasyādhikaraṇasvarūpatvavādināṃ tathetyarthaḥ /
siddhānte tvadhikaraṇavṛttidharmaviśeṣarūpatvaṃ bhedāderiti vivekaḥ /
ekasyaiva pritayogibhedena nānāvyavahārasādhanatvaṃ nidarśanamukhena draḍhayati hrasve ti /
ekatraiva ṣaḍaṅgulimite vastuni tadapekṣayādīrghaṃ pādarthāntaramapekṣya hrasvavyavahāraṃ hrasvaṃ tadapekṣya dīrghavyavahāraṃ ca tadvastujñānameva tattatpratiyogismaraṇasahakāreṇa janayati hīti bhāvaḥ // 180 //
children.translated_text:
Here the illustration is 'just as.'
Just as the cognition of the ground's own-nature alone, when the pot and the like are not apprehended, together with the recollection of each [absent thing], is accepted by those who hold that absence has the nature of the substratum's own-nature as the instrument for the convention 'the ground is devoid of pot' and the like—so too. This is the meaning.
In the established doctrine, however, difference and the like have the nature of a specific property existing in the substratum—this is the distinction.
He strengthens, through illustration, the point that a single [entity], through difference of counter-positives, serves as the instrument for diverse conventions: 'short' and so forth.
In one and the same thing measuring six <s>aṅgulas</s>, the cognition of that thing itself, together with the recollection of each counter-positive, generates the convention 'long' with reference to something shorter, and the convention 'short' with reference to something longer—such is the purport. // 180 //

body.translated_text: Thus, through being possessed of aspects of many established kinds,
The reality of the manifold that is directly perceived cannot be denied. // 181 //

children.text:
eva miti /
svarūpalakṣaṇasya bhedasyādyakṣaṇa eva dharmigrahaṇe grahasambhavādbhedavyavahāra eva pratiyogismaraṇasyāpekṣitatvācca nānākāravibhinnapadārthasvarūpasya tattvaṃ pratyakṣapramāṇapramitaṃ nāpalapanārhamiti bhāvaḥ /
asādhāraṇākārarūpasya bhedasya svaparanirvāhakatvānnānavasthā /
tatprāgabhāvastatpūrvāvasthārūpaḥ /
dhvaṃsastaduttarāvasthārūpaḥ /
tadatyantābhāvastadadhikaraṇasvabhāvaviśeṣātmakaḥ /
sāmayikābhāvaḥ /
kālaviśeṣāvacchinnatattadadhikaraṇasvarūpātmakaḥ /
eṣāṃ ca tattatpratiyogyuparaktatvena vyavahāre punastattatpratiyogismaraṇāpekṣeti viveko 'tra bodhyaḥ // 181 //
children.translated_text:
'Thus'—thus.
Since difference, which is characterized by own-nature, can be apprehended at the very first moment of perception together with the apprehension of the property-bearer, and since the recollection of the counter-positive is required only for the convention of difference, the reality of the own-natures of things—which are diverse, distinguished by diverse aspects—as established by the valid means of perception, cannot be denied. Such is the purport.
Since difference, which has the form of a distinctive aspect, serves to establish both itself and the other, there is no infinite regress.
The prior non-existence of that [difference] has the form of the prior state of that [substratum].
Its destruction (<s>dhvaṃsa</s>) has the form of the subsequent state.
Its absolute non-existence (<s>atyantābhāva</s>) has the form of a specific nature of that substratum.
Its occasional non-existence (<s>sāmayikābhāva</s>) has the form of the own-nature of each substratum delimited by a specific time.
And [regarding these absences,] since in their usage they are colored by their respective counter-positives, the recollection of the respective counter-positive is again required—this distinction should be understood here. // 181 //

body.translated_text: Scripture, being oriented toward injunction, is not a valid means for such a [metaphysical] matter;
Even if it had authority, it would not generate cognition, since the meanings of its terms cannot form a syntactic connection. // 182 //

children.text:
evaṃ bhedaprapañcasya sattva eva pratyakṣaṃ pramāṇam , na sadasadanirvacanīyatva iti sthāpitam /
śāstrasyāpi na tatra prāṇāṇyamityāha āgama iti /
āgamaḥ - śāstraṃ , kāryaniṣṭhatvāt - kāryārthapratipādanatatparatvāt , īdṛśeṣar'the -kāryānanvayini siddhe prapañcānirvacanīyatvādau , na pramā - na pramāṇam /
mīmāṃsakamatenedam /
siddhāntimatenāpyāha prāmāṇye 'pīti /
siddhārthe śāstrasya pramāṇabhāve satyapi śāstrasya pramāṇaśabdamātrasya vā nānirvacanīyatvādau pramāṇatvam , na sannāpyasannityāderananvitārthakatvena śabdabodhājanakatvādityarthaḥ /
tat tatpratipādakatayeva pratīyamāno 'pi sandarbho 'viruddhārthaparatayā neya iti hārdam // 182 //
children.translated_text:
Thus it has been established that perception alone is the valid means for the reality of the differentiated manifold, not for [its] indeterminability as real or unreal.
That even scripture is not a valid means for that [indeterminability], he says with 'scripture' (<s>āgama</s>).
'Scripture' means: the <s>śāstra</s>. 'Being oriented toward injunction' means: having its purport in teaching what is to be done. 'For such a matter'—that is, for an already-established matter like the indeterminability of the manifold, which has no connection with what is to be done—'it is not a valid means.'
This is according to the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> view.
According to the view of the established doctrine too, he says 'even if it had authority.'
Even if scripture has authority regarding established [ontological] matters, neither scripture nor the word 'valid means' alone has authority for [establishing] indeterminability, because [expressions] such as 'neither existent nor non-existent' and the like, being syntactically incoherent in their meaning, cannot generate verbal cognition. This is the meaning.
The inner purport is: even a passage that is apprehended as teaching that [indeterminability], should be led to a non-contradictory meaning. // 182 //

body.text: nāsat pratīteḥ , bādhācca na sadityapi yanna tat /
body.translated_text: 'Not unreal' because of experience; and 'not real' because of sublation—if [you say] this is not so,

body.text: pratītereva sat kiṃ na , bādhānnāsat kuto jagat ? /
body.translated_text: Why should it not be real precisely because of experience? And how is the world unreal because of sublation?
Therefore, this <s>avidyā</s> of yours is itself resorted to through <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). // 183 //

children.text:
athānumānasyāpi sadasadanirvacanīyatve na pramāṇatvamityāha nāsa diti /
prapañcaḥ sadasadbhinnaḥ pratīyamānatve sati bādhyamānatvāditi yuktirapi na satī, prapañca sadasattvavān tata evetyābhāsa samānayogakṣematvāditi bhāvaḥ /
nirupādhikasattvāsattvayorvirodho 'trā bhipretaḥ /
tasmā diti /
anirvacanīyatvasyāprāṇāṇikatvāttadupapādakāvidyākalpanaṃ bhavadajñānakāryamevetyarthaḥ // 183 //
children.translated_text:
Now, he says that inference too is not a valid means for [establishing] indeterminability as real or unreal—'not unreal' and so forth.
The reasoning 'the manifold is different from both the real and the unreal, because while being experienced it is also sublated'—this too is not sound, because the counter-argument 'the manifold possesses both reality and unreality precisely for the same reasons' has equal logical force. Such is the purport.
The intended contradiction here is between unconditioned existence and unconditioned non-existence.
'Therefore'—thus.
Since indeterminability is not established by any valid means, the postulation of <s>avidyā</s> to account for it is itself a product of your own ignorance—this is the meaning. // 183 //

body.translated_text: Moreover, the property of falsity (<s>mithyātva</s>) attributed to the differentiated manifold—

body.text: mithyā vā paramārtho vā nādyaḥ kalpo 'yamañjasā // 184 //
body.translated_text: Is it itself false or ultimately real? The first alternative does not work straightforwardly. // 184 //
If that falsity is [itself] false, then the reality of the manifold would be hard to deny;
And even if it is ultimately real, by that very [admission] your non-duality would be undermined. // 185 //

children.translated_text: (Thus the refutation of the falsity of the manifold in the form of separation from both the real and the unreal.)

children.text: pramāṇābhāvāddūṣitaṃ sadasadanirvacanīyatvarūpaṃ mithyātvaṃ prakārāntareṇāpi dūṣayati kiñceti /
children.translated_text: Having refuted through the absence of valid means the falsity that takes the form of indeterminability as real or unreal, he also refutes it by yet another method with 'moreover':
If the falsity of difference is itself false, then the reality of difference is established.

If the falsity of difference is ultimately real, then since the reality of something different from <s>Brahman</s> is thereby accepted, there is a self-contradiction—and the undermining of non-duality. This is the meaning.

children.translated_text: Thus. 'By mutual non-identity' — by being mutually different. The triad is the triad of categories characterized as knower (<s>jñātṛ</s>), known (<s>jñeya</s>), and knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>). Here, the sacred utterance of the revered <s>Parāśara Bhaṭṭa</s> should be recalled: 'If the difference between self and cognition is made manifest in [the experience] "I know this," then let even the external [world] be one. If the cognition too is false according to the doctrine that its object is false — if they could endure even that, then long life to their doctrine!' (202)
And no inference operates in contradiction to perception.
For the non-heat of fire is not inferred from [the reason of] its being a substance. (Verse 203)

children.text:
pratyakṣeti /
pratipakṣaṃ - viruddham /
vahneranuṣṇatvānumānamiva pratyakṣabādhitamarthajñātroḥ saṃvidaikyānumānaṃ bhavadīyamiti proktaṃ bhavati // 203 //
children.translated_text: 'Perception' — thus. 'In contradiction' — opposed. Just as the inference of fire's non-heat [from its substancehood] is contradicted by perception, so your inference of the identity of the object and the knower with consciousness is contradicted by perception — this is what has been stated. (203)

body.translated_text: Moreover, this reason [co-apprehension] is contradicted (<s>viruddha</s>), since the co-existence of the two

body.text: tavāpi na hi saṃvittiḥ svātmanā saha bhāsate // 204 //
body.translated_text: [shows that] for you too, consciousness does not shine forth together with itself. (Verse 204)

children.text: kañci sāhityaṃ bhedaniyataṃ jñānārthayorhetughaṭakaṃ tadabhedasādhane viruddhamityāha
children.translated_text: He says that co-apprehension, which is invariably accompanied by difference, constitutes the logical reason, and that in proving non-difference it is contradicted:

children.text:
kiñce ti /
saṃvitsaṃvidā sahopalabhyata iti hi tavāpi na sammatam /
tatsaṃvidā tatsaṃvidā sahopalabhyamānamarthajātaṃ niyamena tadbhinnameva bhavediti yāvat // 204 //
children.translated_text: 'Moreover' — thus. That consciousness is apprehended together with [another] consciousness — this is indeed not accepted even by you. Therefore the class of objects apprehended together with consciousness is invariably different from it — such is the extent [of the argument]. (204)

body.translated_text: The continuous stream of pure, transparent, mere consciousness, free from the disturbance of blue and the like,
Shines forth in deep sleep and the like; but not so does the object [shine forth] separately from cognition.
Therefore consciousness is real; but the object, being [merely] cognized, is unreal. (Verse 205)

children.text:
atra śaṅkate nīlādyupaplave ti /
arthoparāgamantarā jñānaṃ bhāsate svāpādau /
naivamartho jñānādvinā kadāpi bhāsate /
tatpratibimbasyevārthajātasyamithyātvaṃ saṃvidi kalpitasyeti bhāvaḥ // 205 //
children.translated_text: Here [the Buddhist] raises an objection with 'free from the disturbance of blue and the like.' Consciousness shines forth in deep sleep and the like without the coloring of an object. But the object never shines forth without consciousness. Therefore, like a reflection, the class of objects is false, being superimposed on consciousness — such is the purport. (205)

body.translated_text: This very [argument] of yours is an utterance in which the self-contradiction of your own words has not been considered,
Since the invariable rule of co-apprehension is thereby undermined. (Verse 206)

children.translated_text: He refutes with 'this very [argument].'

children.text: arthaṃ vinā saṃvido bhāne tāṃ vinār'thasyāpi bhānaṃ siddhiprāyamiti sahopalambhanirūpabhavaduktahetvasiddhiriti pūrvāparasvavacanavirodhamapi na parāmṛṣṭavān bhavānevaṃvadanniti yāvat // 206 //
children.translated_text: If consciousness shines forth without the object, then the shining forth of the object without consciousness too is nearly established — thus the reason stated by you as being of the nature of co-apprehension is unestablished. And in saying this, you have not even considered the contradiction with your own earlier and later statements — such is the extent. (206)

body.text: yasmādṛte yadābhāti bhāti ya(ta) smādṛte 'pi tat /
body.translated_text: That without which something shines forth — [the former] shines forth without the latter too.
Just as the pot [shines forth] by itself, independent of the cloth that shines forth independent of the pot. (Verse 207)

children.translated_text: (Thus, by the refutation of the non-duality of consciousness, the veridicality of the distinction between cognition, cognizer, and cognized is established.)
(This much alone of the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s> portion is available.)

Thus, in the <s>Siddhitraya</s>, blessed by the revered <s>Bhagavān Yāmuna Muni</s> — the foremost champion in the propagation of the <s>Viśiṣṭādvaita Siddhānta</s> — [is completed] the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s>.

nirbhāta iti śatrantātpañcamī /
nirbhātādityarthaḥ /
ghaṭādṛte bhātātatpaṭādṛte bhānaṃ ghaṭasya yathā sidhyati , tathār'thaṃ
children.translated_text: He establishes the very non-establishment of the reason with 'that without which.' 'Shining forth' — the fifth case ending is ablative in the <s>śatṛ</s> (present participle) form; the meaning is: 'from that which shines forth.' Just as the pot's shining forth independent of the cloth — when the cloth shines forth independent of the pot — is established, so

children.text:
vinābhātājjñānādvinā bhānasarthasya sidhyatīti sahopalambhaniyamo nanīladitaddhiyāṃ sidhyatītyarthaḥ /
nanu jñānenaivārthaprakāśasya vācyatvājjñānasya ca svaprakāśatvājjñānabhānaṃ vinārṃ'thabhānaṃ na yujyata iti cedevamapi sahopalambhaniyamo na yujyata eva jñānaviśeṣeṇa jñānasāmānyena vā , pūrvatra vyabhicārāt uttaratra paramate 'siddhaśce /
idamartha eva sahopalambhaniyama iti 197 tamaḥ ślokaḥ , sa cātrānusandheya iti prāgevoktam /
evaṃ mitimātṛmeyabhidāyāthātmyaṃ na nihnotuṃ śakyata iti vyavasthāpi tamatreti dhyeyam // 207 //
children.translated_text: the shining forth of the object independent of consciousness — since consciousness shines forth independent [of the object] — is established. Thus the invariable rule of co-apprehension — 'blue and the cognition of blue [are always together]' — is not established. Such is the meaning. Objection: Since the illumination of the object is to be stated as occurring through consciousness alone, and since consciousness is self-luminous, the shining forth of the object without the shining forth of consciousness is not tenable. Response: Even so, the invariable rule of co-apprehension is not tenable — whether with a specific cognition or with cognition in general — because of deviation in the former case and non-establishment [of the reason] in the latter case according to the opponent's own view. That the co-apprehension-rule [holds only] in this sense — this was stated in verse 197, and it should be recalled here, as was said earlier. Thus, the veridicality of the distinction between cognition, cognizer, and cognized cannot be denied — and the determination [of this] should be meditated upon here. (207)

Descended in the illustrious lineage of the author of the <s>Śrībhāṣya</s>, skilled in elucidating the purport of the <s>Śrībhāṣya</s>,

body.translated_text: A treasure of wisdom, the best of teachers, in the city of <s>Bhūtapurī</s> (Mannargudi), <s>Rāmānujārya</s> of great renown shines forth — he is my preceptor.
I, who have obtained enlightenment through the service of his lotus feet, who am sheltered at the feet of the teacher-father known as <s>Kṛṣṇārya</s>,

children.text: aṇṇaṅgarārya iti ca prathitābhidhāno vyākhyābhimāmakaravaṃ prativādibhīkṛta
children.translated_text: And who am well-known by the name <s>Aṇṇaṅgarārya</s> — I have composed this commentary, which strikes fear into opponents.
By the grace of the teacher's feet, having crossed the ocean of <s>Yāmuna</s>'s utterances,

body.translated_text: This beautiful commentary has been composed for the delight of the teacher's feet.
Whatever merits are herein — they are born of the teacher's grace.
The faults, however, are mine — this should be reflected upon by the discerning.
This garland of words is offered upon the chest of <s>Śrī</s> (Lakṣmī).
May <s>Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa</s>, the Supreme Person (<s>Puruṣottama</s>), be pleased by this.
This work was completed in the <s>Vikrama</s> year marked by the digits for seasons, sky, and eyes (2006),
On the full-moon day of <s>Āṣāḍha</s>, in the city of <s>Vṛttālaya</s> (Tirutturaipūṇḍi).

children.translated_text: Thus, by one whose ancestral home is the divine site of <s>Nagapurī</s> (<s>Tirunāṅgūr</s>), of the lineage of <s>Prativādibhayaṅkarācārya</s>,
the ornament [of the lineage], the best among the learned, son of the distinguished teacher known as <s>Kṛṣṇamācārya</s>,

one thoroughly versed in the <s>Catustantrī</s>, whose fame has spread to all directions, an embodiment of compassion, descended in the divine lineage of the illustrious author of the <s>Śrībhāṣya</s>,
a connoisseur residing in the sacred <s>Bhūtapurī</s>,
the foremost among all scholars, of the <s>Hārīta</s> [gotra], the revered <s>Āsūri Rāmānujācārya Deśikendra</s>,
who has mastered the heart of the word, sentence, and means of valid knowledge through devoted service to the lotus feet [of his teacher],
by the servant of the <s>Śrīvaiṣṇavas</s>, the revered
<s>Aṇṇaṅgarācārya</s>, a crest-jewel of logic and grammar,
learned in both <s>Vedāntas</s>,
has been composed this commentary on the <s>Saṃvitsiddhi</s>,
[named] <s>Siddhāñjana</s> — [now] complete.

body.translated_text: May it be victorious!
